Powerful meaty-brothy thiol with roasted coffee and a sulfury, faintly eggy depth. The saturated partner to 2-methyl-3-furanthiol, rounder and less burnt, used sub-ppm in meat, coffee and roasted gourmand accords.

Perfumer's Apprentice lists it under the earthy family with the odour description floral, orris, earthy, supplied as a yellow liquid. Perfumers who work with it single it out as the earthier reading of iris rather than the soft powdery one, one describing it as smelling exactly like oil paint. That is the useful distinction: this is the rhizome and the damp root, the linseed and cellar side of orris, not the violet-ionone top that most iris accords are built from. Used as a body base it gives an iris formula weight and a mineral floor underneath whatever ionones and orris naturals sit above it.

The Good Scents Company gives the odour type as green and the description as fresh green sweet ozone melon, evaluated at 1% in dipropylene glycol, with medium odour strength and 20 hours substantivity at full strength. It is a branched unsaturated aldehyde, related to the trimethylhexanal family but more delicate, less metallic and more floral-green than those. In a formula it supplies a clean cut-stem greenness with a watery melon lift, and because it is an aldehyde a very little goes a long way at the top. It is a workhorse of functional and fresh perfumery, where it builds accords with melon, citrus and nitrile fresh-fruit materials.

A green rose-geranium note with a metallic, herbal edge and a grapefruit nuance: the rose-oxide effect, softer and rounder, so it blends in rather than dominating. Tetrahydro-2-isobutyl-4-methyl-2H-pyran, the saturated analogue of rose oxide.
Fresh, clean, woody-floral note with a soft fruity-woody character and good spreadability. A versatile, mild woody material widely used in functional and fine fragrance.

The oriental-market adaptation of Ambre 84 DL in the Symrise de Laire line, written Ambre d'Or(ient) at source. Scentspiracy describe rich, resinous and spicy notes with a sophisticated gourmand touch, opulent in character and built with oud as a central element, made for markets where the sweeter nuances of Ambre 83 and Ambre 84 are less preferred. In a formula it is an amber fond that arrives with its own oud and spice already in place, so it reads darker, drier and less confectionery than Ambre 84 DL and needs far less resin and spice work over the top of it; it is a market variant rather than a renovation of a vintage base.

Bedoukian's own FL-841 spec sheet gives a sweet hay character reminiscent of green and black tea, with cream notes appearing at lower levels and dry green notes that carry dried herbs. Perfumer & Flavorist list BRI 841 in the 2026 fragrance range as anisic, spicy, herbal, green and lactonic, and TGSC records fruity, straw, caramel and burnt at 10% in dipropylene glycol. It is among the most powerful odorants known, an aroma determinant of tea, apricot and oxidised wine detectable at parts per trillion, with the receptor OR1A1 highly selective for it. In a formula a trace builds hay, tea and tobacco character or lends anisic-lactonic warmth to a gourmand; an overdose turns burnt and prune-like and will swallow everything around it, so weigh it only from a very dilute solution.

Watery marine freshness with herbal, woody pine and balsamic facets, plus an aldehydic lift. Useful in aquatic accords and fresh fougere compositions. IFF's ingredient, sold by Fraterworks; a synthetic aroma chemical, not pine essential oil. Supplier composition needs review before allergen or IFRA clearance.

Sulfurous thioester with a cheesy, sour-dairy pungency that reads as rotten cabbage neat and as ripe tropical fruit in dilution. Adds overripe body to pineapple, passion fruit and cheese accords at ppm level.
Waxy citrus aldehyde with a distinct mandarin-tangerine peel character. Used in traces to boost mandarin and citrus naturalness.

The other pillar of smoke aroma: dense, sweet woodsmoke and smoked-meat phenolic with a soft, almost balsamic roundness compared to guaiacol's sharpness. Combine both for photorealistic smoke in leather and incense work.

Fraterworks 432836: a proprietary diffusive floral blend offered as an alternative to Hedione and high-cis methyl dihydrojasmonate grades. It is not Paradisone, Hedione or a single molecule. The SDS declares methyl dihydrojasmonate at 50-100% and a cyclohexylethyl propanoate at 1 to less than 5%, without an exact recipe. Supplier strength 4/10 and blend impact 8/10 describe a moderate direct odor with strong influence in a blend. The supplier reports 80 hours on a blotter. The IFRA 51 certificate lists no Category 4 restriction; this is not a comprehensive safety assessment. SDS: H401, toxic to aquatic life.
Damascone-like red fruity-rose radiance with a distinctive rosemary-thujonic twist. Exceptional lift and diffusion; pairs with aldehydes C-11, C-12 MNA and armoise for modern herbal-fruity effects.

Drier, more sophisticated orange than the sweet oil, with bitter-peel, slightly woody and fresh-marmalade facets. Prized in colognes and amber compositions for a grown-up citrus opening; phototoxic in leave-on use.

Sweet fruity-rosy ester with tropical and green geranium facets over a waxy base, warmer and considerably longer than citronellyl acetate. Standard rose-fruit modifier for geranium, rose and soft floral bases where the acetate flashes off too fast.

The 95 percent gamma-methyl ionone grade: soft, powdery violet with a velvety orris depth and a creamy, almost cosmetic quality. Where the 70 is dry, woody and leathery, the 95 is all finesse, and the higher purity is what buys the smoothness. About 184 hours on a smelling strip. It builds violet, iris and orris accords and adds powdery radiance and diffusion to almost any composition, bridging floral top notes into woody-amber bases; it is the ionone behind the Grojsman accord that underpins Tresor and much of what followed. Sold and priced as a separate article from the 70, and it does a different job.

Rare Tasmanian floral absolute rich in natural beta-ionone: warm violet and freesia with fruity, hay-like, spicy and tea nuances. Precious enhancer for violet, osmanthus, mimosa and fruity-floral compositions.
Fresh, sweet, aromatic floral-rosy with leafy-fruity facets; tenacious deep rose, jasmine, lily, pear, tea and berry.

Dry green tea and tobacco-leaf character with hay, smoke and slightly phenolic earthy facets. Signature green-tea depth in fougères and vetiver compositions; a defining note of classic masculine greens.
Roasted peanut and nut skin with earthy, sweet-toasted and maple-like warmth. A trace pyrazine for nut, coffee, cocoa and toasted gourmand accords.
Soft, dry, powdery woody note with a subtle earthy-cedar character; a smooth, inexpensive woody fixative. Used to add body and roundness to woody-floral accords.
Warm, spicy-herbaceous with woody and slightly camphoraceous nutmeg-like facets, rounder than oregano. Adds culinary-herbal warmth to fougères, spice accords and men's classics.
Dry woody notes with sweet amber warmth and patchouli-like earthiness. Supplier-classified heart note; reported blotter life exceeds 20 hours, not an exact lifetime or skin measurement.
True olibanum: fresh terpenic pine-lemon lifting a warm balsamic incense heart. The meditative resin at the core of incense and amber accords.

Symrise describes it as warm and woody in a cedar direction but slightly camphoraceous, with a distinct patchouli note and ambergris nuances; Moellhausen reads the same molecule as soft woody like cedar, weak amber, balsamic, with a patchouli note. Odour strength is medium but the blotter life is very long, around 284 hours neat, so it works as a quiet structural base woody that carries the drydown and bridges cedar to patchouli without shouting over the rest of the formula.
Bland, light-textured non-volatile carrier oil from Carthamus tinctorius with quick skin absorption. Used as a carrier and in massage oils to speed a slow-absorbing blend.
Extremely potent trace constituent of patchouli responsible for much of its odor impact; intensely woody-earthy and patchouli-typical. Used in trace to boost patchouli character.
Fresh green sesquiterpene with a crisp green-apple bite over a soft woody-herbal base. Lifts chamomile, hop and green accords and thins the heaviness of sesquiterpene woods without adding sweetness.

Helichrysum italicum absolute: extraordinary maple-syrup and curry-spice warmth over honeyed tobacco, hay, fenugreek and dried-fruit facets. Powerful signature material for tobacco, amber and boozy-gourmand themes; dose carefully or it takes over.
Fresh floral-fruity green note with winey apple, rum and berry facets; a fresh top-note modifier lending citrus, raspberry, peach and apricot nuances.

Warm saffron-leather note from Givaudan with spicy, rosy-ketonic and slightly medicinal tobacco facets, evoking saffron threads over suede. The go-to material for modern saffron-rose-oud and soft leather accords.

Steam-distilled Isparta otto: fresh lemony-green rose over a clean waxy petal body, with only a light honey where the Bulgarian turns jammy. The otto to reach for when the rose must stay luminous, and a natural lift under citrus tops and modern rose-oud hearts.

Clean, ambrette-like alicyclic musk, less fruity and more classically powdery-musky than Helvetolide, with a fresh laundered transparency. A cost-effective modern white musk with good performance in functional products.

The waxy pre-absolute extraction: fatter, greener and more animalic than the absolute, with creamy-carnal tuberose over a camphoraceous-wintergreen top and orange-blossom facets. The plant wax mutes diffusion and carries a green vegetal edge the absolute loses; artisans use it directly where a heavier, less polished tuberose is wanted.

Ethiopian olibanum distinguished by a huge octyl acetate content: sharp, fresh and fruity-green with a lemon-verbena bite, far brighter and less balsamic than carterii or sacra. The frankincense to reach for when an incense accord needs a luminous top rather than a church-resin body.
Luxury methyl ionone base with natural flowery iris nuances. Powdery violet-iris character with long odor life on the smelling strip.

Sulfurous mustard-seed note over roasted hazelnut and a coffee-like depth, the thiophene counterpart to 2-acetylthiazole and rather less bready than it. Used in trace for coffee, popcorn, nut and mustard effects, and to lend a savoury edge to gourmand and tobacco bases.

Givaudan's specialties catalogue calls it a reconstitution of the natural oil which it can replace in equal amounts, built only from synthetic ingredients and plant-based naturals, reflecting all the typical warm, animal, leather-like notes. The catalogue odour index reads animal, leather, castoreum extract. It is a highly interesting note for chypre, tobacco, leather and fougere types, and perfumers describe the Givaudan reading of castoreum as rounder and slightly sweeter than other houses' versions, more perfumery than literal. It is worked in traces: suppliers recommend a 1% solution or less.

dsm-firmenich files it in the Gourmand family and describes it, in a tiramisu note, as bringing a roasted, brown coffee cup note with some cocoa and cappuccino undertones. The house says what makes the note intriguing is its seamless balance between indulgent creaminess and sophisticated richness, and rates it lighter and more elegant than some other coffee varieties: a velvety base that evokes cappuccino, with a subtle fruity tang on top. In their trial formulas it enhances freshness, softens harshness and adds a creamier, biscuit-like quality, landing as a gourmand cocoa powder effect reminiscent of tiramisu; set against oud it diminishes the mushroom aspect and softens the raw edge while adding weight and intensity. Firgood is a solvent-free process that uses electromagnetic waves to release the plant's own water, so this reads closer to the fresh roasted bean than a solvent absolute does.

Fresh, sweet floral-herbaceous with linalool/linalyl acetate softness, camphoraceous facets and a hay-like dryout; French high-altitude qualities are finest. The heart of every fougère and aromatic composition, blending seamlessly with coumarin, oakmoss and citrus.
Elegant erogenous macrocyclic musk with powdery balsamic warmth, clean skin-like intimacy and subtle animalic radiance. Enhances florals and skin-musk accords.
Very volatile ethereal-rummy top note with a green, tart-fruity lift; used in trace for sparkle in berry, rum and cognac accords.
Diffusive fruity-solventy top note with apple and pear facets. Widely used commodity ester for fresh fruit accords.
Soft, dry, woody-balsamic oil with a faint spicy-cedary and slightly earthy character. A mild, sustainable woody fixative from New Caledonian conifer wood.
Biotech patchouli-derived material with a clean, woody, ambery-musky character rich in patchoulol but free of the dark, mildewy heaviness. A sustainable, radiant patchouli-woody base.

Rich creamy coconut with fatty, sweet peach-butter facets, the classic 'coconut aldehyde' of suntan lotion. Essential in coconut, fig leaf, osmanthus and tropical gourmand accords; powerful and long-lasting.
Soft, mild woody-cedar alcohol with a faint balsamic-earthy tone. A gentle fixative and woody rounding agent derived from cedarwood.

Robertet describes it as floral, fruity, jam, indolic and long lasting, a niche and rich jasmine note that recalls the absolute, and lists it among the house's best sellers. It is the heavier of the two jasmine Floralines: the jammy fruit and the indole give it the narcotic, slightly dirty depth a plain jasmine reconstitution lacks, so it reads as absolute rather than as flower. In a formula it holds through the heart and pushes white-floral accords toward richness and body. Applicable for a perfumery use only.

Zeon describes it as diffusive, fresh green and violet-like, and its catalogue expands that to powerful, natural, fresh, green, violet leaf, fruity and vegetable. It is the wet, cut-stem green rather than the sharp leaf-alcohol green: cucumber and melon rind under a violet-leaf top, with a fruity edge that keeps it from reading purely vegetal. In a formula a trace opens the top and pushes air through everything behind it, which is what makes it the standard lift for violet leaf, cucumber, melon and green florals, and what makes overdosing it read as crushed foliage or a fresh-cut vegetable across the whole composition. Note that this is the (3Z,6Z) isomer, a different material from the (2E,6Z) nonadienol usually sold as violet leaf alcohol, and it does not substitute for it one to one.

Warm woody-honeyed absolute with a camphoraceous-fruity top and a dry orris-violet undertone; the tenacity is extraordinary and a blotter still reads weeks later. Traces fix woody, tobacco and orris accords, but the alantolactones make it a severe sensitizer and IFRA prohibits alantroot in fragrance.

Synarome's own page: created by Hubert Fraysse in 1926, this specialty starts with a fresh citrus top fused with sophisticated leather, and the floral and luminous heart gathers refined orris and violet notes with a spicy touch, rounded off by precious woods and musky tones. Suppliers give the same reading as a fresh bergamot top over an orris-violet spicy heart on precious woods and musk. It belongs to the range Synarome built to reproduce the birch-bark-tanned Spanish leathers, but it is the warm floral end of that range rather than the tarry one: perfumers compare it to Suederal and find it smoother, more floral and softer in the base. The house gives it a week of tenacity on the blotter, suggests low single-digit percentages, and recommends it with rose, neroli, chypre, tobacco and oud. Buyers describe it as extremely powerful and diffusive, so it is easy to overdose.

Symrise gives Floral, Rose Petals, Powdery, Balsamic. It is a soft, slightly waxy rose-petal alcohol with a geraniol shade but far better tenacity, and it carries a powdery, cosmetic, faintly balsamic tail. In a formula it adds the powdery, cosmetic facet to a rose creation and works either as a quiet modifier or as bulk floral body; Symrise's use level is a wide 2 to 20 percent, and it survives soap.
Waxy-fruity orange note with green, slightly mushroomy-earthy facets and a jasmine-like softness in dilution. Used to give orange accords body and a natural peel waxiness.

Robertet describes it as floral and fruity with a narcotic connotation, and notes that it is widely used in functional perfumery. It is the fruitier, more carrying of the house's two tuberose Floralines, where 75 is the milky one: the narcotic edge supplies the heady white-flower effect while the fruit keeps it from turning heavy. Its functional-perfumery track record means it is built to survive a base and bloom out of it, so it suits soap, detergent and fabric work as readily as fine fragrance. Applicable for a perfumery use only.
Soft woody-floral alcohol related to the ionones, with dried fruit, tea and gentle orris-violet nuances. Naturalizer for osmanthus, tobacco and violet accords where a muted ionone effect is wanted.
Sweet balsamic ester reminiscent of storax and Peru balsam. Gentle amber-balsamic fixative for opulent bases.
Fatty, rancid-cheesy, sweaty odor. A trace-use acid for cheese, dairy and body/skin nuances in animalic and gourmand accords.

Ferociously potent catty blackcurrant thiol, sulfurous and urinous neat, but juicy, tart and mouthwatering at ppm dilution. The keystone of cassis bases; used in extreme dilution to animate fruity and exotic accords.

Phenolic-sweet mossy note with woody, leathery and slightly marine-inky facets that powerfully evokes real oakmoss absolute. Used in traces alongside Evernyl to rebuild compliant oakmoss accords for chypre, fougere, leather and tobacco work.
Sulfurous tropical note of passion fruit, blackcurrant and grapefruit, exotic and sweaty-fruity, extremely potent. Used in trace amounts for realistic passion fruit, mango and cassis effects.
Roasted chocolate and nutty hazelnut-peanut facets. Top filing follows the catalog's pyrazine convention, not measured evaporation or longevity.
Grapefruit-citrus fused with dry woody-vetiver tonality, with a certain kinship to nootkatone. Carries sparkling citrus character deep into the drydown of modern woody-fresh compositions.

Sulfurous raw onion and leek at the slightest trace, opening into a brothy cooked-meat depth with a roasted, faintly metallic edge. A parts-per-billion material only, used for allium, broth and savoury effects and to put a raw vegetal bite under cumin and green accords.
Soft waxy, oily-fruity floral note with a faint leafy-brandy nuance. Smooth fixative-like ester for fruity-floral accords.

Fresh, tangy-bitter citrus peel with a subtle sulfurous, juicy pulp nuance from trace nootkatone and mercaptans. Used for sparkling modern freshness; often boosted with methyl pamplemousse or a trace of grapefruit mercaptan.

Almost odorless crystals with a sharp lemon-sour taste. Used in perfumery as a chelating agent to remove iron (Fe) contamination from oils and compounds picked up from steel drums or during distillation.

Fraterworks Lotus Storm 766840, a compounded blue-lotus impression by Bertrand Duchaufour. Jasmine and creamy white florals combine with watery foliage, galbanum, fruity and earthy nuances, beeswax and a lightly spicy musky finish. Supplier reports more than 24 hours on a smelling strip, not exact hours or skin longevity. The linked IFRA 51 certificate gives a 17.07% Category 4 finished-product ceiling. Identifier mapping and incomplete constituent/allergen disclosure require review; this is not a safety clearance.
Fruity apple-damascenone character with rosy and slightly camphoraceous facets. A modern specialty for fruity-floral radiance.

Fresh green leaf and foliage with a bark-like cortex edge and a soft balsamic storax undertone, turning floral-melony on dilution. The unsubstituted parent of the Lilial and Bourgeonal family: cheap, powerful and used low for crushed-stem greenness in hyacinth, lilac and muguet accords.

An IFF specialty musk built on a quinazoline skeleton unlike the nitro, polycyclic and macrocyclic musks it sits beside. Bulkaroma describes it as a clean, powdery musk, soft, with a sweet and warm top note and a pleasant hedonic profile, and tags it clean, floral, musky, powdery, soft and sweet. The warmth in the opening is what distinguishes it from the flatly laundered polycyclic musks: it reads soft and skin-like rather than detergent-clean, so it works as the rounding musk under powdery florals and soft ambers. Supplied as a colourless to pale yellow liquid to solid.

A dry, resinous amber base with agrestic earthiness and moderate sweetness, supported by Mysore sandalwood and Aceh patchouli. A composed fragrance base and fixative rather than natural opoponax essential oil.

The molecular-distilled alcohol fraction of vetiver oil, khusimol-rich: rich, sweet and balsamic over the woody-rooty heart of vetiver, with the smoky and grapefruity extremes distilled out. Used where vetiver character is wanted without the oil's dirt, and as the precursor to vetiveryl acetate.

Moellhausen presents it in BoldBases #3 as the dry balsamic touch of memories and past: a sweet building block whose vanilla side gently meets the woody note of labdanum. It is a compounded house base, not a single molecule, so it arrives as a finished amber accord: the vanillic sweetness and the dry resinous labdanum are already balanced against each other. Used as the house intends, it is a foundation you build a base on rather than an accent, giving the drydown a warm balsamic floor without having to construct one from separate resin and vanilla materials.
Dry, dusty East African wood oil with a faint sandalwood echo over an earthy, slightly tobacco-like base. A cheap and very tenacious sandalwood extender and fixative for woody and amber bases.

Strong sulfurous coffee note with onion, garlic and radish-mustard pungency, turning mushroomy and earthy as it fades. Gentler and far easier to dose than furfuryl mercaptan, which makes it the practical choice for roasted coffee bodies.

Persian otto from the Kashan fields: warm spicy rose with a resinous-honeyed depth and a dry balsamic tail the European ottos do not have. A specialty otto for attar-style and amber-rose work, where the rose has to sit inside the resins rather than float above them.

Intensely green, leafy aldehyde of privet, tomato leaf and crushed stems with a fresh muguet lift; smoother and rounder than linear aldehydes. Adds natural green freshness to florals, fougeres and functional bases.
The most characteristic sandalwood constituent, soft, creamy and diffusive with a smooth milky-woody warmth. A key marker of sandalwood quality and a building block for reconstitutions.

Givaudan says it brings a spectacular blooming and natural, transparent and fresh rose petal effect with fruity-juicy undertones. The point of the material is bloom: it opens a rose accord out rather than deepening it, giving petal freshness where citronellol and geraniol would give weight, and Givaudan's perfumers describe it as very easy to blend in almost all olfactive directions. It is claimed at roughly five times the performance of citronellol, so it is used in small proportion against a classic rose base. The molecule is a biodegradable, non-sensitising Givaudan captive with no published CAS.

Deep fruity-rose ketone of stewed plum, blackcurrant jam and honeyed tobacco, warmer and jammier than the alpha isomer. Transforms roses, ambers and tobacco accords with a trace; IFRA-restricted rose ketone.

Nearly silent: a faint candle-wax, oily-fatty note with a whisper of orris that gives waxy texture and body more than scent. Methyl hexadecanoate, a low-melting fatty ester reported in champaca and jasmine absolutes.
Powerful fresh-minty, camphoraceous note with woody pine and earthy-patchouli undertones. Works in pine and patchouli directions.

Soft, sweet, balsamic-spicy with hyacinth-floral and faint cinnamon nuances, much gentler than cinnamal. A blender that bridges spicy, floral and balsamic notes in lilac, hyacinth and amber bases; a listed allergen.

Nearly odorless UV-B filter occasionally incorporated in fragrance and cosmetic bases to slow photo-degradation and color change of the perfume oil. Functional additive rather than an odorant; cosmetic regulations cap its level.

Givaudan's own specialties brochure explains that the characteristic fragrance of heated birch leaves in a sauna bath was studied by headspace analysis in its research department and reconstructed as this base. Suppliers describe it, in decreasing intensity, as birch-leaf, herbaceous, vegetal, fresh and green-spice: an airy, astringent verdancy carrying shades of tea and spice, particularly cardamom, coriander seed and betel leaf. It is powerful and diffusive and takes a wide use range, where around 2% adds a modern green top to masculine colognes and up to 3% gives a herbaceous vegetable effect in shampoo and beauty care. It is the green signature of Calvin Klein Escape for Men.

Sweet balsamic with a cinnamyl heart over amber, spicy, fruity and woody depth. It is a compounded synthetic stand-in for tolu balsam absolute, and the supplier rates its cinnamic heart as arguably nicer than the natural. Its reason to exist is colour: natural tolu is intensely dark brown, this is a pale golden liquid, so it carries balsamic warmth into compositions a dark absolute would ruin, with no supply-chain risk behind it. Sold already cut to half strength in triethyl citrate, which makes an otherwise unpourable material easy to weigh.
Sharp, fresh, resinous-coniferous oil with a sweet-balsamic and slightly herbaceous pine character. Used in forest, pine and functional fragrance accords.

Fujian and Guangxi sambac absolute: cleaner and more tea-like than the Indian, with apricot-peach fruitiness and a fresh green edge in place of the banana-indole heaviness. The origin behind jasmine-tea accords; it lifts a white floral where Indian sambac would weigh it down.
Extremely powerful alliaceous, cooked-onion and savory sulfur odor. Ultra-trace for tropical fruit, savory and truffle effects.

Mane describes a nice radiant ambery scent with elegant facets reminiscent of white woods, and trade coverage adds that it reads as a cedar-ambery character rather than a sweet balsamic one. Its speciality Driftwood is designed around the molecule and shows what it does at length: an ambery-woody note with salty and marine facets, arboraceous rather than resinous. In a formula it is a radiance and drydown material, giving amber warmth without the syrupy weight of labdanum or vanillin, and it sits comfortably under white florals and clean woods. It is a captive with no disclosed structure, reachable to independents only inside the Driftwood speciality.

The earliest maturity grade of cold-pressed Citrus reticulata peel: sharper and greener than yellow or red, with a bitter leafy edge over the dusty anthranilate sweetness all mandarins share. The choice when a mandarin note must read crisp and unripe rather than syrupy.

Intense butter and butterscotch note, creamy and mouthwatering at trace levels but rancid-cheesy when overdosed. The reference buttery molecule for caramel, pastry and cream accords, used in tiny amounts.

Sweet anisic-green estragole warmth with celery-like herbal facets, brighter and greener than basil. Classic anisic-herbal topnote for fougeres and green chypres; its estragole and methyl eugenol content is what carries the IFRA limits.

Soft woody-amber acetate: a brief acetate lift settles into a smooth woody tone that recalls vetiveryl acetate and creamy sandalwood, with a hint of clary sage, and without the harsh dryness of many synthetic ambers. Very tenacious (about 280 hours on a strip) and stable in functional bases. Acetoxymethyl isolongifolene.

Robertet presented it at SIMPPAR 2026 as a 100% pure and natural, soluble and clean ingredient offering tones of grated coconut and pineapple, obtained by conversion of coconut flesh followed by supercritical CO2 extraction. In a formula it is a ready-made pina colada facet: a fleshy, creamy coconut carrying a tart tropical fruit lift on top, which gives a solar, monoi or gourmand accord a natural body and a slightly fibrous, real-fruit texture that a coconut lactone on its own cannot supply.
Powerful maple syrup, celery-curry and burnt-sugar character with hay-like and nutty-immortelle depth, driven by natural sotolon. In traces it enriches maple, caramel, tobacco and immortelle accords.
Herbal-rue note with fruity, waxy and powdery orris-like undertones remarkably close to iris root. An affordable orris extender that also serves rue and fig leaf reconstructions.
Sweet woody-herbal bergamot-like ester with pine-coniferous freshness and soft lavender undertones. Functions like linalyl acetate but woodier; ideal for colognes and fougeres.
Dry, green-herbal absolute with hay-like, slightly smoky and tannic tea facets. Adds a natural tea-leaf realism to green, fresh and cologne accords.

Nearly odorless fragrance-protection additive from Fraterworks, current Solgard (E) grade with tocopherol. UV protection and antioxidant support, not an aroma ingredient or sunscreen. Supplier guidance: typically 0.5-4% in fragrance, or 10 g per kg ethanol for pre-fixing alcohol. Supplier specifies a 15% maximum for UK, NZ and EU destinations; this is separate from its unrestricted IFRA 51 Category 4 certificate. Full product safety and local regulatory review are still required. Solgard B with BHT is discontinued and is not this grade.

Fresh waxy-clean ester with a rose body and sweet fruity-honey facets; saturating the double bond trades the lift of citronellyl acetate for wax and stability. The workhorse rose ester for soap and bleach-bearing bases, where geranyl acetate would discolour or drift.

The historical soul of muguet: sweet, dewy lily-of-the-valley with linden-blossom honey and a soft melon-watery freshness. Still the most naturalistic muguet material, though IFRA-restricted as a sensitizer, always check current limits.
Waxy-fruity, brandy and apricot odor with a floral nuance. A soft fatty-fruity note for wine and cognac accords.

A long lasting fresh tropical amide (Givaudan) of guava and passionfruit with nuances of grapefruit, rhubarb and cassis. It can be overdosed heavily in tropical fruit accords or used lightly to give a juicy twist to other fruity notes and to bring bloom in shampoos and shower gels.
Sweet, ethereal-fruity odor with pear and celery-like nuances. A simple ester for fruity top-note work.
Expansive green-edged rose with geranium freshness and a distinctive metallic sharpness that gives realism beyond simple rose alcohols. Extremely diffusive and persistent; dose with a light touch.

Rich, dark roasted-coffee character with smoky, earthy, slightly winey and burnt-caramel facets true to fresh espresso. Powerful in coffee gourmands and adds roasted depth to amber, tobacco and oud accords.

Deep sweet green-fruity with a Concord grape skin core and jasmine, orange blossom and lilac florals behind it. A substantive green-floral that greens up white florals and grape accords without evaporating away from them.

Advanced Biotech's natural chocolate speciality, a yellow to brown liquid with a chocolate odour, sold as a natural flavouring and fragrance preparation and used in bath and body products, candles, air fresheners and perfumes as well as in food. The Choclatone range is built on 5-methyl-2-phenyl-2-hexenal, cocoa hexenal, carried in mid-chain triglycerides, so it smells as the molecule does but softened by the odourless carrier: aldehydic, bitter cocoa and nut skin over green, sweet chocolate with fruity and slightly butyric edges. Because it arrives pre-diluted it is the more forgiving way to place a real cocoa note into a gourmand, giving the roasted bitterness without the aldehydic bite of the neat material, and it sits comfortably beside vanilla and other sweet brown notes.

Symrise describes it simply as smelling like pear, and supplier listings fill that out as juicy, pear-bright and lightly green, an immediate burst of fresh sun-ripened pear that is both juicy and sweet. It carries a ripe pear character that is fresher and rounder than the classic pear esters alone, so it works as a fruity heart that reads natural rather than candied. It blends readily with florals such as jasmine and peony, with citrus, and into gourmand accords. The molecule was developed from by-products of corn fermentation and is an exclusive Symrise captive.

Rich, heavy pineapple note, sweeter, waxier and far more tenacious than allyl caproate, with a slightly animalic-fruity depth. Carries pineapple into the heart of tropical compositions; IFRA-restricted.

Absolute recovered by solvent-washing the distillation waters left over from neroli production, so it carries the water-soluble half of the flower: honeyed and indolic over a dry musty-herbal petitgrain underside the concrete-derived absolute does not show. Used in small amounts to give a neroli or orange-flower accord the green transparency of the living flower.

IFF specialty base delivering indolic-animalic warmth in a stabilized, non-discoloring form: fecal-floral depth with civet and jasmine facets. Practical substitute for raw indole/civet in bases where discoloration matters.
Fresh, sweet and balsamic like crushed fir needles: clean and terpenic at first, a little tart, over a soft woody-coniferous body with a faint grassy edge.

Sweet orange-blossom ether with mothball-naphthalenic, acacia and slightly fruity-grape facets; a 19th-century classic. Small amounts give vintage neroli-mimosa warmth; overdose smells of old wardrobes.

Rosy-herbaceous ester with a honeyed, faintly tobacco-like tail and much less fruit than the lower citronellyl esters. Used as a modifier alongside citronellyl acetate and formate where a rose needs a dry herbal-honey body rather than more petal.

Menthone acetal coolant with a light green-minty odor, softer and rounder than menthol itself. Gives a fast-onset, medium-length cold effect; the sibling of Frescolat ML where a little more minty character is wanted.
Fresh herbaceous-green, slightly fruity and lavender-like ketone. Fresh lift for lavender, fougere and green apple notes.
Deep ink-blue oil with a sweet, fruity apple-and-honey character softened by a gentle herby-floral haze and faint camphor coolness. Brings chamomile-like sweetness to florals and aromatic accords.
Clean, cooling camphoraceous freshness, the pure heart of eucalyptus without the terpene roughness. Standard freshening tool in fougères, mint accords and functional perfumery.

Sweet vernal grass absolute with an intensely honeyed hay-coumarin profile, softer and greener than liatrix, with tea and dried-apricot nuances. Lovely in refined tobacco, hay and fougere accords; coumarin-rich so IFRA-relevant.
Warm, ripe fleshy apricot and peach with plum, jasmine and ambrette creaminess; extremely long lasting for a fruity material. Anchors stone-fruit and osmanthus accords deep into the drydown.

Musty rooty earth with a sour cheesy-animalic funk from free isovaleric acid, resting on a warm camphoraceous-balsamic bornyl acetate body. Funkier and more sweat-driven than spikenard, which is drier and spicier; a trace-level fixative that gives leather, chypre and amber bases a living, unwashed depth.

Eugenol-rich allspice, warm and sweet-phenolic with clove and faint aromatic-cineole facets, coarser and without the fresh peppery lift of the berry. The cheap allspice workhorse and a high-eugenol backbone for fougere, amber and masculine grooming accords.

A sensual woody profile beaming with rich smoky facets, with refined leathery undertones and an elegant ambery warmth. Firmenich present it as a feminine reading of oud: the smoke and the leather are there but the animalic side is not, so it stays clean and wearable where the Oud Assafi specialties go barnyard. Supplied at 20 percent in DPG. It behaves as a high-dose base rather than a trace material: under one percent it adds a smoky whisper behind cedar, sandalwood or patchouli, and at a few percent the leather comes forward and the whole composition gains body and fixation.

Tropical-saffron aldehyde with herbal, clean tobacco and rose-oxide facets over a damascone-like fruitiness. The structural bridge between safranal and the ionones: use in traces for saffron, black tea, tobacco leaf and osmanthus, where it lifts dry and bright without safranal's phenolic harshness.

Givaudan describes it as floral, green, fresh and deep, with a lily-of-the-valley character; the base was built around an exclusive Givaudan aromachemical and the smell of blooming linden trees in early summer. In a formula it is used as a central note, but the house notes it is also very effective in the top notes and in the dry down, so it carries a linden signature across the whole wear rather than only in the heart. Suggested use is up to 10 percent, and about 4 percent in a violet accord adds pleasant floral volume. The 151/7 grade is the 2026 reformulation of the discontinued Givco 151 and was reported to perform similarly to its predecessor in both olfactory and GC comparison.

Cone oil of Humulus lupulus: green herbal myrcene over a resinous, spicy-woody humulene body with the unmistakable bitter-beery signature. The natural source of the humulene note and a quick way to give green, fougere and craft-beer accords an authentic dry bitterness.

Functional cooling agent with only a faint minty odor: delivers a gentle, long-lasting physiological coolness without menthol's harsh smell. Used in fresh colognes, aquatics and body sprays to make freshness literally felt on skin.

Sweet herbal-floral violet alcohol with a light balsamic warmth and a soft woody tail, the reduced form of beta-ionone and considerably softer than it. A naturalizer for violet, osmanthus and tea accords where beta-ionone would read too dry and too diffusive.
High in alpha- and beta-santalol, giving a rich, creamy, milky-woody profile close to album but with a fresher, slightly spicy edge. Prized as a premium natural sandalwood in fine fragrance.
A nitro musk base formulated to replace Musk Xylol, with a powdery sensual aroma evoking fresh laundry, soap and skin. Contains IFRA-compliant Musk Ketone; free of Musk Xylene.

Woody and balsamic. A blended reconstitution of aloeswood, very true to the natural essential oil: intensely woody, reminiscent of vetiver, with sweet balsamic undertones. Being a full reconstruction rather than a specialty built around a natural oud, it is the economical way to carry an agarwood note through a woody base, and the vetiver-like dryness lets it blend cleanly into cedar, patchouli and vetiver accords instead of sitting on top of them.

Oak-like woody base with liquor, cognac and smoke facets. Ventos blend sold by Perfumer Supply House, containing natural oakwood extract alongside synthetic ingredients; distinct from natural oakwood absolute or CO2 extract.

Sharp sulfurous alliaceous note of onion, garlic and horseradish, with a minty edge and a roasted coffee facet as it thins out. A ppm-level material for coffee and savoury roasted bases, less explosively volatile than furfuryl mercaptan.
A more affordable oud-type oil from Aetoxylon sympetalum, drier and more woody-leathery with less of the deep animalic sweetness of true Aquilaria. Used to extend or build oud accords.

Kao describes it as fresh-herbal with fruity-flowery undertones, and gives the descriptor triad Herbal - Chamomille - Fruity. The chamomile reading is the distinguishing one: a soft, slightly tea-like aromatic freshness rather than the sharp herbaceousness of a lavandin or a sage material. As a small pivalate ester it opens fast and lifts, so in a formula it is a top-note freshener that puts an herbal-fruity brightness over a fougere or a floral accord without the camphoraceous bite that a lavender note would bring.

Advanced Biotech specifies a dark brown liquid and describes the odour in one word, fruity, which is the jammy lift that sits on top rather than the whole picture. The product is declared in the EU as a thermal process flavouring, meaning a Maillard reaction product, and the maltol-praline name is the house's claim for the sweet caramelic body underneath that fruity opening. Soluble in water as well as in most organic solvents, dense at roughly 1.08 to 1.12, with a two-year shelf life. In a formula it is a ready-made caramelic praline base for gourmand work, saving the perfumer from building maltol, furanone and nut notes by hand, and it holds low in the drydown. It is brown and assertive, so it goes in as a trace under vanilla, tonka or coffee rather than as a body note in its own right.

Sparkling, sweet-tart citrus with a distinctive floral-lavender and slightly spicy tea-like nuance, more refined than other citrus oils. The backbone of colognes and fougeres; perfumers use it generously in top notes to lend elegance and lift.
Nutty, roasted cocoa and coffee note with a fermented, slightly musty chocolate character, milder than trimethylpyrazine. Rounds roasted and fermented facets in chocolate and nut gourmands.

Powerful watery-floral aldehyde with a metallic, dewy transparency and light woody-citrus undertone; diffusive and long-lasting for an aldehyde. Excellent for wet-petal and morning-dew effects in muguet, freesia and marine florals.

Sweet licorice-anisic and warm, softer and rounder than star anise with a faint green seed nuance and no fenchone bite. The traditional natural for pastis, licorice and anise effects in gourmands, ambers and aromatic fougeres; estragole content carries its own constituent limit.

Symrise gives the odour as citrus, mandarin, orange and coriander leaf. It is an isomer mixture of tridecadienenitriles with, in Symrise's own words, outstanding strength and tenacity, which is what a citrus nitrile is for: it holds a juicy mandarin and orange note in places a cold-pressed peel oil would fade or discolour. It boosts those notes, enhances fruity fragrances, and combines well with orange blossom components. The published odour threshold in air is 0.0063 ug/l and it boils at 296.4 C, so it is both loud and long, unusual for anything reading as citrus. Symrise recommends 0.01 to 2 percent.

French flower oil of Lavandula hybrida, cultivar Super, Payan Bertrand E4712. Lavender-like, floral and herbal, with a camphoraceous aspect. A separate cultivar from Grosso, not a synonym or substitute identity. Supplier blotter life: 4 hours. Impact 5/10 is an uncalibrated application estimate, not a supplier rating. The supplier IFRA 51 certificate lists Category 4 as not restricted; declared constituents still contribute to whole-formula limits. SDS: H315, H317, H318, H412. The expanded allergen declaration includes the oil itself as Lavandula Oil/Extract.
Powerful, fresh, natural marine note with a distinct sea-breeze character, combining ozonic, rosy and honeyed nuances reminiscent of sea salt and the mineralic, slightly dirty aspect of seawater.
Deep green with a distinct tea and herbaceous facet, drier and more sophisticated than other leaf esters. Valuable in green-tea, mate and galbanum-type accords.
Soft creamy sandalwood with a clean, slightly urinous-woody nuance in the classic style. A dependable, economical sandalwood volumizer beneath the fancier santal molecules.

Mane's potent woody-ambery molecule with a fresh, rosemary-camphor sparkle on top of a dry, radiant amber body. Brings both lift and enormous drydown power; a signature of several contemporary masculine ambers.
Earthy, rooty and dry with a distinct orris-like powderiness and woody undertones. Bridges top and base notes and brings a natural iris facet to florals and chypres.
Bland, stable fixed carrier oil with a near-ideal balance of mono- and poly-unsaturated fatty acids, high vitamin E and gamma-oryzanol. Used as a base and carrier oil.

Fresh fruity-rosy ester, richer and rounder than citronellyl acetate with a distinct berry nuance. Used in modest doses to lift rose, geranium and muguet bases, and it sits well next to bergamot in citrus structures.

Sweet fresh rose with geranium-leaf and light fruity-citrus facets; one of the two pillars of rose chemistry alongside citronellol. Ubiquitous in rose, geranium and floral bouquets of every kind; IFRA-restricted allergen.

Woody, leathery, ambery and animalic. Very powerful and complex, with the richness and diffusivity of natural oud oil. Firmenich build it on their own Oud Assafi natural at 3 percent, so it carries genuine agarwood depth rather than reading as a pure reconstruction; the name means exceptional. In a formula it is an entire oud accord in one bottle: a few tenths of a percent give an oriental or leather base the animalic-woody signature and the diffusion a synthetic oud alone will not deliver, and it holds through the drydown.

Fresh, fruity-rosy ester with a green pear and lavender-like sweetness; smoother and lighter than geraniol itself. Bridges citrus top notes into rose hearts and adds a natural sparkle to geranium and neroli accords.

Fine orris-violet of great elegance with soft woody-floral tonality, considered the noblest of the methylionones. Used in high-quality iris accords, mimosa and violet flowers where refinement matters more than raw power.

Symrise gives Floral, Orange Blossom; The Good Scents Company calls it a highly diffusive and intense floral-fresh aromatic reminiscent of orange blossom. It reads as orange blossom with an anthranilate-like sweetness and a peely, fresh-green edge on top. In a formula it is the high-impact key to orange blossom and neroli reconstructions and a booster for floriental accords, and because it is a benzofuran ketone rather than an anthranilate it does not discolour a base the way methyl anthranilate does. Symrise describes it as very substantive and puts the use level at 0.01 to 2 percent.
Rich plum and raspberry with peach, dried-fruit and soft floral facets. Useful for dark stone-fruit, berry, osmanthus and gourmand effects.

Givaudan's specialties brochure describes it as an economical reconstitution of the rare natural Geranium Bourbon oil, reproducing the fresh green sparkling and minty herbaceous characteristics with a rosy floral volume. It sits exactly where geranium oil sits in a formula: a rosy-green bridge from citrus tops into a rose or fougere heart, sharpening and de-sweetening rose accords and giving lift to lavender and herbal masculines, with a consistency and a price the natural Bourbon oil does not offer.

Indian grandiflorum absolute from Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh: greener, sharper and markedly more indolic than the Egyptian, with the same banana-ester fruitiness over a leafier, less honeyed body. The two origins are not interchangeable; the Indian puts an animalic bite into a white floral where the Egyptian rounds it off.
Rich, diffusive sandalwood with a fresh, spicy-cedary and slightly floral top over a creamy woody base. A high-impact synthetic sandalwood used in prestige compositions.

A separate product from the Malto-Praline line, specified by Advanced Biotech as a dark brown liquid with a fruity odour and declared in the EU as a thermal process flavouring. It is the lighter of the two houses' praline reaction bases: specific gravity around 1.015 to 1.040 against Malto-Praline's 1.08 upward, a flash point near 32 C that says a volatile carrier is present, and a twelve-month shelf life rather than twenty-four. The effect is a nutty confectionery praline with the fruity top the spec names, softer and less molasses-heavy than the malto grade. In a formula it lifts the sugared-nut facet of gourmand accords without dragging the whole base brown, which is what makes it worth keeping alongside Malto-Praline instead of choosing between them. The short shelf life and the low flash point both argue for buying small and working it diluted.

Bright, sharp, juicy-fresh lemon peel with a zesty, slightly aldehydic sparkle. Used for instant freshness in top notes of colognes, chypres and functional perfumery; fades quickly so it is often paired with citral or Lemonile for persistence.

Symrise describe it as Green, Floral, Chrysanthemum Leaves, Grapefruit: bruised chrysanthemum foliage with a bitter grapefruit-peel edge over it. Their sheet says it shows an elegant bitterness in grapefruit and coniferous accords, gives volume, complexity and depth to white floral creations, and blends pleasantly with lactones to create a lively fruitiness. Recommended use level is 0.05 to 3 percent, with an odour threshold of 0.1585 micrograms per litre.
Iron-distilled dark patchouli: deeper, damper and more camphoraceous-chocolate than the light molecular-distilled grades. The vintage chypre patchouli character.
Pungent acidic note of rancid butter and rotten cheese; used in trace amounts for fruity-ester and cheese effects.

Australian myrtle leaf oil running 70 to 80 percent citral: a loud, sweet lemon-drop citrus sitting on a green-medicinal, faintly eucalyptus underside inherited from the tea tree side of the family. A cheap natural way to make a lemon top note actually carry; push it and it turns citronella, so keep it underneath the expressed oils rather than in front of them.

Zeon lists this optically active grade as natural, milky, creamy, against the plain racemic delta-Decalactone in the same table which it lists as creamy, nutty. It is the soft dairy lactone: warm milk and cream with a ripe stone-fruit edge and a faint coconut roundness, rounder and less nutty than the racemate. Zeon's stated position is that the odour quality of optically active substances is much superior to that of racemic compounds, and that using the resolved material makes it possible to reproduce genuinely natural flavours and fragrances that racemic material alone could not; the R grade is supplied at 80.0 to 83.0 percent ee, which matches the R-heavy ratio found in peach. In a formula it is the creamy body under fruit and gourmand accords, softening sharp fruity esters and giving skin-like warmth in the heart, and because it is the same substance at a resolved grade a perfumer typically weighs it lower than racemic delta-Decalactone for the same creaminess.
Dry, woody-ambery diol with a soft cedar and slightly spicy character and good fixative power. A supporting woody-amber note for masculine and woody accords.

A supercritical CO2 extract of eucalyptus leaves and twigs from Mane's Jungle Essence range. Perfumer & Flavorist describes a high-quality extract that evokes the living eucalyptus tree with a typical blackcurrant facet, less minty and fruitier than a classical eucalyptus essence, revealing a dynamic freshness in perfumes. In a formula it is a top note for crisp, fruity, aromatic openings, and it is the route to a eucalyptus that reads green-fruity rather than medicinal or camphoraceous, which is what a distilled globulus or citriodora oil gives instead.
Rich green-herbaceous, hay-like and coumarinic lavender-type absolute with great naturalness. Body and depth for lavender and fougere hearts.
Warm, sweet-floral absolute with heady, slightly spicy and powdery facets recalling a cross of tuberose and orange blossom. Traditional Indian attar flower (moulshree).

Soupy sulfur alcohol, leek and cooked cabbage over a broth-like sweetness. The alcohol version of methional, roughly a thousand times weaker but far more tenacious, so it holds a savoury vegetable body under gourmand and fermented accords.

Soft, muguet-rose alcohol with a fresh peony petal character, clean and slightly green-citrus. Excellent hydroxycitronellal-free muguet builder and a smooth rosy volumizer that is very stable in functional bases.

Bedoukian gives it a tropical, ripe, juicy, sweet green, fruity scent. The supplier listing expands this to sweet, juicy tropical fruit notes with an aromatic, slightly woody impression and a creamy coconut dry-down, and The Good Scents Company types it fruity with an exotic, musty, characteristic pink-guava character. It is a fruit-realism material rather than a candy one: at traces up to about 2% it puts the ripe, faintly overripe guava and mango facet into fruity and floral accords and leaves a creamy tail behind the fruit.

A sweet floral base with the character of orange blossom, built on methyl anthranilate at roughly eight percent and blended with orange blossom, petitgrain and neroli. It was first used in Coty's L'Origan in 1905 and later in Houbigant's Coeur de Jeannette. The anthranilate gives it the slightly heady, grape-skin edge of real orange flower, so a modest dose turns a thin neroli accord into a full blossom without reaching for indole. Being a compounded base it already carries its own petitgrain-green counterweight, which is what separates it from dosing the bare molecule.
Fresh green with sweet fruity-winey undertones, bridging cut grass and orchard fruit. Handy in apple, pear and green floral topnotes.
Mild floral-herbaceous note suggesting lilac and rose leaves with a slightly earthy, cool nuance. Fixative-blender in lilac, lily and rose accords, valued for stability in functional bases.

Takasago's own product page classifies it as floral, orange flower and musk, and supplier listings describe an orange blossom or neroli aroma with a grape and musk undertone. The house presents it as a novel methyl anthranilate note that is extremely stable and resistant to discolouration, and states it can be used to replace methyl anthranilate outright. That is exactly what it does in a formula: it gives the grapey orange-flower effect of an anthranilate but holds up where anthranilates yellow and turn, with good stability reported from acidic softeners and antiperspirants right through soap and powder detergent, and only fair performance in bleach. Takasago places typical use levels below 5%.
Lilac-pine floral blend of terpineol isomers, slightly harsher and more terpenic than pure alpha-terpineol. Economical workhorse for lilac, lily and general floral bouquets in soaps and detergents.

Full cinnamon-stick spice with a sweet balsamic body and none of the scorched edge steam distillation leaves behind, its cinnamal bite softened by the eugenol and cinnamyl acetate the CO2 carries over. The rounder choice for amber and gourmand warmth; still dominant, so dose it like the oil.
Soft, clean muguet-pyranol with fresh petal, light rose and subtle green-fruity facets; transparent and unobtrusive. A backbone volumizer of post-Lilial muguet accords, usable at very high levels.

Spicy, woody and sweetly peppery with a clear cardamom-like aromatic top and a warm ginger-adjacent bite. The sesquiterpene body makes it rounder and less sneezy than black pepper, so it works as a modern spice accent in colognes, rose-pepper themes and woody-amber tops.

Synarome's own listing says Muscarome opens on a warm and entrancing Tonkin musk note, soft and smooth like buckskin, and Perfumer Supply House sells it as strong, animalic, musky, woody, dry and sensual, the synthetic rendition of Tonkin musk tincture. It is the material perfumers reach for to put the alive, breathing quality back into a musk accord that clean macrocyclics leave flat. The house positions it as a rounding agent for the background rather than a feature: it adds a natural musky effect, lift and diffusion, and blends into masculines, orientals, leathers and opulent florals. Suggested at low single-digit percentages, with roughly a month of tenacity on the blotter. The J5 grade carries ethylic alcohol; the AMCR grade is the alcohol-free version in triethyl citrate and is a separate product.

West African flower absolute: a green jasmine-hyacinth carrying a strange mushroom-earthy undertone and a faint anisic sweetness. Traces give white florals a wild, unpolished naturalness that jasmine absolute on its own cannot reach.

Kao describes it as a spicy-woody note with a floral tendency and a damascone character, and files it under the descriptor triad Spicy - Woody - Floral. The damascone reading is what makes it useful: it carries the dry, slightly stewed rose-and-fruit warmth of a rose ketone in a carbonate that sits lower and quieter in the blend. In a formula it works as a bridging modifier rather than a headline, warming woody bases and giving a floral heart a spicy, dried-rose edge; it is a carbonate, not an acetate, so it behaves differently from the tert-butylcyclohexyl acetates a perfumer may reach for by name association.

Extremely powerful fenugreek and maple-caramel lactone with curry, lovage and celery facets, the ethyl homologue of sotolon and roughly an order of magnitude stronger. Works at parts per billion for maple, immortelle, rum and tobacco realism, and turns soupy and savoury the moment it is overdosed.

Soft, sweet violet with woody-orris undertones and a subtle raspberry fruitiness, smoother and more floral than the beta isomer. Cornerstone of violet accords and a rounding agent across floral, fruity and woody compositions.
Sharp penetrating green-floral chrysanthemum note with rosy-jasmine facets, a metallic edge and grassy warmth on dilution. Key note of Indian kewda; lifts florals.

Pseudevernia furfuracea lichen absolute (harvested from conifers): drier, more resinous-piney and tarry-leathery than oakmoss, with smoky forest-bark depth. Used in fougeres, leathers and pine-woody bases; IFRA-restricted like oakmoss, with low-atranol qualities available.

Deterpenated mandarin: the sweet anthranilate heart of the oil with the limonene bulk stripped away, rounder and less peel-sharp than the cold-pressed grade and noticeably more floral. Concentrated body plus far better oxidation stability, so it holds a true mandarin note in the top where the whole oil would go thin and rancid.

Givaudan's specialties catalogue presents it as a cost-effective reconstitution of sampaquita, the jasmine sambac of the Philippines: the delicate fragrances of carnation and ylang together with a slightly green note grafted onto a rich basic accord of jasmine, tuberose and honeysuckle. The catalogue odour index reads jasmine, fruity, and suppliers describe a powerful, rich, creamy jasmine with a slight fruity nuance behind it. In a formula it is used in traces to exalt mid florals and to add narcotic depth, and it blends readily into rose, ripe fruit, coconut and tropical accords as well as musks.

IFF's own compendium describes Ylanganate as a booster of white floral notes carrying a non-discolouring orange flower character, offering gentle complexity and calm sensuality. Suppliers list it as floral, ylang, orange flower and grape, strong. In a formula it reads as bright creamy orange flower touched with ylang and gardenia, and it lifts and rounds fruity, sweet and vanillic-balsamic accords rather than sitting on top of them. It is a low-dosage booster, so it works as a corrector inside white floral, orange flower, ylang and gardenia accords more than as a soliflore in its own right, and it will not yellow a base.
Warm caramelized-sugar and buttery-furan character with chamomile-like and slightly musty facets. Published descriptions vary, so evaluate the actual grade before use.

Fresh, watery-green floral aldehyde with cyclamen, muguet and cucumber-melon facets and a clean aldehydic lift. Core modifier of muguet and marine-floral accords; also flags a rosy freshness in fougeres.

Robust camphoraceous lavender with a rougher, greener and more penetrating profile than true lavender, higher in camphor and cineole. The economic backbone of fougère and functional perfumery; blends well with rosemary and coumarin.

A synthetic sandalwood oil that reproduces the extremely fine, powerful, rich and sweet sandalwood odour. It is a complex mixture of captive and patented aroma chemicals together with essential oils, but contains no sandalwood oil at all. It can replace the original oil in equivalent proportions, with an exceptional cost/performance ratio and very good substantivity, so in practice it is the sandalwood body of a formula rather than a topping-up material; the house also notes that adding it at around a tenth of the total volume of other sandalwood ingredients makes them read more natural.
Classic macrocyclic ketone musk considered by some superior to muscone, enhancing diffusion, depth and longevity. Less powdery than Exaltone, with a smooth animalic-clean muskiness.

Nez names Vertonic as an IFF captive that fuses at the top of Nicolas Beaulieu's Speed Smelling 2022 composition, and in Delphine Lebeau's it supplies the freshness of detergent alongside an aqueous apple accord and soapy aldehydes. The documented character is therefore green and laundered-clean, a freshness used at the opening to knit the top notes together rather than to stand out. IFF publishes no structure, CAS or technical sheet for it.

Givaudan describes it as a floral, rosy, geraniol note with an elegant, fruity airiness, and calls it versatile, comforting and diffusive, giving perfumers a new perspective on petally radiance. The geraniol descriptor is a facet of its character rather than an identity, so it reads as the leafy-rosy side of a rose without the material's usual density. It is a Givaudan captive from the same floral trilogy as Rosabloom, developed in the Zurich and Shanghai research labs, and no CAS is published on the house page.
Phenolic antioxidant with a very faint waxy odor, used like BHT to retard oxidation of citrus oils and aldehydes in concentrates. Often combined with chelators for maximum shelf-life protection.
Penetrating, cooling medicinal note, dry and slightly minty-woody, instantly evocative of mothballs and tiger balm. Traces sharpen lavender, rosemary and spike accords; also cools mint compositions.

The definitive clean 'white musk': sweet, powdery, slightly woody-floral with a fresh laundered softness and enormous substantivity. Usually supplied at 50% in IPM or BB; can form a large percentage of a formula as a fixative bed.

Soft, velvety musk with a quiet fruity pear sweetness over a clean powdery body that reads as warm skin rather than laundry. An epoxide musk, unusual in a field of macrocyclics and polycyclics, used to round white florals and give a composition a linear, enveloping skin tail.
Modern rose-lychee petal effect: dewy, pink and slightly citrusy, with remarkable diffusion. The transparent rose of contemporary fine fragrance.
Cold-pressed Thai coconut carrier oil with a natural coconut odor. Used as an emollient base for massage-oil and roll-on perfume preparations.

Perfumer's Apprentice describes it as a "rich combination of natural ingredients that captures the warm, leathery and tobacco nuances of a rich black tea with hints of sweet gourmand notes". It is the brewed and dried leaf rather than a fresh green tea, so it reads warm and dry, with a tobacco-leaf facet that carries it well past the heart, and only a hint of sweetness underneath. The colorless grade is the practical point: it delivers that character into a pale juice without staining it, which the naturally dark tea materials will not do. Works as a warm dry anchor under fruit or spice, and against amber or woods.

Takasago describes it as giving volume and diffusion with a touch of muguet, sitting across floral, green, citrus and white-floral character. It is soft and bright on the strip and opens over hours into a muguet-cyclamen of real tenacity and diffusive power, with lily and magnolia edges; suppliers note it reads subtle on a blotter and only comes alive in a composition and on skin. In a formula it is the fixative half of the muguet pair, effective at low dose, with excellent substantivity on dry fabric, blending readily into most accords, and over five weeks of blotter life. Derived from renewable resources.

Medicinal phenolic bite with spicy cinnamon and a cooling wintergreen lift, sharper and far more austere than benzaldehyde. Traces give fougere, hay and heliotrope accords an antiseptic edge; overdose reads as disinfectant.

The dextro isomer leads with a citronella-green, geranium-like edge before the rosy petal body opens, over a waxy-oily base. Drier and coarser than the laevo form that dominates rose oil, so it suits geranium and functional rose work more than a fine rose heart.
Green-fruity ester of unripe banana peel and grassy character with waxy depth. Extends leafy green notes into the heart.

The waxy hydrocarbon extract of Acacia dealbata blossom, and the form most mimosa actually trades in: the same soft powdery-honey floral as the absolute, but heavier, fattier and blunted by its high wax load. Use it where the wax itself is wanted as a fixative, in solids and balms, or as stock for a home-washed absolute.

Green, fruity and floral. This diffusive specialty imbues any fragrance with the green, fruity, floral character of blackcurrant buds combined with the freshness of the boxwood shrub: tart juicy berry over crushed blackcurrant leaf, with a rosy edge that makes it read as floral as much as fruity. It is the reference cassis note and the standard stand-in for blackcurrant bud absolute, but it is potent and sharply sulphurous at the top, so it belongs in traces; overdosed it turns scented-candle. Firmenich now supply version 345F in its place, which is greener, cooler and tarter with a longer shelf life, so the two are not interchangeable in an existing formula.

Warm, spicy-woody rooty oil with a leathery, slightly cinnamic and earthy sweetness. Classic old-school fixative note for chypre, leather and amber compositions. Payan Bertrand's Korean calamus oil (steam-distilled rhizomes) is classified H317, H319 and H411, and its IFRA 51 certificate caps it at 0.447% of a fine fragrance: the oil carries 2.24% cis- and trans-asarone, a prohibited-as-such material allowed only as a trace inside a natural, plus 0.51% methyl eugenol, 0.58% thujone and 0.07% estragole, all with standards of their own. The declared allergens are linalool 2.19%, limonene 1.93%, citronellol 0.38%, geraniol 0.24%, citral 0.20%, isoeugenol 0.012%.

Givaudan describes Gyrane as a radiant green floral with spicy geranium aspects that supports the fresh green top notes of a fragrance, and classes it floral with geranium and green facets. It is an isomer mixture of butyl dimethyl dihydropyrans, also carrying CAS 24237-01-2 and 24237-02-3, and the house pairs it with Cyclal C, NeoFolione and cis-3-hexenol derivatives. In a formula it acts as a top-note amplifier more than a note in its own right: it widens a green accord, pushes a geranium or rose top outward, and holds up in alkaline media such as shampoo, fabric detergent and powders, with only medium substantivity on damp substrate.

Robertet describes fir balsam undertones under a fruity-blackcurrant top note, carrying what the house calls a strong pine trees forest headspace, over a balsamic dry-down. The vendor adds a second image for it: dried fallen leaves in autumn warmed by hot sunshine. In a formula it is a whole forest floor in one bottle, the co-extraction giving you the resin, the needles and the cedarwood body together rather than asking you to build them. Use it as the spine of a coniferous or fougere accord and let ordinary cedarwood sit behind it. Perfumers report it takes over a blend quickly, so it wants careful dosage, and the material thickens toward a gel with age, so warm it before weighing.

Steam-distilled tulsi (Ocimum sanctum), a sweet, pungent, clove-like green-herbaceous oil rich in eugenol with a warm balsamic-woody undertone and a lift of methyl chavicol. Adds spicy herbal warmth and a sacred, clove-basil character to aromatic, herbal and amber accords, dosed with care for its eugenol and estragole content.

Distilled from the wood rather than the berry: dry pencil-shaving wood over a green terpenic-resinous top, without the gin-like sparkle the berry oil is bought for. A quiet dry-woody body note for fougere, forest and masculine accords.

Perfumer's Apprentice lists the odour as floral, powdery, green and files it under the floral family, supplied as a light yellow solid. It is a reconstitution of orris butter, not the natural concrete, so it arrives as its own SKU weighed and diluted differently from a natural orris butter. In a formula it does the orris job: the powdery violet-root cushion that sits under a floral heart, softening aldehydes and rounding a woody or iris accord without the price or the batch drift of the natural.
Smooth, sweet, powdery polycyclic musk with a soft fruity-floral roundness, in the Galaxolide-Tonalide family but creamier. Historically used in high-impact functional perfumery.

Plantation-grown Santalum album from Western Australia: the true album santalol profile, creamy and milky-woody, but a touch drier and greener on top than Mysore and slightly less buttery in the drydown. Now the dominant legal supply of genuine album oil and the grade an independent perfumer can actually buy.

Sweet hawthorn-mimosa floral, more refined and less chemical than acetophenone, with coumarinic and slightly fruity nuances. Classic in mimosa, cassie and hawthorn reconstructions and powdery spring florals.
Bitter-orange leaf and twig: fresh, green, floral-woody with a soapy citrus cleanliness. The affordable backbone of colognes and fougeres.

Earthy pea-pod pyrazine with raw potato, galbanum and slightly nutty green facets; one of the most potent odorants known. Trace amounts lend earthy realism to vegetable-green, iris and vetiver themes.

The Good Scents Company records the odour at 100 percent as tropical fruity floral musk, and gives tropical as the odour type. It is a synthetic tercyclopentanol, C15H26O at molecular weight 222.37, offered by Zeon at 95 to 100 percent assay as a colourless to pale yellow liquid. Its published physical data, a boiling point near 338 C and a logP around 4.8 with water solubility of only about 2 mg/L, put it firmly in the heavy, low-volatility band, so it behaves as a substantive musk that sits under a composition rather than as a top note; that placement is read from the physical constants, not stated by the source. Not found in nature, and designated for fragrance use only, not for flavour.
Green, fruity-jasmine ester similar to verdyl acetate but sweeter, softer and more substantive. Cost-effective green-floral body for functional white florals.

A de Laire osmanthus signature built without a drop of osmanthus absolute. Round, soft facets of a velvety skin touch come from iris powder and violet flowers, over the smell of apricot flesh and juicy pear carried by the Symrise Pearadise captive, whose pear reads green, fresh and crisp. It was designed to hold only the flowery-fruity side of the little Chinese flower, deliberately leaving out the leathery facet that is essential to the natural absolute, so it lands brighter and cleaner than the extract and at a fraction of its cost. In a formula it works as the osmanthus itself in a heart, or as an apricot-skin roundness under tea, peach and violet accords.

Radiant, metallic-clean macrocyclic musk with a hot-iron, freshly laundered linen character and a slightly fruity glow. The signature of modern white-musk laundry accords; blends seamlessly with aldehydes and clean florals.

Rich balsamic-resinous frankincense with sweet-woody depth, a terpenic incense warmth and a light smoky facet. Very long-lasting and a strong fixative in incense, woody and amber accords. Alcohol-extracted absolute of Boswellia carterii gum from Somalia (Biolandes).

The benchmark sandalwood: soft, creamy, milky-woody and warm with a persistent balsamic sweetness. A precious fixative and heart-base note that lends roundness and skin-like warmth to florals, ambers and chypres.

Sharp camphoraceous-herbal greenness with a cool cineolic bite over a sweet hay-and-tobacco base; the chamazulene fraction gives the oil its ink-blue colour. Sits between blue tansy and German chamomile in herbal work and lends a bitter-green backbone to fougeres and aromatic hearts.

Givaudan describes Elintaal as having a natural and fresh muguet note with herbaceous undertones, and classes it floral / green / muguet. It is the ethoxyethyl acetal of linalool, 3-(1-ethoxyethoxy)-3,7-dimethylocta-1,6-diene, and the house rates it stable from acid cleaner through powder detergent, which is why it keeps its lily-of-the-valley freshness in media that flatten more reactive muguet materials. In a formula it builds the fresh white-floral heart of a soap, shampoo or fabric base at a low single-digit level, and its herbaceous edge lets it sit under green top notes without turning soapy-sweet.
Sharp, tart fruity note with buttery butterscotch facets; also serves as a mild solvent.

Sweet honey and pineapple with a chamomile-herbal freshness and a cocoa depth underneath, sharper and vastly more tenacious than the simple allyl fruit esters. A few tenths of a percent boost citrus and fruity tops and add body to chocolate and honey accords; IFRA restricts it, and like all allyl esters it needs free allyl alcohol below 0.1%.

Minty, herbal and eucalyptus-like, soft and slight rather than sharp: TGSC types it minty-herbal-eucalyptus, and Takasago describes a slightly minty material giving a fresh cooling sensation. The molecule occurs in lemon eucalyptus leaf. Its cooling profile is close to menthol but far more stable and much longer on skin, and it doubles as an insect repellent and a skin-penetration enhancer. Chosen over menthol when the cold effect has to survive a harsh base, and over the odourless coolants when a little green-minty character in the smell is welcome.

Solvent-extracted damask rose: deep, jammy, honeyed and slightly spicy rose, richer and darker than the otto with more phenethyl alcohol body. Gives immediate, opulent rose character to hearts and works beautifully with oud, saffron and patchouli.

Robertet describes it as floral, milky and honey, and characterises the product as a rich reconstitution of the tuberose note. The milky, lactonic side is what distinguishes it: it gives the fleshy, almost buttery petal quality of tuberose rather than the fruity-green side of the flower. Used as the tuberose heart itself, it also rounds and creams other white florals sitting alongside it. Flash point above 100 C. Applicable for a perfumery use only.

Firmenich calls it green, fruity, floral and extremely powerful, the purest expression of a classic green galbanum-type note with an amazing pineapple effect in fruity green accords. Its character is dose-dependent in a way few materials are: floral around 0.01 percent, green around 0.1 percent and fruity around 1 percent, so the same bottle does three different jobs depending on how hard it is pushed. It is the same molecule as Dynascone and Galbascone but made by a different synthesis route, and is reported greener, cleaner and less fruity than those, so it is weighed differently rather than swapped in one for one. Extremely diffusive, it holds well over 72 hours on a blotter and is typically dosed at trace level to give a green accord bloom.

A compounded vetiver speciality base rather than a single molecule. The Good Scents Company files it under vetiver specialty with the odour reading woody vetiver powdery at full strength, odour type woody, and Perflavory characterises the family as one of the iconic woody bases, very rich. In a formula it does the job a vetiver oil does without the raw material's variability: a dry, earthy-woody floor with a soft powdery lift that fixes and lengthens the base of chypres, fougeres and masculine woods. Vigon's documentation declares the CAS as MIXTURE and names geranyl acetone and nerolidol on the shipping papers, consistent with the green-woody smoothing those two give the vetiver body.

The supplier describes it as floral, green, indolic, with an orange blossom note, and very close to the original sambac flower scent. It is produced by solvent-free molecular distillation of Jasminum sambac concrete, and the house is explicit about why that matters: the process keeps the most volatile notes that are lost in the traditional conversion of concrete into absolute. The practical consequence is that it opens with the living flower rather than the jammy, tea-like heaviness an absolute leads with, while still carrying real indole underneath. In a formula it is the choice when a jasmine has to smell freshly picked at the top of a white floral, and it can be used alongside the absolute, which supplies the depth this one deliberately trades away.
The classic fine lavender: fresh, sweet-herbaceous and floral with soft woody-balsamic undertones. The backbone of fougeres and aromatic colognes, calmer and rounder than spike lavender.

Denser and sweeter than the distilled oil, with the rooty-earthy vetiver core wrapped in a balsamic, tobacco-like richness and a soft smoky drydown. A concentrated fixative for chypre and amber bases where the oil reads too dry and grapefruity.

Cool spearmint-like minty note with a camphoraceous herbal body, drying down sweet and woody with a light spicy, caraway-like edge. The chill is softer than menthol's. Lasts about 20 hours on a strip. p-Menth-8-en-2-ol, sold as a mixture of stereoisomers.
Camphoraceous-woody with a musty, slightly earthy nuance, cheaper and rougher than borneol. Functional camphor-woody note for pine and herbal accords.

Givaudan specialty with a transparent watery pear-skin note carrying pineapple and slightly metallic green nuances. Bridges fruity top notes into aquatic accords, giving juicy freshness without heaviness.

Aniseed and tarragon over a fruity licorice-cherry sweetness, softer and rounder than the methyl ester. Works in heliotrope, cherry and powdery balsamic bases where the anisic note has to stay edible rather than medicinal.
Extremely powerful, diffusive green pineapple with fruity-herbaceous galbanum freshness; typically supplied at 10% in DPG. Traces add remarkable modernity and lasting pineapple naturalness.
Fresh spicy-herbal note recalling basil, chamomile and sweet red bell pepper with a green aromatic lift. Adds crisp herbal freshness.
Warm herbaceous camphor-mint note, deeper than eucalyptol and less sharp than menthol, recalling dried herbs in a warm room. Adds old-fashioned aromatic warmth to fougeres.
Sweet hawthorn and mimosa floralcy with powdery anise, vanilla and slight honey facets. Indispensable in lilac, heliotrope, mimosa and hawthorn accords, and to sweeten fougeres and ambers.

Symrise gives the odour as fruity, dried fruit and brandy: a raisiny, boozy dried-fruit note rather than a fresh one. In a formula it underlines damascone-like aspects, provides brandy-like connotations and adds a natural fruity twist to floral notes, which makes it a cheap way to read damascone-adjacent without spending a rose ketone. It is the quietest material in this Symrise fruity set, with a published odour threshold in air of 0.7943 ug/l, so it works as body and not as a booster. Symrise recommends 0.1 to 5 percent.
Lush tropical plumeria: creamy-fruity white floral with apricot, coconut-suntan, honey and green-tea facets. Adds exotic solar warmth to tropical bouquets, tiare and ylang themes.
Fresh fruity-floral note with citrus and green nuances; a versatile rose-ketone family intermediate that lends bright fruity lift.

Pell Wall carries it as a Firmenich recreation of tuberose absolute: floral, dense, sweet and slightly bitter, very tenacious, radiant and characteristic of the flower.
