The house description is deliberately general on facets: Souroubea gives attractive new effects in floral bouquets, and provides richness and natural sophistication. What it does in a formula is documented more precisely than what it smells of, and it is described as useful across top, body and base notes, so it is used to enrich a bouquet throughout rather than to sit in one register.

The sesquiterpene that turns up wherever a green thing is also faintly fruity: apple skin, ginger, basil, the pith of a grapefruit. On its own it is soft and diffuse, more texture than statement, greening a top without the sharpness a leaf alcohol brings and leaving a dry herbaceous trail behind it. It holds at percentage rather than trace, which few greens tolerate. It oxidises, so keep it cold.
Medicinal, terpene-green freshness with earthy, slightly nutmeg-like terpinen-4-ol character. Mostly functional, but micro-doses can add a raw 'crushed leaf' medicinal realism to herbal accords.

Symrise's own datasheet gives the odour as citrus, rosy, waxy, cinnamon and coriander, and elsewhere the house calls it citrus-like and fruity-floral with rosy and cinnamon nuances. It is the mixed (E)/(Z) 3-methyl-5-phenylpent-2-enenitrile at min. 94 percent, a clear colourless to pale yellow liquid. The nitrile group is what earns it a place: unlike a citrus oil or an aldehyde it does not go sour or fade, so Symrise recommends it as the main ingredient for building stable citrus accords and to prolong citrus top notes, and it blends well into floral rosy and balsamic oriental directions where the waxy cinnamon facet gives the top a little body instead of a thin lemon flash.
Pungent sweaty-cheesy acid used in trace amounts for realism in animalic, leather and human-skin effects. Essential in minute doses for natural fruit and cheese nuances.

Deterpenated lemon: stripping the limonene bulk concentrates the citral-rich body, giving a rounder, fuller and far more tenacious lemon than the cold-pressed oil, with much better stability against oxidation. The workhorse for lemon that has to survive the first hour; dose against citral rather than against oil weight.

Sweet red-rose ester with a fruity honeyed body and a faint balsamic storax tail. The missing rung between PEA acetate and PEA butyrate, giving rose hearts fruit and honey without the acetate's jammy top.

IFF gives a fruity pineapple, peach and mango top note with amber and chocolate nuances; TGSC lists the odour at medium strength as "fruity amber chocolate anise basil". It is the isobutyrate of the same tricyclodecenyl alcohol that gives Cyclacet and Cyclaprop, and IFF notes it carries markedly less of their anise-basil edge. What separates it from ordinary fruity esters is persistence: TGSC publishes 344 hours on the blotter at 100%, so it works as a heart-note fruit that does not evaporate off the accord in the first hour.

Opens on a surprisingly bright, linalool-rich rosewood sparkle, then settles into a woody-amber heart and dries down to a leathery, pungent base. Built around Acetarolle, Mysoral and Myrrhone Neo. In a formula it is the rosewood-to-amber bridge: it gives a woody accord a lit top and a leather-amber floor at the same time, which is why it is used for masculine woods, oud-style effects and amber-woody hearts. The supplier's own caution is to keep it below the point where the pungent topnotes dominate and let the amber drydown do the talking.
Clean, cooling balsamic pine with cedarwood, sandalwood and sweet camphor nuances. A versatile blender-modifier from pine to rose accords; blends especially well with ionones.
The most lifelike damp-earth material next to geosmin; camphoraceous on top, opening into pure petrichor and decaying leaves in dilution. Roots florals in soil and naturalises compositions.

An intensely vibrant neon green experience featuring crisp creased leaves, ozonic air freshness, tropical fruit hints and subtle metallic-sulfuric facets, making a hyper-modern green accord. Fraterworks stresses that this is deliberately not another green base loaded with the usual cis-3-hexenol and its esters: it reads fruity, woody and tropical instead of herbal, and Mane's own show note calls it the crispness of bitter orange leaves freshly rubbed with ozonic fruity hints. It is built on an overdose of the Mane captive Bigarane. In a formula it is the green that stays legible against a modern clean-musk or aquatic structure, and the listing notes it carries no sensitising materials. Lasts more than 24 hours on a smelling strip.

A Givaudan captive launched 21 April 2023 into the Gaia collection. The house describes it as petrichor, the smell that comes from the ground when rain falls after a dry period, and says it brings green, earthy and watery tonalities to a fragrance. It is 100% biodegradable. In consumer testing 81% detected an after the rain effect in compositions carrying it at significant levels, so it is weighed as a real accord rather than a trace signature. In a formula it is the wet-soil bridge between a green top and a woody or mossy base, and it sits alongside Phytogaia, built around the forest tree, and Thalassogaia, built around the marine environment.

IFF high-cis methyl dihydrojasmonate: a transparent, radiant jasmine with a citrus lift, more petal and bloom than plain Hedione because the odour lives in the cis isomer. Used at high levels to give volume and natural bloom to floral and citrus accords rather than as a smell of its own.
Warm peppery-woody herbaceousness with earthy nutmeg and tea-tree facets. Naturalizes nutmeg, marjoram and herbal accords and adds body to lavender-spike notes.

Wintergreen: sweet, medicinal-phenolic and rooty with a warm balsamic body, present naturally in ylang and tuberose. Traces give authentic depth to ylang, tuberose and carnation; larger doses turn medicinal; IFRA-restricted.
Pungent rancid-butter and sharp cheese note that, at extreme dilution, gives creamy, buttery, fruity realism. A trace-level tool for butter, cheese, cream and realistic fruit accords.

Sweet candied strawberry with floral-jammy and slightly musty facets; despite the trade name it is a glycidate ester, not an aldehyde. The classic strawberry note of perfumery, used in fruity florals and gourmands.

LMR gives it as an aromatic and floral note with a clean fresh character, fruity nuances and a hay effect that altogether brings it closer to a lavender oil than to the lavandin it came from. It is the oil hydrodistilled and then fractionally distilled, and the cut is more elegant and markedly less camphoraceous than whole lavandin, with a pronounced coumarin profile that pushes it gourmand. In a formula it lets you place lavandin where the raw oil would have been too rough: it holds the fougere and aromatic function without the camphor spike, and its hay-coumarin tail hands over cleanly to tonka and amber bases. LMR Naturals, SIMPPAR 2026.
Sweet, green-floral salicylate close to isoamyl but slightly cleaner and more clover-like. Interchangeable workhorse for fougere and floral-salicylate sunshine effects.

The house describes it as the glamorous and roasting touch of mellow fragrances, the gourmand sensation of a sweet breakfast. In a formula it supplies a roasted coffee accord that darkens and warms a gourmand drydown, and it is the kind of building block used in small strokes because the roasted character reads loudly and will pull an accord toward the burnt side if overdosed.
The mixed alpha/beta sesquiterpene alcohols responsible for sandalwood's odor: creamy, milky, warm-woody and long-lasting. Used to boost or reconstruct natural sandalwood character.

Perfumer's Apprentice carry IFF's description as sweet, smooth, balsam, vanilla: a balsamic-vanillic resinous base with powdery amber undertones, built as a direct working substitute for Siam benzoin resinoid. In a formula it does the resin's job rather than imitating a single molecule, bringing sweetness, warmth and fixation underneath amber, oriental, gourmand and floral accords at 1 to 15% of the concentrate, with a blotter life past 400 hours. It is a compounded base sold as a mixture, so it carries no single CAS.

Evernia prunastri lichen absolute: profound forest-floor odor of damp earth, bark, seashore and ink with leathery-phenolic depth; the irreplaceable foundation of the chypre and fougere families. Strictly IFRA-restricted for atranol/chloroatranol - modern low-atranol qualities exist and should be specified.

Perfumer's Supply House describes it as a pleasant citrus accord that evokes freshly squeezed tangerine peel, blended with floral, marine notes that give it an unusual sparkling zest, with a fruity undertone reinforcing its natural character. It is remarkably diffusive and long-lasting, and holds up in functional bases where a real citrus oil would collapse. In a formula it works as a top and middle note that gives freshness and volume to citrus, floral and green accords, so it is the lift material rather than the citrus body: it buys sparkle and staying power at the top without the fading and the colour problems of an expressed tangerine oil.
Smooth, transparent, velvety woody-ambery note with a dry, slightly cedar-and-amber tone and a distinctive skin-like radiance and diffusion. One of perfumery's most ubiquitous woody-amber materials.
Delicate, honeyed green-floral absolute with soft muscat-wine and hay nuances. Gentle transparent floral for fresh, fruity-floral and cologne accords.

Weak vanilla with a fruity edge: TGSC types it simply vanilla-fruity, other suppliers calling it a faint vanillic, slightly acidic odour. The smell is not why it is bought. It is the warming counterpart to the Coolacts, a sensation felt immediately on application, building rapidly within about the first five minutes and holding for roughly two hours, and it also enhances the perceived cold of cooling agents dosed alongside it. In a formula it sits under a gourmand or amber base and warms it physically as well as olfactively.
Rosy-musky floral with a fresh petally smoothness. Bridges rose hearts into musky drydowns.

Powerful cooked-potato and vegetable-broth sulfur aldehyde with a creamy, faintly meaty body and a tomato-leaf edge. A trace molecule for savoury and gourmand accords; fleeting on the blotter and unpleasantly cabbage-like above a few ppm.

Perfumer's Apprentice list it in the floral family with the odour given as floral, soft, sweet, spicy, supplied as a colourless clear liquid carrying a mixture CAS. It is an IFF Oliffac speciality, the house's reconstitution line, usable from trace levels up to twenty percent of a compound, with a blotter tenacity given as 200 hours or more. In a formula it is a stable stand-in for ylang oil that keeps the soft, sweet, clove-spiced creaminess of the flower without the colour, viscosity and batch variation of the natural, and it holds through the heart far longer than the oil does.

Sweet balsamic cinnamate with a soft cocoa-powder warmth and an ambery drydown, heavier and far more tenacious than the methyl or ethyl esters. A quiet sweetener that stretches tolu, benzoin and cocoa accords without adding spice bite.

Sharp, juicy pineapple ketone with green pear and fresh apple facets, a slightly fatty green edge and a dry, dusty, fruit-skin note that makes pineapple accords read more natural. Bright and short-lived at the top. Mane's fermentation-made 9-decen-2-one.
Ultra-powerful blackcurrant-box tree thiol, green-sulfurous and catty with tropical guava facets. A ppm-level tool for realistic cassis, guava and sauvignon-blanc effects.

Standing, noble and extremely passionate, described by the house as the majestic touch within a daring perfumer's palette. It is woody and slightly spicy, and in a formula the base adds a powerful veil of darkness into oriental compositions. One of the seven finished branded bases in the BoldBases collection, which Moellhausen presents as a creative expression for creative perfume makers, so it is dosed as a single line item rather than built up from components.

Deep, sweet balsamic-ambery absolute from Cistus ladanifer gum with leathery, honeyed, dried-fruit and animalic undertones; the closest natural material to the smell of ambergris. Cornerstone of every classic amber accord (with benzoin and vanillin) and of chypre and leather bases.
Soft, sweet balsamic-solar salicylate with a subtle woody-amber warmth, very skin-like and diffusive. Modern fixative for solar white florals and suntan accords.

Givaudan's speciality base is listed green, herbaceous and vegetable, built from multidimensional analytical work to carry the smell of heated birch leaves and the Scandinavian sauna they belong to. The supplier positions it as an originality and freshness donor for back-to-nature themes: around 2% in a masculine cologne for a contemporary green lift, 2 to 3% in shampoo and beauty care for the herbaceous vegetable effect, and no more than a fifth of the compound overall. It is a base, not the tar: it reads as living leaf rather than the smoky birch tar distillates.
Fresh balsamic woody fir-needle oil with a clean coniferous character.

Also known as Dimethyl Octanol (3,7-dimethyl-1-octanol). A soft, sweet rose alcohol with minute fatty/aldehydic facets; stable and long-lasting, favoured for rose notes in functional and fine fragrance.
Stable, soapy-clean floral, linalool-like

Fresh clean citrus ester with bergamot and lime facets over a soft lavender-like body; the acetate of dihydromyrcenol, rounder and less metallic than the alcohol. Built for citrus tops in soap and detergent bases, and it carries lime notes that natural oils cannot hold.

Woody, green-citrus sesquiterpene with a sweet orange-peel character, subtle but persistent. Used to give citrus accords a natural woody drydown and as the precursor-cousin of nootkatone in grapefruit bases.
Strong musty roasted-nut character, hazelnut and toasted almond, with sweet hay-coumarin warmth and a softer coconut-milky undertone.

Balsamic-leathery resinoid from Liquidambar with a distinctive styrene-like, glue-cinnamon odor and sweet floral-lilac undertones. Essential in leather, incense and classic floral bases (hyacinth, lilac); IFRA-restricted, so dose carefully.

The signature molecule of orris root: dry, powdery iris with violet, woody and faintly waxy-carrot facets of exceptional refinement. Used sparingly to give true iris character where orris butter is too costly or too fatty.

Almost odorless crystalline coolant with only a faint minty trace; the effect is physiological cold, not smell. Longer-lasting and far less harsh than menthol, used to make aquatic, mint and fougere freshness felt on skin.
Woody-ambery ketone with a warm, dry, slightly floral-woody character used to smooth and extend woody accords. A supporting base note in woody and fougere compositions.

Sweet coconut-vanilla coumarinic note, creamier and more lactonic-gourmand than coumarin itself. Prohibited by IFRA for fragrance use due to photoallergy; its tonka, hay and dessert applications survive only in flavors.
Fruity-herbaceous apple and hay character from angelate esters, warm and slightly tea-like. Small doses add natural fruity-herbal complexity to lavender accords, tea notes and aromatic hearts.

Bitter green hop cone with a resinous myrcene-humulene body, a dry woody-beery undercurrent and a clear blackcurrant lift. Carries the gin and beer signature far better than the distilled oil, and earns its place in amber-herbal and green-woody accords wherever a genuine bitter edge is wanted.

Clean, warm macrocyclic musk with creamy, waxy and pronounced powdery elements over a dry woody, sandalwood-like facet. The same 16-membered lactones as Habanolide in a different isomer balance: softer and more diffuse, without its metallic hot-iron bite. Lasts about two weeks on a blotter.

The house describes it as juicy, young and fun, like biting a rich and tasty peach during summer, enriched by the notes of a flowery apricot. In a formula it is a narrow-profile building block that carries a ripe stone-fruit heart, giving a fruity accord flesh and a sunlit, slightly floral roundness without the flatness of a single lactone or ester used alone.

TGSC classifies 4,8-dimethyldeca-4,9-dienal (generic name magnolia decadienal) as floral, described as "floral aldehydic magnolia lily muguet" and as a concentrated fresh cyclamen floral note with intense power. The aldehyde carries the lift, but the impression is white-floral rather than soapy: magnolia and lily over a cyclamen freshness. Blotter life is given as greater than 48 hours at 100%, so unlike most floral aldehydes it holds through the heart and is used to give muguet, cyclamen and magnolia accords reach without adding weight.

A green, fruity note that evokes the odour of freshly crushed black-currant leaves. It gives freshness and diffusion to citrus and green accords, produces a grapefruit twist with a fresh vegetable effect, and offers excellent malodour coverage on base. Sold as 180/4. It is the crushed-leaf side of cassis rather than the berry, so it works as a top-note sharpener where a berry material would only sweeten.

Fresh, bitter-herbal and camphoraceous, opening with a light tangerine-lemon brightness over pine and wormwood, then settling into green herbaceous, slightly medicinal depth. For bitter herbal, fougere and chypre accords. Essential oil of Artemisia abrotanum (Egypt).

High-cis ambrettolide isomer considered the supreme form of this musk; closer to true ambrette seed and stronger than standard ambrettolide. Elevating, radiant macrocyclic musk with elegant sweetness.

Practically odorless phenolic antioxidant added at 0.05-0.1% to protect citrus terpenes, aldehydes and other oxidation-prone materials from degradation and discoloration. Standard stabilizer in fragrance concentrates and finished alcoholic perfumes.

Cherry and bitter almond over a soft sweet base, with a faint musty cherry-pit nuance; supplied as a mixture of the 1,3-dioxane and 1,3-dioxolane acetals. Far less volatile and far more stable to air than benzaldehyde itself, so it carries an almond-cherry note through soap, candles and long drydowns where free benzaldehyde would oxidise to benzoic acid.

Fraterworks 199662A, a compounded honey base combining French beeswax absolute and modern aroma materials. Honey sweetness with floral undertones. This is not Honey Absolute, Honey Provence FirAbs or Honey Signature. Supplier recommends a 10% working dilution and reports more than 400 hours on a smelling strip; the duration is only a lower bound. IFRA 51 Category 4 maximum is 5% in finished product. Several trace declarations conflict, so aggregate constituent review remains required.

Dry, warm peppery-woody terpene with an oily herbaceous body and faint terpenic citrus and pine edges; modest tenacity, gone from a strip in a few hours. A main source of the bite in black pepper, nutmeg and carrot seed oils. Bicyclic monoterpene, sold as a natural isolate.

Despite the name, the supplier describes it as a muguet note with nuances of anise and cyclamen, and calls it diffusive. It is a floral speciality base, not a mimosa base: the anisic facet gives the muguet a sweet-spicy edge and the diffusion means it pushes a floral heart outward, so it is dosed carefully rather than used as a bulk floraliser.

TGSC describes this dioxolane as "very strong, green, wet, earthy, fruity and radish-like, also reminiscent of chrysanthemum and gardenia", and recommends diluting to 10% or less merely to smell it. It is not the muguet floral aldehyde its trade name suggests; it is an acetal, and the effect is stem and crushed leaf rather than bloom. Blotter life is under 4 hours at 100%, so it is a top-note wetting agent: a trace gives white florals and gardenia accords the impression of a flower just cut, and overdose turns the whole formula to radish.
Intensely fruity, green-apple and unripe-fruit character with a sharp juicy lift; powerful in trace for apple and berry accords.

Fruity-rose ketone with a fresher, more apple-and-mint character than the beta isomer, plus blackcurrant and tea facets. Adds naturalistic rose-fruit sparkle to modern roses and fruity florals at trace levels.

Fresh, sweet menthol coolness with green herbaceous body and a slightly creamy-chocolate dryout in fine Mitcham qualities. Used in traces for cool lift in fougères and gourmet mint accords; IFRA-restricted for pulegone/menthofuran content.
Strong herbal-spicy saffron natural with leathery, honeyed and violet-narcissus facets. Authentic saffron signature for amber and leather accords.
Roasted and nutty thiophene aldehyde with sweet almond, cherry, woody and furfural-like bread facets. A trace material for baked, toasted and nut accords.
Crystalline woody sweetness with refined aged-cedar dryness and mellowed clove-pepper warmth. Connects spicy tops to woody bases in spice reconstructions.
Fresh, clean, piney-coniferous note with a soft camphoraceous woody character, brighter and more synthetic than bornyl acetate. A workhorse for pine, forest and functional accords.

A Givaudan speciality base listed as citrus, mandarin, grapefruit and yuzu over a juicy tropical fruit background. It combines the sweet-peel facets of mandarin and grapefruit with the dry, powerful character of Japanese yuzu, so it reads as a finished citrus top rather than a single peel oil. Supplied pre-diluted in triethyl citrate, which makes it easy to weigh and gives it a longer, less volatile citrus opening than a cold-pressed oil. In a formula it is the ready-made yuzu accord: dose it as the whole head note of a cologne or a fresh floral instead of building the citrus from separate zest materials.

The 50% cut of Galaxolide in isopropyl myristate, sold as its own article beside the neat material. IFF's description carried by Perfumer's Apprentice: a clean, powerful and versatile iso-chroman musk having exceptional persistence and a superb fragrance quality approaching the tone of macrocyclic musks. Supplier odour tags are musk, floral, woody, clean; ScenTree reads the musk itself as musky with berry and milky facets and calls it one of the freshest and headiest musks. It gives bloom, lift and longevity and holds a blotter past two days. IPM is an odourless, non-discolouring, skin-friendly carrier, so this grade is dosed straight from the bottle at roughly twice the weight of neat Galaxolide.

IFF's turnkey agarwood base, built from several of the house's own specialities. Perfumer's Apprentice describes it as balsamic, creamy and animalic, opening on the sweetness of tobacco and dried fruits, with animalic dark leathery middle notes and a slightly smoky, mossy base. Fraterworks traces the same arc: a sweet tobacco and dried-fruit top developing into a creamy-animalic dark leather heart, drying down to a resinous, incense-like smokiness over damp moss. A light brown liquid that holds for days on the strip. In a formula it delivers a complete oud effect at a few percent without a drop of real agarwood, and it is one of the more polite oud bases, so it sits under fruity-rose and spice accords rather than flattening them; the supplier suggests red-berry materials such as dulcinyl or raspberry ketone alongside it.

Velvety, warm macrocyclic ketone musk with a distinctly animalic, slightly powdery civet-like nuance and excellent tenacity. Adds plush skin-warmth to florals and ambers where a hint of dirtiness is welcome.

Floral, honey, indolic, rich, warm and jammy. Robertet calls it a powerful product and says it delivers a long-lasting orange flower note. It is the heavy, animalic reading of orange blossom rather than the fresh one: the indole and honey carry it deep into the drydown, which is what makes it worth reaching for over a neroli when a formula needs the flower to persist rather than sparkle. Being flagged powerful by the house, it wants a light hand and will dominate a white floral accord if dosed like an ordinary base.

Robertet's descriptors are animalic, powdery, scatol, leathery, powerful, and the house calls it a powerful and persistent floraline, its term for a reconstitution enriched with natural ingredients. The skatolic, faecal-warm core is wrapped in powder and soft leather rather than left raw, which is what makes it wearable. Robertet suggests it blends with agarwood bases and oriental accords; a trace animalises a floral heart and holds it for days, while a heavy hand takes over the whole formula. The house states it is applicable for perfumery use only.

Fresh green-floral ester with jasmine, cyclamen and slightly fruity-woody facets; extremely stable and substantive. A functional-perfumery staple that gives lasting green-jasmine freshness to soaps and detergents.

Zeon lists it as diffusive, sweet, noble jasmin, and its catalogue as very natural, diffusive, floral, sweet and reminiscent of natural jasmine petal; a retail listing describes it as a bright, transparent and completely ethereal jasmine breeze with some sparkling citrus. It is highly epimerised methyl jasmonate, carrying roughly five times the epi-isomer of JASMONEIGE, and Zeon's own claim is that the epi-isomer's threshold is well under a thousandth of the other isomer's, so a very small dose does the work. In a formula it is used as the noble lift inside a jasmin base and the other white florals, lily of the valley, gardenia and honeysuckle, adding petal realism, radiance and lasting warmth under the top rather than a jasmine note of its own. Treat it as distinct from ordinary methyl jasmonate: the epimerised grade is dosed far lower for the same effect.

Sharp, green-fruity gardenia note with rhubarb, earthy-mushroom and slightly solvent facets; the unmistakable signature of gardenia petals. Essential to gardenia and tuberose accords and a daring green flash in rose and chypre tops.

Violently catty and sulfurous neat, opening into blackcurrant bud, boxwood and broom at ppb dilution. The backbone of cassis and Sauvignon Blanc accords and the material widely known as cat ketone; dose at ppb, because anything above a trace reads as cat urine rather than fruit.

Carbon dioxide extract of dulse, the red Atlantic seaweed, and a cleaner reading of the sea than the Fucus absolute we also carry: none of the solvent drag, none of the sulphur. Salt and wet mineral first, then a savoury depth that sits oddly close to food, and a long mossy tail that keeps it in the base. Where a synthetic marine note gives you the idea of an ocean, this gives you a particular shoreline. Strong enough that a trace does the work.

Symrise gives Citrus, Grapefruit, Clary Sage, Grape; The Good Scents Company files it as herbal and reads it as sweet herbal clary sage bergamot petitgrain tropical citrus. It is a fresh green citrus-herbal top with a peony-like floral edge and the fruity bite of grapefruit peel and clary sage oil. In a formula it gives citrus aldehydic accords a sparkling champagne lift and builds a very natural clary sage impression in fougeres; Symrise calls it a multifaceted booster from top to heart at 0.5 to 10 percent. Blotter life is short, under an hour by Perfumer's Apprentice's measure.

Musty nut-skin and walnut with bready, coumarinic and faint licorice-cherry shading, weak and diffuse rather than sharp. Rounds the roasted pyrazine and thiazole palette from underneath, filling in the nut-skin and baked-crust body those trace-level materials leave hollow.
Sweet nutty-coconut lactone with caramel and hay nuances, bridging gourmand and fruity territory. Used in coconut, tobacco and dried-fruit accords for creamy sweetness.

Indian frankincense with a distinctive fresh, green-limey and slightly fruity terpenic profile (alpha-thujene rich), lighter and sharper than carterii/sacra qualities. Good economical incense top note with a clean resinous drydown.

Perfumer Supply House, on the Robertet product: "This specialty blend of natural aroma chemicals is a fruity accord that captures the juicy and sweetness of a freshly ripened apricot." The character is lactonic and warm rather than fresh, the soft velvet side of stone fruit, so it holds into the drydown where a fresh-fruit top would already be gone. Dose it as the fruit inside a floral or a gourmand, where a single lactone on its own would read synthetic.

Mild sweet floral-balsamic jasmine with a waxy balsamic softness, quieter and rounder than amyl cinnamic aldehyde. The alcohol partner to that aldehyde, chosen when the aldehyde's discoloration and reactivity in soap or alkaline bases cannot be tolerated; an IFRA-restricted allergen in its own right.

dsm-firmenich place it in the Ambery family and give the odour as amber, dry, woody, leather, animal and smoky. It is a well balanced association of ingredients, some of which are captives, blended to reconstruct the complexity of natural ambergris with no animal extract, and it ships as a thick brown to dark brown viscous liquid that can set solid when cold. In a formula it behaves as a whole base-note structure rather than one effect: it brings warmth, depth and diffusion to ambery orientals, spicy fougeres and rich chypres, and it is more even and more structured than a natural tincture, so it adds depth without taking the composition over.
Watery-fruity note of apple, pineapple and berry with a fresh, slightly floral transparency. A smooth, stable fruity heart material for juicy modern accords.
Green stem-like flower-shop note, watery and sappy, evoking cut stems and outdoor freshness. Sold as a 50% dilution; gives natural cortex lift to floral, hyacinth and green accords.

Warm herbaceous bay with basil and rosemary facets, medicinally sweet, over a crushed-cardamom undertone and a green tobacco tail. The camphor that dominates laurel leaf oil is almost absent here, leaving a tenacious base-note herb for fougeres, chypres and tobacco accords.

Schiff base of hydroxycitronellal and methyl anthranilate: sweet, long-lasting orange blossom-muguet with honeyed grape and mimosa facets and an amber-orange color. The most used Schiff base in perfumery, fixing white-floral themes for hours.
Fresh green, fruity note with herbal-leafy facets. Adds a natural green-fruity character to florals and fruits.
Sweet floral-bergamot ester, fruitier and rounder than linalyl acetate with pear-like nuances. Bergamot, lavender and clary sage accords.
Fresh camphoraceous-spicy bay leaf with cineole, clove and slightly medicinal facets. Gives aromatic culinary lift to fougères, bay rum and Mediterranean-themed compositions.

A supercritical CO2 capture of real gingerbread, baked from a recipe prepared by a baker, extracted cold so the molecular complexity survives. It holds not only the smell of the ingredients but the Maillard reactions of the oven itself, which is why it carries the aroma of baked sugar and butter and is described as close to reality. Until this existed a perfumer could only reconstitute the note by assembling ginger, vanilla and tonka into an accord; here the whole pastry arrives as one material, warm, honeyed and comforting, to sit in the heart of a gourmand and give it an oven-warm centre a built accord never quite reaches.
Soft lilac with powdery sweetness, floral nectar and jasmine-rose depth. Intended for lilac effects and classical muguet, hyacinth and lilac bouquets.

Symrise gives the odour as green, vegetable-green, green bell pepper, asparagus and rooty. It is sold as a fragrance booster: highly diffusive and extremely substantive, typical for petitgrain, galbanum, vetiver and patchouli compositions, and it achieves a crisp and radiant effect in green fruits. It also keeps its olfactory character in bleach, which is why it survives in functional bases. It is dosed out of a 1 percent solution, at 0.001 to 5 percent of that solution, so the working amount in a concentrate is a trace.

Warm ginger-spiced grass: a fatty-sweet herbal body over green hay, lifted by rosy geranium nuances and closing dry, woody and lightly peppery. The scruffier, cheaper cousin of palmarosa, useful where palmarosa's clean rose reads too polite.

Crystalline Symrise powerhouse with an extremely powerful, sharp woody-amber note of metallic, cedar-like dryness and week-long tenacity. Defines the loud 'woody-amber' accord of contemporary masculines; dose in traces from a 10% or 1% solution.

Soft powdery-honeyed floral of Acacia dealbata blossom with green stem, cucumber-watery, waxy and hay-like beeswax facets. Gives tender powdery naturalness to violet, heliotrope and spring-floral accords.
Sweet fruity-plum note with dried prune, floral and slightly woody facets. Key material for plum, damson and osmanthus accords.

Dry, oud-like woody amide with a vetiver tone, a grapefruit, nootkatone-type brightness on top, a touch of spice and a faint animalic shadow. Tenacious: the original patent reports over 24 hours on a strip, Fraterworks over 96. N-Ethyl-N-(3-methylphenyl)propanamide.

Fresh green violet-leaf note with vibrant fruity pear and galbanum-like facets, cleaner and more stable than the acetylenic carbonates. Modern replacer for violet leaf effects in fine fragrance and functional perfumery.
A contemporary iris-flower accord with a fresh, clean floral character, interpreting the flower's delicate scent. A formulated base rather than natural orris root extract or iris butter.

Mild, fresh lemon-citral note with a green, slightly earthy nuance, far more stable than citral in alkaline media. Used for lemon freshness in soaps and functional bases where citral would discolor or fade.

Absolute pulled from the waters left when bitter-orange twigs and leaves are distilled for petitgrain: deep bitter green, true to a leaf torn off the tree, with a musty hay warmth, a faint smoky edge and only a ghost of orange-flower sweetness underneath. It bridges petitgrain and orange blossom, and a trace lends real-flower naturalness to neroli, jasmine and gardenia accords.
Warm, earthy-spicy and woody with a fresh gingery-carrot top and a soft, curry-like turmerone body. Adds exotic golden warmth to spicy-woody ambers and modern gourmand-spice accords.
Juicy nectarine-peach fruity note with tropical undertones. Modern fruity booster for lush fruity-floral compositions.

Floral and green, but also opulent orange flower notes. Robertet offers it explicitly as a substitution for jasmine sambac absolute on price to quality ratio, which sets its job in a formula: it takes the sambac slot at a fraction of the absolute's cost while keeping the green facet that separates sambac from grandiflorum. The orange flower character means it also cross-reads into neroli and white floral accords rather than sitting only in jasmine.

Sweet fruity balsam with a musty-powdery middle; lighter and more volatile than isoamyl benzoate. A cheap volume material for ylang and tuberose reconstructions, where it adds sweet balsamic bulk and helps solubilize crystalline florals.
Fresh woody needle oil with citrus brightness, nectar-like sweetness and a radiant character. Steam-distilled in New Zealand from the needles and twigs of Pseudotsuga menziesii.

Sesquiterpene sold as the gamma isomer, and it smells of the balsams rather than of wood: opopanax and myrrh, warm and softly spicy, with orange-blossom sweetness above and a thin fruit-peel edge below. A material for giving a resinous accord body without the smoke a real resinoid brings.

Low-odor glycol solvent with a faint sweetish note, used to solubilize fragrance into water-based and surfactant systems (room sprays, cleaners, wipes). Better coupling ability than DPG in aqueous media.
Deeper, warmer and more powerful than the alpha isomer, contributing the rich creamy body of natural sandalwood. Highly prized in sandalwood reconstructions.

Firmenich's own marketing sheet files it under balsamic and gives the olfactive description as coumarin, lactonic, tonka and phenolic with a very natural tobacco effect; The Good Scents Company adds sweet tonka bean with a tropical coconut lactonic tone. In a formula it replaces or enhances coumarin, and because the sheet calls its strength overpowering it is dosed about ten times below coumarin, which is why the house sells it only as this 10% triethyl citrate solution. It sits as a heart-and-base sweetener that lasts about a week on a smelling strip and is more stable than coumarin in detergent.

IFF specialty with a dry ambergris-tobacco odor, slightly woody and rooty, evoking the drier facets of ambergris tincture. Useful in tobacco-amber accords and to add naturalness to ambroxide-based bases.

IFF calls it a powerful floral muguet note with a fresh green, aquatic naturalcy that gives distinct floralcy by significantly increasing the body of a fragrance; the fuller descriptor set is green, marine and fruity with fresh-floral, watery, juicy and aldehydic nuances. Impact is highest in the top with medium heart and base impact, and substantivity runs beyond 48 hours, so it opens a formula wet and keeps a muguet transparency behind it. It is used to build transparent fresh, cyclamen and muguet florals with a watery feel, typically up to a few percent of the concentrate.

Perfumer Supply House describes it as a sweet, heavy, narcotic green floral with fruity and herbaceous aspects, also honey-like and animalic, reminiscent of daffodils, jasmine and tuberose. Suppliers carrying the same Firmenich base report a sharp green, snapped-stem opening that settles into a narcotic white-floral heart where narcissus meets jasmine and tuberose, then dries down honeyed and faintly animalic with a mossy, chypre-like cast. In a formula it is the floral heart itself: it will carry a narcissus soliflore on its own, adds narcotic weight and tenacity to orientals and chypres, and pairs naturally with coumarin in fougeres through its hay-like facet.
Strong narcotic floral with mothball/naphthalene, erogenic-animalic and jasmine facets; less fecal than indole, good for gardenia, orange-flower, narcissus and cassie.

Givaudan describes a floral jasmine note with a rich sweet herbaceous character and hints of tea. Against the standard grade the house calls Forte a broader-cut, lower cost option that is slightly more tenacious and has a more pronounced green mushroom facet, so it sits deeper and greener under a jasmine accord than the regular cut and holds longer. It is a body material rather than a lift: it fills the herbaceous-tea middle of white florals and carries well in functional bases, where Givaudan rates it strongly for burning performance and stable across most pH conditions in liquid detergents, fabric conditioners and all-purpose cleaners.

The Good Scents Company gives the odour type as floral at medium strength: floral, heliotrope, tropical, mimosa, berry and green, noting that it is bright and penetrating with sweet mimosa and apple-seed undertones. Ventos records it as floral-sweet, heliotrope, mimosa and powdery with green nuances. The molecule is p-methyl-alpha-amyl cinnamaldehyde, a ring-methylated relative of amyl cinnamic aldehyde, and that added methyl steers it away from jasmine and toward powdery mimosa and heliotrope. Blotter life is over 48 hours, so it behaves as a floral fixative as much as a floral: it holds a mimosa or heliotrope accord together deep into the drydown and lends powder and body to florals that would otherwise thin out.
Sweet apple-pear note with a distinctive jammy, slightly earthy-woody chamomile nuance, smooth and rounded. A stable fruity heart material for apple accords in fine and functional perfumery.

Sweet dried-raspberry ketone with rose, cherry and a cassie-mimosa floral undertone; the methyl ether of raspberry ketone, sweeter and less phenolic than the parent. Adds jammy berry depth to rose, cassie and mimosa bases and rounds fruity-floral accords.

Herbal anise sweetness with a hawthorn-balsamic body and a soft powdery tail. The missing partner to anisyl acetate and anisyl alcohol, useful wherever a hawthorn or heliotrope accord needs anisic backbone without anisaldehyde's punch.

Floral, fresh, magnolia. A soft, full floral for use in any floral perfume or magnolia accord: a luminous white-floral body with a green nuance and the citrusy, slightly lemony accent typical of a magnolia flower on the branch, settling into a delicate honeyed sweetness. It is the shortest route to a convincing magnolia in a formula, and because it is a compounded base rather than a single molecule it also rounds and lifts other white florals, giving jasmine or ylang the fresh living top that a soliflore built from single materials usually lacks.
Fine fruity ester: pineapple and sweet apple with passion fruit, woodruff and strawberry nuances.

Honey, sweet, edible, diffusive and powerful. A FirAbs co-extraction whose natural part is cera alba, beeswax and honeycomb collected from beekeepers in the Var, Drome, Hautes-Alpes, Alpes Maritimes and Vaucluse, extracted together with synthetic ingredients including captives. Firmenich call it incredibly gourmand and flavour-like, yummy rather than animalic, which is the distinction from a honey absolute: there is no urinous or barnyard edge to manage. The beeswax fraction is what makes it read as real, and users report a faint sweet tobacco nuance alongside. It is extremely potent, with experienced users reporting that a quarter of a percent will overtake a blend and half a percent will dominate it, so it is a trace material. Reports on its persistence differ, some finding it fleeting and others that it runs well into the drydown.
Fresh green aldehyde with a bright open-air character, a cool dewy greenness and a light waxy-citrus edge. Lifts muguet, lilac and freesia and adds a cool sheen to woody bases.

Sweet, soft balsamic ester with honey, cocoa and warm resinous nuances; a major constituent of Peru and Tolu balsams. Quiet but valuable fixative that smooths amber and heavy floral bases; listed as an allergen and IFRA-restricted.

A soft, ethereal fruit ester: fresh grape skin and green apple peel with a winey, faintly pineapple-tropical lift, juicier and quieter than the plain butyrates. Ethyl 3-hydroxybutanoate, a hydroxy ester reported in grape, wine and passion fruit.

Roasted cocoa and toasted nut with a dry medicinal-earthy edge and a roast-beef savoury nuance. The most used of the three dimethylpyrazine isomers, working in traces to give cocoa, coffee and praline accords their roasted backbone.

Damp forest-floor woodiness: vetiver-like and mossy, with weedy green-herbaceous, lightly leathery and almost salty facets and a faint earthy, potato-like nuance. Used below about 2% for moss and refined leather effects, as an alternative to isobutyl quinoline. 2-tert-Butyl-1,4-dimethoxybenzene.

Extremely powerful oily-fatty green aldehyde that turns creamy, milky and dairy-like on dilution, reading as warm butter or biscuit at trace. The standard route to lactonic and milky effects in gourmand accords; anything above a trace turns fishy and rancid.

Hydroabietyl alcohol: a colorless, tacky, almost odorless resin alcohol used as a high-grade fixative and plasticizer with a barely-there balsamic tone. Extends drydown longevity and improves substantivity on fabric.

CO2 extract of the fermented South African bush tea, sweet in a dried-plant way rather than a floral one: honey and black tea at the top with an almost liqueur-like fermented edge, violet and berry through the middle, cured hay and vanilla underneath. A bridge between tea, hay and honey accords rather than a lead. Not rooibos, which is the neighbouring bush and a woodier, tobacco-ish thing.

Odorless, water-miscible glycol carrier used for water-compatible fragrance dilutions, cosmetics and some flavor work. Less universal for aroma chemicals than DPG (limited solvency for very nonpolar materials) but ideal where water miscibility is needed.
Explosive fresh-brewed coffee aroma at extreme dilution, becoming sulfurous, burnt and rubbery when overdosed. The character-impact molecule of roasted coffee, used only in ultra-trace amounts.

Firmenich's own supercritical CO2 extract of elemi gum (939865), described as spicy, peppery, lemony: a fresh top note with a green facet over a bottom note that evokes frankincense and pink peppercorn. Extraction at low temperature and pressure preserves the natural profile of the raw gum, so it is cleaner, more vertical and more faithful to the resin than the steam-distilled oil, with more depth behind the lemon. Firmenich position it to add a fresh note to woody, spicy and zesty perfumes, mainly masculine ones; it pairs naturally with pink pepper, cardamom and olibanum for a resinous spice opening.

Sweet rosy-floral ester with a peach-apricot fruitiness, sweeter and less acid than geranyl acetate and far less prone to turning sour on storage. Common in rose and geranium reconstructions, and it warms chypre, fougere and lavender bases.
Sweet, heavy orange blossom-pineapple ether, fruitier and rounder than yara yara with acacia-honey warmth. Persistent fixative-floralizer for orange blossom, mimosa and tropical soap accords.
Fresh-cut-flower impression with pronounced floral-iris qualities and green foliage aspects. Freshens violet, orris and mixed floral compositions.

Fresh green with a tart granny-smith apple core, pear flesh and a snow-pea vegetal nuance. Rounder and more fruit-forward than the isobutyrate and without the tea-dry facet of the tiglate, so it suits crisp apple, pear and green fruity-floral tops.

The Good Scents Company records a strong jasmone odour with a hint of parsley which gives a jasmin absolute connotation; IFF's own line is a good jasmin note that is extremely rich and stable. It is a body material rather than a top effect, used to build reconstituted jasmin, tuberose and gardenia, where it adds creamy lactonic petal weight and a green herbaceous edge that keeps the accord from going flat. Exceptionally substantive, 356 hours measured neat on the blotter, and used up to 10 percent of the concentrate.

Robertet publishes it as "Floral, rosy, less spicier but closer to the rose petal than the initial absolute", a fractionally distilled Turkish Rosa damascena absolute whose methyl eugenol has been cut back. Taking that constituent down is exactly what removes the clove-spice edge and leaves the petal, so it reads softer and more transparent than an ordinary rose absolute. Use it where you want real absolute depth in a rose accord without the spicy-phenolic weight the standard grade drags in, and where the restricted constituent in ordinary rose absolute is what caps your dosage.
Fresh waxy-citrus aldehyde with green mandarin-peel, slightly floral and clean fatty facets. Naturalizes citrus tops and adds a modern transparent aldehydic lift to colognes and florals.

Kao describes it as fruity, pear-like natural, with the descriptor triad Fruity - Green - Pear. The house's emphasis is on the natural reading rather than the intensity: a rounded, juicy pear with a green stalk edge instead of the sharp solvent-like pear of the simpler acetates. In a formula it is the pear itself, a top-note fruit that gives a fresh floral or a gourmand accord an edible opening, and its green side keeps it from collapsing into candy the way a pure ester pear does.
Buttery, creamy material with caramel and toffee sweetness, toasted nut nuances and subtle fruitiness. Its dairy character supports custard, butter-cream and baked-goods accords.

Grape-like anthranilate: sweet, deep and fruity with a floral berry nuance and only a faint orange-flower undertone. Warmer and rounder than methyl anthranilate, and it lends tenacity and richness rather than pungency. A modifier for jasmine, neroli and orange-blossom bases, and the anthranilate of choice when a grape-petitgrain lift is wanted without methyl anthranilate's musty bite.

Symrise gives the odour as balsamic, tonka and orange flower, and files the material under balsamic. In a formula it provides a soothing, powdery richness to floriental fragrances, underlines typical heliotrope characteristics, and adds balsamic aspects to fruit notes like grape and plum. The published odour threshold in air is 0.0050 ug/l, but it is dosed generously by the standards of that figure, which tells you it blends rather than dominates. It ships as white to beige crystals and needs dissolving. Symrise recommends 0.1 to 5 percent. Note the name carefully: this is benzofuran-2-yl methyl ketone, not the plain benzofuran that the word coumarone usually denotes, and it is not coumarin either.

Symrise gives the odour as animalic, floral, civet and leather, and files the material under animalic. It is a crystalline acetal sold as a key component for white flower notes and as a less discoloring alternative for skatole and indole, which is its practical point: it brings the indolic, slightly dirty depth that jasmine, tuberose and orange blossom need, without the yellowing those two cause in a finished product. The published odour threshold in air is 0.0063 ug/l. It ships as pale white to white crystals, so it has to be dissolved before use. Symrise recommends traces up to 1 percent.
Sweet chewing-gum mint dominated by l-carvone, warmer and less icy than peppermint with a green herbaceous edge. Small doses freshen fougère topnotes and pair beautifully with lavender and patchouli.
Elegant orris-woody note with nuances of tobacco, leather and animalic warmth; low in profile but profound and long lasting. Harmonises woody, orris and leather accords, beautiful with Cashmeran.

Symrise gives the odour as fruity, floral, plum, rose and tobacco; The Good Scents Company records the same profile at 10 percent in dipropylene glycol and rates the odour strength high. In a formula it blends well with rose ketones, lends power and body to floral-fruity creations, and implements tobacco-like aspects in oriental compositions. The published odour threshold in air is 0.0008 ug/l, so it behaves like the rose ketone it is: dosed low, and dominant if it is not. Symrise recommends 0.1 to 2 percent.

A faint fatty-waxy, petal-like ester with soft honey and orris nuances; it lends a lipid smoothness to iris, violet, mimosa and tuberose bases rather than a scent of its own. Methyl tetradecanoate, reported in champaca absolute and violet root.

Fresh green with a rum-like winey lift over ripe pear and apricot, closing on a dry woody-waxy nuance. The C7 step between hexyl and octyl acetate, useful where the pear needs a boozy edge rather than a clean fruity one.

Tahitian vanilla absolute: sweet vanilla lifted by a distinctly anisic-floral, heliotrope-almond character from the anisyl compounds that dominate its volatiles, where Bourbon planifolia is phenolic, rummy and dark. A different species (Vanilla x tahitensis), priced above planifolia and used where the vanilla should read floral and powdery rather than balsamic.

UV stabilizer with a delicate rose-geranium odor, historically added to protect perfumes and soaps from light-induced discoloration while contributing mild fixation. Regulatory pressure has curtailed its use; check current restrictions before formulating.

Symrise gives it as Citrus, Lime, Fruity; Perfumer's Apprentice lists it as Citrus, Lime, Herbal. It is acid-isomerized citral, so it smells of a fresh, sparkling lime top with a soft floral shade underneath, cleaner and less lemon-candy than plain citral. In a formula it is a lime top-note booster and the working note for natural lemon and lime accords, and it also lifts coniferous and pine directions. Symrise's stated use level is a wide 0.1 to 20 percent.

DSM-Firmenich's modern freshwater note: sweet, watery, transparent floral with light fruity nuances, like a softer, cleaner Calone without the oyster facet. Readily biodegradable and easy to formulate; 0.1-0.2% already gives a convincing cascade-water transparency.

Sharp green vegetal thiazole that smells of tomato stem and vine rather than ripe tomato, with sulfurous, earthy and faintly metallic facets. The tomato-leaf molecule and a fine fragrance staple: trace levels build green tomato, fig-leaf and galbanum-adjacent accords and sharpen the top of green florals.

Green leafy violet-leaf ester with a mild fatty, faintly oxidized-nutty nuance and a cucumber-apple edge. Slower and rounder than nonadienol or nonadienal: use it where the violet leaf trio needs to hold into the heart instead of flashing off, in green florals, cucumber and melon accords.
Soft vanilla with milky, creamy, powdery and caramel facets. A smoother vanilla modifier than a blunt ethyl-vanillin effect.
High-end sandalwood molecule, soft, warm, creamy and milky with excellent tenacity and a very natural feel. Used to lend refined sandalwood richness in fine fragrance.

Solvent-extracted oud keeping the smoky-woody depth of the distilled oil but with a smoother, sweeter balsamic-honeyed body and far less barnyard bite. Easier to dose and far cheaper per drop than the distilled oil, which makes it the practical oud base for indie work.

Bedoukian describes a powerful green note with a strong floral character and honey undertones, aimed at gourmand and green-floral work and at hyacinth in particular. TGSC reads it neat as sweet green honey fruity hyacinth with papaya, guava and pineapple, and at high dilution as sharp, sweet green, fresh, fruity apple and pear with a slight floral nuance; strength is rated medium and blotter life is a little over an hour. In a formula it puts a wet honeyed stem under a hyacinth or white floral accord and keeps a fruity top from reading candied, working as a top-note lift rather than a body note.
Sweet floral ether with hyacinth, lilac and slightly medicinal green facets. Classic for lilac and white floral bases.

Nepalese high-altitude leaf and flower oil: fresh pine-resinous green with a balsamic sweetness and an unexpected fruity-floral lift on top. A distinctive natural for conifer, incense and herbal-green accords where pine needle oil alone smells flat.
Intense, powerful synthetic sandalwood with a rich, warm, natural creamy-milky character and subtle musky facets; far stronger than the natural oil. A workhorse for modern sandalwood accords.

Advanced Biotech gives the same two-word odour as for Green Note Natural, green and leafy, on a colourless to pale yellow liquid, but the rest of the sheet separates the two clearly. This one is declared in the EU as a natural flavouring substance, meaning a defined material rather than a preparation, it carries no ethanol dilution, its specific gravity is higher at 0.880 to 0.910 and its flash point is 57 C against the other's 24 C. In practice that makes it the concentrated leaf note: less volatile, more persistent and considerably stronger in the hand than the ethanol-carried Green Note. Its name states its job, which is to be added at trace to sharpen an existing green rather than to be the green itself, and at anything above a trace it takes over and turns an accord into cut grass. Work it dilute and treat it as a lift, not a body.

Givaudan describe it as a rich, warm, economical rose with all the fresh, natural character of a rose blossom, its olfactive structure resembling that of natural Turkish rose oil. Suppliers give the profile in decreasing order as floral-rose, fresh, sweet, with a waxy petal edge. In a formula it blends into all types of composition, enriching and underlining the floral bouquet character rather than dominating it, and it is very long-lasting, performing especially well in agarbatti; typical use runs from about 1% up to 20% of the concentrate. The current material is the revised version, reformulated after Lyral was withdrawn from cosmetic use.

A high impact bicyclic ester (Firmenich) with a fresh herbal green profile of rosemary and crisp basil over ripe pineapple, banana and blackcurrant bud, closing with a faint warm estragole spice. Powerful and tenacious, it works as a fruity-green top note booster in citrus, tropical, herbal and fougere compositions.

Intense, diffusive herbal-green ketone with a thujone-like, sage and wormwood bite, a cool minty-camphoraceous edge, a leafy green close to the alkyne carbonates and a tropical-fruit nuance. Very powerful; used in small amounts in aromatic, ambery-woody and herbal accords. A tricyclic undecenone once made by Firmenich.

Named after an orchid native to Borneo, Givaudan's specialties brochure describes it as having a delicate scent similar to lily-of-the-valley with a touch of privet and watermelon. The brochure places it in floral, fresh, transparent and aqueous accords of the eau fraiche type. In a formula it works as a ready muguet heart with a green, watery-fruity lift, giving a transparent floral its shape without the sweetness or weight a heavier muguet accord brings.

Nutty roasted oxazole with toasted Dutched cocoa and nut-skin body over a roasted-vegetative, slightly pyridine-like green background. The oxazole counterpart to trimethylthiazole, drier and less sulfurous than it, with a 5 ppb threshold: trace levels build cocoa, coffee and toasted-bread accords.

The industry standard dried plum base from Firmenich, printed under FRUITY in the house catalogue as code 975617. It presents a powerful, complex note of ripe plums with dried fruit sweetness, a smooth velvety texture and subtle coconut nuances. In a formula it adds velvet fruit texture to fine fragrance and builds rich gourmand and oriental accords; small amounts contribute a gentle sweetness while overdoses work very well in a modern gourmand context. It blends well with the rose ketones and other fruit bases and makes particularly beautiful accords with patchouli. It has withstood the test of time, featuring in classics such as the original Dior Poison and Chanel Egoiste, and holds more than a day on a blotter.

PFW's odour description, as carried by Perfumer's Apprentice, is dry, woody, labdanum, rose, musk, orange flower, and the supplier files it in the wood family. The reading is a dry woody-labdanum core with a rose inflection, sitting over a musky orange-flower softness. In a formula it behaves as a dry ambery-woody base note that lends labdanum warmth without the sticky resinous weight of a labdanum absolute, and its musk and orange-flower side lets it sit under florals and smooth a rose or neroli accord from below. The supplier recommends assessing it in a 10 percent solution or less, so it is not a material to smell neat on a blotter.
Sharp, fresh, camphoraceous-herbaceous coniferous oil with a strong thujone-driven green-woody bite. Used in trace for forest, herbal and functional pine accords.

The house describes it as expressing the whole richness of the flower, the sensuality of its plump petals, reproducing the inebriating, unique and powerful scent of gardenia. In a formula it is a ready-made white floral heart, standing in for a flower that yields no usable essential oil, and its stated power means it will dominate a floral accord unless the other florals are built around it.

Soft, long-lasting muguet-lily with a sweet hydroxycitronellal-like warmth and a gentle cyclamen freshness. Prohibited under IFRA and banned in EU cosmetics since 2021; retained here for legacy formula reference.
Very soft floral-balsamic sesquiterpene alcohol with delicate peppery sweetness. Gentle fixative also prized for skin-care benefits.
Green, anisic-spicy basil leaf, sweet and peppery. Electrifies citrus colognes and fougere tops.
Sharp, pungent, sour vinegar note. A trace acidic modifier best used at 1 percent or 10 percent dilution.

Sweet creamy vanilla with cocoa-chocolate and a dairy-powdery body, a shade softer and more phenolic than vanillin itself. The non-discolouring vanilla for soap, candles and amine-containing bases: it carries the note without the brown staining vanillin causes.
Natural-smelling sandalwood note with an amber-woody character; acts as a fixative.

Green, fruity-floral cyclopentanone with pear-apple juiciness, celery nuance and a soft jasmine-muguet body. Works in jasmine, lactonic and celery-tinged floral accords as a lighter alternative to cis-jasmone.

Givaudan describes Frutonile as having an intense peach character with lactonic undertones, and notes that it is stable across the whole pH range, allowing a stable fruity effect at low concentration in any application including bleach systems. The house publishes a blotter tenacity of two weeks, far longer than the peach lactones it stands in for, and rates it strongly for soap bloom and for substantivity on damp surfaces. In a formula it is a small-dose peach heart: a fraction of a percent lifts a fruity-floral accord and survives soap, detergent and bleach where gamma-undecalactone would be destroyed, so it is dosed by the drop and overdoses read as canned fruit.

Henri Robert's de Laire muguet base, built on hydroxycitronellal: the delicate and enchanting scent of lily of the valley, soft floral transparency carried on a green, vibrant edge. Its best known use is Chanel No 19, where it sits alongside the other de Laire muguet base Mayciane. Current material is a restoration described as an elegant, modern lily of the valley without vintage stuffiness. It functions as a finished muguet heart, so it replaces a hand-built lily accord outright and lifts a green floral from the inside rather than sitting on top of it.

Penetrating smoky-phenolic note of charred wood, smoked ham and medicinal tar with an underlying sweetness; a core smoke molecule of burnt materials. Traces build convincing smoke, whisky, leather and incense effects; harsh if overdosed.
Fresh, green-fruity apple-and-pear ester with a mild leafy nuance; used in fruity and green-floral accords.
Sweet, soft sandalwood-like note with soapy, floral and slightly powdery woody nuances. A mild, transparent sandalwood extender for functional and fine perfumery.

Tahitian gardenia absolute: creamy, salicylate-rich white floral with coconut-monoi warmth, green gardenia freshness and a sunny, suntan-lotion sensuality. Rare and costly; used in tropical white-floral and gardenia reconstructions.

Dark, powerful natural extract of Fucus vesiculosus: iodine-rich seashore, salty-marine and green-algae notes drying to leathery, tobacco- and hay-like depths. The key natural for realistic ocean and rockpool effects; use in small amounts as it easily dominates and discolors. Payan Bertrand's Fucus absolute has no restriction in IFRA category 4 (an earlier amendment had it at 0.1%), and its allergen declaration finds only coumarin at 0.007% and limonene at 0.004% at or above the quantification limit; benzyl alcohol, estragole, benzaldehyde and a trace of toluene sit below it.

Opens warm and leathery-animalic: smoky, phenolic in a calamine-lotion way, and unmistakably castoreum, with clear birch-tar facets and a sweet resinous undertone that softens the smoke. It develops a musky sensuality and turns faintly fruity in the drydown. Firmenich's animal-free reconstruction, a co-extraction of natural and synthetic parts that per the house glossary contains no castoreum at all. In a formula it supplies animalic warmth, leather character and phenolic depth to chypres, fougeres, leathers and orientals, and holds on a blotter for well over two weeks.

Symrise's sheet gives Aldehydic, Floral, Marine, Airy; The Good Scents Company reads it at 10 percent as aldehydic muguet waxy watery hyacinth floral green. It smells of lily of the valley and orchid seen through a cold, airy aldehyde, with fruity, green and waxy edges rather than the fatty soapiness of a straight-chain aldehyde. In a formula it underlines fresh spring-blossom elements such as cherry and apple blossom and sits very well on top of established cool watery floral notes; Symrise calls it a top-note booster at 0.1 to 2 percent, though it holds 72 hours on the blotter neat.
Crisp, light floral odor similar to linalool but slightly more chemical-metallic; a stable bois-de-rose type modifier.

Sweet, warm-spicy vanillic note capturing the cooked, pungent-sweet aspect of ginger; less volatile and rounder than ginger oil. Bridges spicy and gourmand territory in gingerbread, chai and amber-vanilla bases.

Extremely powerful fresh green note of violet leaf and cucumber, with melon-rind and galbanum facets over a light waxy body. The reference material for violet leaf and cucumber effects; use in traces at high dilution.

A high-impact violet material: floral violet over a sharp green violet-leaf and tagette edge, lifted by a fruity, faintly banana-like top. The Good Scents Company files it as a floral odour type of high strength and advises assessing it at ten percent or less, which is the honest warning on this one. In a formula it gives the green, crushed-leaf side of a violet accord without leaning on ionones, so it opens green florals, muguet and fresh aldehydic bouquets and keeps a hyacinth or galbanum top from going flat. It holds around twelve hours on the blotter, long for something that reads as a top-note effect, so it stays audible under the heart.

Mild sweet carnation-clove with a delicate woody-floral warmth, much softer than isoeugenol and free of its phenolic bite. Smooth spicy floralizer for carnation, ylang and amber bases; IFRA-restricted.

Ripe pineapple with banana and apple flesh over a green edge, turning faintly sour and cheesy at strength. Heavier and more tenacious than isoamyl butyrate, so it carries a tropical fruit accord past the topnote.
Minty-herbaceous coolness with a slightly musty green edge, milder than menthol. Cooling modifier for mint, geranium and herbal-fresh accords.

A strong woody amber with a sweet earthy, musky odour and a delicate animalic tonality. IFF reports high impact in both heart and base and substantivity beyond forty-eight hours, with very good stability and performance in fine fragrance, soap, shampoo and antiperspirant deodorant, at levels from traces upward. In a formula it is the workhorse ambergris-woody fixative: it lends volume and skin-like radiance to a whole composition rather than smelling of one thing, extends woods and musks, and survives hostile bases where naturals do not. Distributor specifications identify it as the ambroxan molecule at over ninety-nine percent by GC, supplied as a crystalline powder; it is naturally derived, fully renewable and vegan suitable.

Soft watery-green aldehyde with ozonic melon, cyclamen and a milky hay-like sweetness; the classic bridge between marine notes and white florals (famously in L'Eau d'Issey). IFRA-restricted material, so check current standards when dosing.
Briny sea-spray saltiness with iodine-rich seaweed over a powdery, mossy body, plus a discreet orange flower nuance. Darker and more mineral than the melon aquatics of the nineties.

Supercritical damascena extract: the fresh green dewy top the otto cooks off plus the honeyed body the otto leaves behind, with no solvent tail and no distillation burn. The most faithful rose available; use it where the rose is the subject rather than a support.

Symrise's own sheet gives it as Floral, Iris, Orris, Green. It is a raw, penetrating green-fatty iris note with enormous diffusion and radiance, the nitrile reading of orris rather than the buttery irone reading. In a formula it is the fastest way to put orris and violet volume into a floral-woody or green-floral accord, and it pushes the dry, powdery, cosmetic side of iris rather than the creamy side. Symrise recommends 0.05 to 0.5 percent and sells it pre-diluted at 1 percent, which is a fair warning about how little of it a formula wants.

Classic Synarome ozonic marine base (pre-Calone, 1950s). Opens with a delicate rosy accent over a marine cascade of lily, with a background reminiscent of sand and shells. Gives a natural aqueous facet to compositions.

Symrise gives the odour as fruity, plum, apple and star fruit. In a formula it gives volume, strength and naturalness to green fruity notes, has an interesting lifting and harmonising effect, and provides a deep fruitiness to floral notes. A light crotonate ester boiling at 192.9 C with a published odour threshold in air of 0.0398 ug/l, so it reads at the top of a fruity accord and is the lifting partner to the heavier Datilat in the same range. Symrise recommends 0.1 to 5 percent.

Non-volatile fixed plant oil used as a carrier and in massage-oil blends. Bland, nearly odorless with a light texture and quick skin absorption; added (roughly 10-30%) to speed up a too-slow-absorbing carrier blend.

dsm-firmenich's own OTNE article, made by green synthesis with more than half renewable carbon. Suppliers describe a woody, velvety amber note that gives fullness and strength to any fragrance: a smooth delicate cedarwood with ambery, powdery and violet undertones. It holds about a week on a smelling strip. Reseller copy and user reports call it deeper and more bottom-heavy than Iso E Super, so it is used as a base volumiser and fixative rather than for the airy woody lift.
Refreshing aldehydic bergamot-lemon with citronella and verbena facets over a dry orange body. Uplifting citrus top note with unusual six-hour substantivity for its family.

Robertet's listing gives a delicate and sweet honey and spicy anisic aroma, and states the product is a low-temperature extraction captured onto natural nerolidol. Suppliers and perfumers describe it as delicate, fresh, yellow floral with a potent anisic note, less herbal than traditional mimosa absolute and much truer to the living flower, without the green and woody aspects the absolute carries. Because the aromatic material is already borne on a nerolidol carrier it is far less concentrated and far less sticky than the absolute, so it is dosed generously rather than in traces. In a formula it is the mimosa to reach for when the absolute would go herbal or muddy, and its anisic sweetness makes it a good modifier in fruity, powdery and soft oriental accords.

Moellhausen's own amber article describes it as an ambergris-type accord: the cutting animalic and salty notes come directly to the head, while its enveloping ambery notes and the earthy side given by musks find a great harmonization with the heart notes. Built like every BoldBase from fewer than eight elementary components, so it is a building block rather than a finished accord: the house's use for it is to uplift notes inside an amber formulation, salting and animalising an amber or musk base and giving it the mineral, slightly marine lift of grey amber.

Sweeter, more vanillic smoke than guaiacol: warm clove-woodsmoke with whisky-cask, spicy and slightly leathery facets. Excellent in smoky vanilla, peated-whisky, leather and incense accords at trace levels.
Nepalese pepper with surprising grapefruit and pomelo brightness, a coriander seed quality and balsamic hints from natural cinnamates. A rare, versatile modern spice note.
Fresh green-spicy dill herb with caraway-like carvone facets and a grassy sweetness. Adds crisp culinary greenness to herbal topnotes and aromatic-aquatic accords.

Bedoukian sells it as a melange of fruity floral, soft milky notes for skin care and fine fragrance, and describes a powerful, warm jasmine odour with milky undertones. TGSC reads it as oily jasmin, coconut, milky, dairy, floral, rates the strength medium and measures 36 hours on the blotter. In a formula it is the creamy filler under a white floral: it rounds jasmine, tuberose and orange blossom, lays a coconut-milk skin over a fruity accord, and blurs the hard edge of indolic materials without adding sweetness of its own.

Fresh, sparkling frankincense: lemony-terpenic and peppery opening (alpha-pinene, limonene, octyl acetate) over a resinous, balsamic, old-church body. Bridges citrus tops into resinous bases; essential in incense, amber and modern 'mineral' compositions.

Perfumer's Apprentice lists it as a "juicy accord that captures the sweet and delicateness of freshly picked raspberries". The word doing the work is delicate: this is the soft, just-picked berry rather than the jammy cooked one, so it sits closer to a fresh fruit than to a gourmand. As a compounded all-natural base it gives a whole berry in one line, and it earns its place in the heart of a fruity floral or behind a rose, where berry and rose share the same territory. Overdose flattens the delicacy that is the point of it.

Rich, warm, sweet-spicy eugenol character with fruity and woody undertones, the finest of the clove oils. Essential in carnation, amber spice and gourmand bakery accords; eugenol content triggers IFRA restriction.

Pungent green vegetable aldehyde, intensely fatty and oily with fruity apple-skin overtones, filling the rung between trans-2-hexenal and trans-2-octenal. IFRA prohibits it outright as a fragrance ingredient on dermal sensitization grounds, so it is of reference and analytical interest only.

Crisp, intense green-floral with a clean, watery linalool freshness: sharp leafy-fruity at the top, then soft tea and freesia-like floral notes with a hint of rosewood. Keeps white florals from turning cloying and bridges citrus tops to floral hearts. Leaf oil of Michelia alba (white champaca), about 89% linalool.
Green, fatty and slightly fruity-winey, a blunter cousin of leaf alcohol. Used in small amounts to add naturalness to green and fruity topnotes.

The laevo half of linalool, and the one that smells of lavender rather than of coriander: cooler, woodier and drier than the racemate, with the soft floral sweetness pulled back and a cleaner herbaceous edge left in its place. It is what carries true lavender, where it runs a quarter to nearly half the oil, and ho wood, where it is almost the whole of it. Reach for it when ordinary linalool reads too sweet under a fougere or a lavender accord. The dextro isomer is the other material entirely: warm, herbaceous, the coriander one.
Very powerful green-nutty thiazole with pistachio, roasted coffee, cocoa and sulfurous facets. Best evaluated at high dilution for pistachio, nut and roasted gourmand effects.

An IFF captive released to the open market, chemically cyclooct-4-en-1-yl methyl carbonate. Perfumer's Apprentice gives it as floral, violet leaf, green and marigold with fruity banana notes; ScenTree files it under green with fatty and medicinal facets and calls its effect in violet leaf compositions fresh, heady and aromatic. It is an intense violet-leaf material with a genuine floral quality rather than the flat crushed-stem greenness of the classic violet leaf chemicals, and the banana-ester edge is what separates it from Folione. Head to heart impact, holding a blotter past six hours, with very good damp and good dry substantivity, so it survives soap and deodorant bases.
Green unripe-fruit ester with juicy pineapple and quince facets over a winey, faintly rummy edge. Gives pear, apple and grape accords an underripe crunch that plain saturated esters cannot reach.

Givaudan files it in the ambery family, with an ambrette-leaning dry woody character. Its job in a formula is structural: it gives richness and balance to compounds, strengthening them and adding warmth and fullness, and it can also be used simply as a diffusive woody note. Tenacity on blotter is about one day, so it works in the heart rather than as a long fixative, and it holds up strongly in soap, powder detergent, fabric care and shampoo bases.

Acetylated patchouli oil: the earthy-woody patchouli character made sweeter, smoother and cleaner, soft, balsamic and velvety, with little of the raw oil's camphoraceous, musty heaviness. Extremely tenacious. It stands to patchouli oil as vetiveryl acetate does to vetiver.

Woody and animalic. Very strong and long lasting, especially in the typical woody animalic facet of oud. A balanced blend of natural extracts and synthetic molecules built by Firmenich perfumers with their Natural Ingredients Innovation Center in Grasse, carrying Oud Assafi at 0.2 percent alongside a high proportion of other naturals including Aquilaria malaccensis and Atlas cedarwood. Drier and more straightforwardly woody-animalic than Anokha, it is the one to reach for when the oud has to persist under the rest of the formula rather than announce itself on top.
Warm, sweet clove led by eugenol, rounder and more floral than the distilled bud oil, with a carnation-like softness, woody-aromatic facets and a phenolic edge. Diffusive and tenacious.

Curry-and-fenugreek herbaceousness from the italidione diketones, lifted by a fruity-tea neryl acetate sweetness and closing dry, honeyed and faintly woody. Distinct from the immortelle absolute, which is a much heavier maple-syrup and tobacco material: the oil is greener, more bitter-herbal and usable where the absolute would dominate.

Bright, terpenic olibanum from Boswellia frereana: fresh pine and green-citrus lift over only a light balsamic incense body, with none of the boswellic heaviness of carterii. The freshest frankincense, used for luminous incense tops and to open resinous bases.
Fresh piney-camphoraceous with a sweet balsamic fir-needle character. The signature ester of conifer needle oils; bridges herbal-camphor notes into woody-pine bases.

Deep warm floral of Acacia farnesiana: violet-ionone and mimosa powderiness over spicy-clove, balsamic, herbaceous and distinctly animalic-honey depth. Precious in violet accords, chypres and floral-ambers where mimosa would be too light.
Warm herbaceous-green terpene of sun-warmed basil leaves with sweet floral and citrus facets. Provides the dewy quality of living gardenia and a resinous mango-peel effect in tropical accords.
Harsh, intensely mentholic mint, less refined than peppermint; usually partially dementholized. Economic source of minty freshness for functional perfumery; pulegone content flags it.

A quiet lily-of-the-valley alcohol that leans rosy where most muguet materials lean green: peony sweetness with a citronellol edge over a faint waxy-woody base. Soft enough to be mistaken for weak, and then it sits on the blotter far longer than anything that soft has a right to.

Dark green minty absolute with a hay-tea sweetness over a soft herbaceous body; the menthol reads as coolness rather than the ice blast of the distilled oil. Used where mint has to sit inside a floral or a fougere without shouting, and it outlasts the oil by a wide margin.

This is not really an odour material and should not be shelved as one. Suppliers describe WS-12 as an odourless white crystalline solid melting around 178 C, and The Good Scents Company file it under the odour type "cooling" with no odour description at all, listing the taste as simply "cooling" and marking the entry information-only, not used for fragrance or flavour. What it does is physiological rather than olfactory: it is a TRPM8 agonist rated at roughly three and a half times the cooling power of menthol and holding that effect for something like half an hour, so you get the cold with none of the mint. Advanced Biotech sell it in the Koolada range for a refreshing sensation on the skin or in the mouth, going beyond what standard mint gives. In a formula it changes how a fresh accord feels, not how it smells, and it contributes nothing to the pyramid.
Dry, pencil-shavings woody note with a soft balsamic sweetness and slightly sour-oily undertone from cedrol and cedrene content. A cheap, ubiquitous woody base and fixative.
Sweet spearmint chewing-gum note, warm-minty and slightly green. The defining molecule of spearmint; freshens fougeres and herbal accords, now IFRA-restricted for sensitization.
Waxy green with orange, aldehydic, rose and mushroom facets.
