Oily-fatty dienal carrying a clear grapefruit and orange-peel citrus lift with a dairy undertone, extending the decadienal effect into the heavier waxy range. Prohibited under the IFRA 2,4-dienals group standard, so it stands as a reference rung rather than a working material.
Crystalline lily of the valley freshness with a watery, lightly aldehydic sparkle and citrus zest hints. A powerful muguet aldehyde for modernising classic floral structures.

Sweet balsamic ester with storax, spicy-cinnamic and faintly honeyed hay facets. The acetate of phenylpropyl alcohol, warmer and more resinous than the free alcohol; used to build storax and balsam accords and to lay a cinnamic-balsamic underlay under hyacinth and lilac hearts.

Sweet, powdery vanilla-heliotrope with a creamy, slightly woody-anisic softness and no free phenol, so it barely discolors. A stable vanillin alternative that adds powdery vanilla-almond warmth to florals and gourmands.

A de Laire tuberose base, revisiting the 1960s Tuberiane, built on an exclusive Tuberose Coeur quality together with the Lilybelle captive. Symrise say it puts forward Lilybelle with its hints of muguet and imparts luminous freshness, adding a velvety feel that enhances a rich and radiant tuberose. The green, dewy, airy lily-of-the-valley of the captive is set against the opulence of tuberose behind it, and it is composed without the muguet molecules that are now restricted. In a formula it supplies a whole modern tuberose heart at once, fresher and more transparent than a tuberose absolute.

DRT, who own the name, describe it as "Minty aromatic, camphoraceous, metallic"; The Good Scents Company records the same material as camphoreous minty, and Privi, who sell it under the generic chemistry name, give "Camphoricious, minty". So the reading is consistent across three sources: a cool, sharp, aromatic-mint top with a camphor lift and a slightly metallic edge, not a sweet spearmint. Privi publishes a tenacity of about three hours, so it is a genuine top note that opens a fougere, a herbal or a functional accord with cold air and then hands off. DRT also note it is very stable in acidic media, which is why it turns up in low-pH home care. The metallic facet is the risk: overdose and it reads harsh and cleaning-product rather than aromatic.

Sharp, green-spicy cumin character with an animalic, slightly sweaty warmth, cleaner and more manageable than the essential oil. Used in traces for cumin, curry and skin-like effects in amber and leather accords.
Juicier and sweeter than regular sweet orange, with a raspberry-like blush and softer zest. Gorgeous in gourmand citrus tops and modern colognes.

Supercritical CO2 extract of cured Vanilla planifolia beans: clean, rounded, creamy-sweet vanilla that reads closer to the split bean than the absolute does, without the molasses, rummy and leathery weight the solvent extract carries. Preferred in fine fragrance where a bright true vanilla is wanted and the absolute's dark tonality would muddy the composition.
Mild, fresh green-gardenia alcohol with a light hyacinth-earthy nuance, gentler than its acetate. Softens gardenia accords and adds a fresh floral-green whisper to white-flower tops.

Fresh, penetrating camphoraceous-cineolic herbaceousness with woody-balsamic undertones; Tunisian is more camphoraceous, Spanish more cineolic. Classic in eaux de cologne, fougères and aromatic masculines for a bracing herbal opening.

The house marketing sheet gives the olfactive description as an elegant amber note with a rich woody character, and files the product under Ambery. On perfumery usage it states that the ingredient provides warmth, richness and elegance to all areas of perfumery from sheer florals to modern orientals, and that due to its power the best effects can be achieved at lower dosages, although higher levels are often used to provide performance and substantivity. It is a solid, behaves as a heart and base note, and lasts a month on a smelling strip. Fine fragrance dosage runs 0.5% to 3%, with much lower ranges across shampoo, soap, detergent and candle.
Soft floral-herbaceous alcohol from lavender with rosy-green freshness and a faint fruity nuance. Naturalizes lavender and adds a fine floral roundness to herbal-floral hearts.
Strikingly realistic juicy pear with green, slightly metallic and brandy-like facets, immensely diffusive. The reference pear material; traces also freshen apple, quince and tropical accords.
Rose and cooked apple with ripe plum depth and a distinctive herbal, wormwood-like edge that sets it apart from its alpha and beta siblings. Subtle tobacco undertones in the drydown; trace use.
Sweet, powdery-aromatic floral crystal with a pronounced neroli and orange-flower character. Classic fixative for colognes and citrus-floral accords.

Mane's own line on the captive is soft green notes of petitgrain, and it is the reason its Bigaflower speciality carries crisp green petitgrain at the top. Read through the bases built on it, it is a clean citrus-green with a woody-dry edge, closer to the snap of a freshly plucked bitter orange twig than to the leaf-alcohol greenness of cis-3-hexenol. Overdosed in Greencatcher it turns loud and neon rather than herbal, which tells you the molecule itself is diffusive and not a quiet modifier. It is a captive: Mane does not sell it neat to independents and discloses no structure, so a perfumer outside the house reaches it only inside Bigaflower, Greencatcher or Florapeel.

IFF describe it as a diffusive floral effect reminiscent of a combination of lilac, rose and geranium, while The Good Scents Company files the same CAS under a leathery odour type and reads it at 10% as leather, red rose, green, dusty, weedy and metallic. Despite the name it is not a patchouli material. In a formula it is an inexpensive, very stable diffusion booster: it lifts and radiates a rose, geranium or lilac accord and leaves a discreet suede-leather shadow underneath. Non-discolouring and stable in almost everything including soap, with a tenacity of about 12 hours on the blotter.

Moellhausen describes this base as warm, spicy and gentle, one of the simple human experiences the third BoldBases series was built around. Like every B.Base it is a building block with a deliberately narrow olfactory profile, under eight elementary components, offered for high intensity and persistency. In a formula it is the spice accent itself rather than a modifier: it carries a saffron character that would otherwise take several materials to assemble, and its gentleness means it warms a composition without the medicinal bite a raw saffron material can push through.

Glycerin-derived dioxolane solvent marketed as Augeo Clean Multi: near-odorless with a faint sweetness, good solvency and moderate evaporation, popular in reed diffusers and as a sustainable DPG alternative. Bio-based and readily biodegradable.

Deertongue leaf absolute rich in coumarin: sweet hay and tobacco with green tea, fig-leaf and slightly medicinal-balsamic undertones. Classic in tobacco and fougere reconstitutions and as a chypre fixative; IFRA coumarin limits apply.

Steam-distilled bitter-orange blossom: fresh, bittersweet, green-floral with citrus sparkle, linalool softness and a clean soapy elegance, much lighter than the absolute. Classic in colognes and bridal white florals, bridging citrus tops into floral hearts.

Powerful phenolic-medicinal herbaceousness dominated by thymol, warm, spicy and slightly tarry. Used in traces for rustic herbal character in fougères, bay rums and men's classics; white thyme is the rectified, milder version.

Sweet powdery vanilla, soft and low-volatility, with the heliotrope-cherry shading of the heliotropin family but none of its crystalline sparkle. A quiet rounder for heliotrope, mimosa and powdery-vanillic accords where piperonal would push too hard.

Pungent, sweet-terpenic pine and turpentine with a dry resinous body and a faint lemon lift; sweeter and far less camphoraceous than alpha-pinene. Sharpens conifer, cypress and juniper accords and gives pine and fougere tops a turpentine bite. Oxidises readily, so keep it fresh and antioxidised.

Citronellol-dominated Chinese Pelargonium: directly minty-rosy and sharply green, harsher and simpler than the bourbon, with little of the citronellyl formate fruitiness that gives Reunion oil its depth. The heart and base fall away quickly, so it reads bright and one-dimensional. The volume-priced geranium: fine for soap, fougere backbones and rose-green tops where cost matters more than roundness.

Perfumer's Apprentice calls it a "beautiful accord that captures the essence of a fresh, green tomato leaf". Note that it is the leaf and not the fruit: this is the sharp, slightly bitter green that comes off the vine when you brush it, not a red tomato. That makes it a green top rather than a fruity one, and it is a strong one, so it wants a light hand. Use it where a formula needs a living, just-crushed stem impression, and read it as a compounded all-natural accord, not as a single-source leaf extract, which is why it carries no CAS of its own.

Givaudan's specialties brochure describes it as an economical reconstitution of the natural fragrance of galbanum oil with all its typical olfactive properties, used exactly as natural galbanum oil to provide a powerful green effect across fragrance formulations. It carries the sharp, bitter, crushed-stem verdancy with the faintly resinous and earthy undertow that perfumers buy galbanum for in the first place. It belongs in a green top accord in traces: work it well diluted and add drop by drop, because it takes command of a formula long before the dose looks generous.
Rich green-floral absolute with a sharp, narcotic, leafy-metallic and slightly earthy character. Classic hyacinth note for green-floral and spring bouquet accords.

Givaudan describes Citrathal as having a distinctive clean-fresh, lemon-lime character and positions it as one of the more chemically stable citrus materials, supplied in three grades of which Tech is the technical one. It is a reaction product of 3,7-dimethyl-2,6-octadienal with ethyl alcohol rather than free citral, which is why the lemon-lime brightness survives in bases where citral itself discolours or collapses. In a formula it is the workhorse lemon-lime top for functional and alkaline media: it tolerates generous use levels, blooms well in soap and holds on damp substrate, though the house rates it weakly in acid cleaners and fabric detergent.
Powerful roasted, nutty pyrazine with nut-skin, roasted coffee and unsweetened cocoa character and meaty nuances. A trace-level modifier for coffee, cocoa and roasted accords.

Harsh green-metallic geranium note with orange-blossom, and slightly phenolic-oily facets; unmistakably 'soap factory' neat. Cheap and powerful for geranium-rose effects in functional perfumery and to give bite to green florals.

Sweet-green fruit ester that reads as firm, unripe apple and waxy apple skin, with touches of strawberry and pear. A pungent edge keeps it crisp rather than candied, and it lasts about three hours on a strip. Hexyl 3-methylbutanoate.

Soft, sweet jasmine-lactonic note, warmer and more floral than Hedione with a slightly waxy, tea-like depth; a genuine jasmine constituent and plant hormone. Adds hushed naturalness to fine jasmine reconstructions.
Fresh, soft white-petal alcohol evoking muguet, magnolia and tuberose petals with a clean, slightly leathery-smooth nuance. Harmonizes white and rosy florals and softens woody-citrus themes.

Synarome's legendary animalic-ambergris base: powerful salty-skanky ambergris with civet-like, seaweed and warm woody-labdanum facets. A drop lends vintage animalic radiance to ambers, ouds and leathers; famously overdosed in classic masculines.

Inspired by an exclusive Givaudan aromachemical and by the perfume that surrounds blooming linden trees in early summer. Rich, sweet and honeysuckle-like, with green and fresh aspects and clear lily, muguet, freesia and petal nuances, plus a soft tropical edge. Suppliers place it as a middle note in the light floral family and give it up to ten percent, noting that four percent in a violet accord adds a pleasant floral volume. It is used as a central note in a formula but is also very effective in the top notes and in the dry down, so it carries linden across the whole wear rather than only at one stage.
Fresh floral heart between linalool and coriander, vibrant and slightly rosy with a warm tropical-air character. Traces add freshness, overdoses give a much-loved modern signature.
Sweet, warm, herbaceous chamomile with a fruity-tea, cognac softness. Roman-type, prized in luxury florals and tea accords.
Soft, sweet-balsamic coniferous oil with a fresh green-woody and slightly citrus-fruity forest character. Used in fine fragrance for a refined pine-forest freshness.

A fresh agrumic fragrance with spicy-herbal and sweet undertones, with green and peppery facets over the citrus; TGSC files it under the aldehydic odour type at medium strength and advises smelling it at ten percent or below. Its value in a formula is durability rather than novelty: as a nitrile it is far less affected by hostile media than a citrus aldehyde or a cold-pressed oil, so it carries grapefruit and citrus effects through bleach, concentrated detergent powder, soap, shampoo and body lotion where the natural would discolour or collapse. It is a clear colourless to pale yellow liquid, minimum ninety-eight percent by GC.
Ambergris, musky and animalic with a warm skin-like saltiness.

Givaudan gives a dry fruity peach note with a fresh green softness. It is tricyclodecenyl pivalate, and the house is explicit about its job: it is a modifier, used alongside other cyclenes and the gamma-lactones to cut their fattiness. That is the whole point of it in a formula. A peach built on lactones alone goes creamy and heavy, and this dries it out and puts a thin green edge back on the fruit without adding sweetness. Several days on the blotter, up to 5 percent in fine fragrance and cosmetics where the profile allows, around 1 percent in soaps and detergents.

Nez describes it as a plump and juicy blackcurrant extract that takes centre stage, mouth-watering without being gourmand. The article is explicit that before this technology a perfumer had only synthetic blackcurrant materials or the bud absolute, and that the bud absolute is a very different thing, greener and much more sulphurous. So this reads as the fruit rather than the bud: ripe and round with far less of the catty thiol bite, which is what lets it carry a fruity top openly instead of being trace-dosed the way a cassis bud or a corps cassis has to be. Mane markets it as Blackcurrant NEO Jungle Essence.

The first, finest distillation fraction of Cananga odorata flowers: intensely sweet, creamy jasmine-like floralcy with banana, spicy clove and salicylate nuances. Essential in white-floral, carnation and classic aldehydic-floral perfumes; IFRA-restricted.
Dry, woody-ambery cedar note with a soft vetiver-like earthiness and good fixative power. A staple base for masculine woody, chypre and fougere compositions.

The archetypal marine molecule: intense watermelon-rind, oyster-like sea-breeze note with a sweet floral undertone, defining the aquatic genre since New West and L'Eau d'Issey. Extremely diffusive; traces freshen florals while overdoses give the classic 90s ozonic-marine signature.

A bright, diffusive resin oil, much fresher than classic myrrh: a piney-terpenic, elemi-like lift with a light citrus sparkle over a soft resinous base. Steam-distilled from the resin of Commiphora wildii (omumbiri), Namibia.
Classic polycyclic indane musk: sweet, powdery, clean with a slightly metallic-fruity nuance, historically the musk of many 1950s-70s functional bases. Useful for retro soapy-musk effects.
Green, peppery-terpenic note with balsamic, hoppy and slightly metallic citrus facets. Used in citrus and verbena reconstitutions to restore the raw terpene freshness of natural peels.

Intense sweet creamy vanilla with vanilla-ice-cream and chocolate-milk nuances, drying down slightly caramellic and rummy. The isobutyrate ester of ethyl vanillin: it does not brown alcohol or alkaline soap bases and releases its vanilla slowly, so it outlasts ethyl vanillin wherever color stability matters.

Japanese sour citrus sitting between lime and mandarin, rounded by an unusually high myrcene content and a waxy-fatty peel sparkle from octanal and decanal. Softer and less biting than sudachi, and notably low in linalool, so it stays fruity-peel rather than turning floral.

Bedoukian lists this separately from Cerezoate on the same CAS, as a fruity-tropical, ethereal character with subtle notes of pear and pineapple; the supplier listing adds juicy pineapple, red fruit and blueberry, a use level of traces to 1%, and tenacity of more than an hour on the blotter. It is the wider-isomer grade of ethyl 2-methyl-3-pentenoate, specified at about 83% sum of isomers against Cerezoate's high-cis cut, and it reads correspondingly less cherry and more pear and pineapple. Use it where a fruity or green accord wants ethereal tropical juiciness at the top.

dsm-firmenich synthetic base 184075 D, described by the house as an olfactive reproduction of the fragrance of wild strawberries. It is a compounded accord rather than a single molecule, built by the house's perfumers together with their natural ingredients specialists and carrying proprietary components. In a formula it places a complete strawberry heart in one line, instead of assembling one from single fruity materials such as Aldehyde C-16.
A fresh light green floral lily / lily-of-the-valley (muguet) base with linden-blossom aldehydic and lilac facets; IFRA-49 and EU compliant drop-in replacement for Lilial.
Natural fruity-green odor of ripe pear with apple and passionfruit nuances. Blends into fruity-floral accords and lifts green notes.
Fresh, clean citrus-lime with a lavender-like, slightly metallic coolness. The backbone of countless fresh masculine fragrances; blends citrus into fougere and aquatic structures.
Powerful green fruity-berry rhubarb note with floral and herbal facets. A primary building block for fresh rhubarb reconstructions.

Sweet, jammy raspberry note with warm, slightly floral-powdery and gourmand facets, quiet but very tenacious. The heart of raspberry accords; also softens roses and adds fruity warmth to musky drydowns.

Roasted nutty pyrazine carrying an unmistakable sulfury edge, reading as fried hazelnut and roasted almond over toasted popcorn and a coffee-caramel background. The sulfur-pyrazine hybrid: threshold sits in the low ppb, so it belongs at trace in coffee, popcorn and roasted-nut gourmands where a plain pyrazine smells flat.

A wild-harvested oud oil from a collaboration between the Bangladeshi distillers Jalali Agarwood and Firmenich. Intensely leathery and animalic, balanced by an elegant woody depth, a rich ambery warmth and a distinct spicy heat, with sweet undertones underneath; buyers reliably read barnyard, clean stable and goat-cheese facets in it neat. In a formula it is a trace material and a powerful fixative: a drop signs a whole oriental or woody base as real oud and anchors everything above it for days on a blotter.
Warm woody-spicy leaf oil with green, fruity-tropical and caryophyllene-rich nuances. Unusual natural for tropical and woody-green effects.
Meaty, spicy and herbaceous. Heart filing is a catalog convention, not measured evaporation or longevity.

Bedoukian describes a long lasting, clean and diffusive raspberry/pomegranate note with ionone and violet undertones. TGSC files the odour type as tobacco and reads it neat as dry, sweet tobacco, nutty and violet, medium strength, with substantivity of 276 hours at full strength. In a formula it is a fixed berry: it holds a raspberry or pomegranate accent for days where a fruity ester would be gone within the hour, and its ionone side lets it sit under violet, orris and dry tobacco accords. Bedoukian points it at chypres, where the berry rides the mossy base instead of flashing off the top.
Extremely powerful dry amber, woody and slightly smoky; pure diffusive amber lift.

Synarome's celebrated all-purpose animalic base: a compounded blend suggesting civet, castoreum and musk with fecal-honeyed warmth, famously described as the animal heart of vintage masterpieces. A tiny percentage animalizes an entire composition.

Givaudan describes it as a clean, refreshing interpretation focusing on the distinctive fresh, green, slightly dry notes of ivy, enhanced by a floral accord. The dryness is what separates it from a wet crushed-stem green: it is leaf rather than sap, with a soft floral lining that keeps it from turning harsh. The brochure notes it is powerful even in small dosages and brings freshness and presence to a wide variety of fragrances, from simple florals through to chypres, so it is dosed as a trace green lift rather than as a body note.
Dry, fruity-saffron note with green apple, chamomile and tobacco facets, fresher and fruitier than safranal. Gives a modern saffron-fruity twist to roses, ambers and fruity-spicy compositions.
Fresh green-fruity gardenia note, sweeter and rounder than styralyl acetate. Gardenia, tuberose and rhubarb effects.
Generic clove: warm, sweet-spicy and phenolic with a numbing carnation bite. The default clove for spicy, amber and carnation accords.

Robertet lists it as "Woody, spicy, smoky, balsamic", steam distilled from Paraguayan Bulnesia sarmientoi sawdust. Ordinary guaiacwood sits as a waxy amber semi-solid that has to be warmed before it will pour; the dehydrated grade is a pourable liquid and reads drier and smokier, with less of the sweet rosy-balsamic softness that makes plain guaiacwood so cosy. It belongs under leather, incense and dry-wood accords as a smoky underlay and a fixative, and it is far easier to weigh accurately than the paste.
Intensely pungent, sulphurous-alliaceous gum oil with a fecal-onion, savory nuance that mellows on drydown. A powerful animalic-savory trace note for amber and gourmand-savory accords.

Cold-pressed from ripe Citrus reticulata peel, an intensely sweet, deep citrus-mandarin top note, rounder and sweeter than green or yellow mandarin, with a rich neroli-like floral undertone and an occasional amine nuance. A juicy natural lift for colognes, citrus and fresh floral tops.

Green floral sesquiterpene ester with muguet, orchid and soft rose facets over a waxy, faintly metallic body; quieter and less balsamic than farnesol itself. A discreet fixative that stretches muguet and green floral hearts without adding character of its own.

Sharp, dry cedar-like Japanese wood oil with a distinct medicinal-camphoraceous bite from its hinokitiol and thujopsene, drier and more astringent than hinoki. A clean, very tenacious woody base for Japanese-style and forest accords.
Soft fruity-berry material with velvety red-fruit sweetness and floral warmth. BASF's BMBcert renewable version is the same chemical identity with different sourcing, not a second olfactory material.
Explosive green-apple note, juicy, sweet and slightly strawberry-like, extremely diffusive. A trace makes fruity tops sparkle with fresh-cut apple; overdose turns nail-polish solventy.
Intense fresh-citrus aldehydic material with marine, ozonic and floral facets. Extremely diffusive; boosts the radiance and elegance of aliphatic aldehyde accords and citrus tops.
Fresh green-herbal oil with minty, hay-like and slightly fruity nuances from the nepetalactones. Lifts herbal, fougere and green-aromatic accords.
Modern blackcurrant note, tart, green and juicy with grapefruit and rhubarb facets but without the sulfurous harshness of thiols. Gives clean, long-lasting cassis effects in fine fragrance.

Peppery and bright with a pronounced lemon-peel citrus lift, a green terpenic edge and a dry woody trail, the smell of red huajiao husk rather than true pepper. Distinct from Timut in being more lemon than grapefruit; the numbing sanshools are non-volatile, so the oil reads as citrus-spice sparkle for colognes and woody tops.

Intense green violet-leaf note with cucumber, fatty-metallic and slightly earthy facets, harsher but longer-lasting than methyl heptine carbonate. Used in strict traces to add leafy bite to violet, iris and moss accords; IFRA-restricted.

The house sheet calls it a very rich and natural floral lactone, with a floral, jasmine petal-like character and a delicate fruitiness reminiscent of peach, apricot and coconut milk, and files it under FLORAL, FRUITY. In use it has a complementary effect with jasmine notes and is effective at relatively low concentrations, the sheet naming 0.1 to 1% and giving fine fragrance dosage in the hundredths to a couple of tenths of a percent, so a little goes a long way; it is a heart note and it lasts two weeks on a smelling strip, which is unusually tenacious for something that reads as a soft creamy floral. Identity warning worth carrying on the row: this is the 3-pentenyl lactone, FEMA 4441, and it is a different molecule from Jasmine Lactone, the 2-pentenyl one at CAS 25524-95-2 with FEMA 3745 and about three days on a strip. The name delta-Jasmolactone belongs to this row and must not be left as a synonym on the Jasmine Lactone row, or an import will silently collapse the two.

Warm sweet spicy-anisic aldehyde with a deep balsamic-cinnamon body and none of cinnamal's harsh bite. Gives amber and gourmand accords a rich cinnamon warmth that sits under the composition rather than shouting from the top.

Fiercely diffusive blackcurrant-catty note with minty, sulfurous and herbal facets from its menthone and thiol content. Used in tiny traces to make cassis and tropical fruit accords smell alive and juicy.
Warm, medicinal-herbal oil dominated by thymol with a sharp, dry spicy-phenolic character reminiscent of thyme and oregano. Used in trace amounts for spicy, medicinal-herbal and amber effects.
Fresh green-rosy ester, lighter and more diffusive than phenylethyl acetate, with chrysanthemum facets. Fresh rose top note.
Fresh ozonic-aldehydic lily with a cyclamen-watery sparkle and citrus overtones. Cleaner and more transparent than cyclamen aldehyde; superb in marine florals.
Fresh green, herbaceous ocimene-epoxide note with a lavender-metallic, sage and pear nuance. Adds a natural green lift to florals and fougeres.
Powerful fatty, fried, chicken-fat odor; at extreme dilution a fresh green-citrus orange nuance. Ultra-trace for fatty-fried and citrus naturalness.
Sweet, honeyed rose ester with fruity raspberry-pear facets and a hint of cocoa; brighter and jammier than PEA. Adds gourmand-tinged rosiness to tops of rose, honey and fruity-floral accords.

Softer and sweeter than nutmeg oil: freshly grated nutmeg with warm woody, powdery and balsamic facets, a milky-creamy touch and a hint of tobacco over a brief terpenic top. It bridges spices and woods from heart to base. Solvent-extracted absolute of Myristica fragrans seeds (Biolandes).

Kao describes it as a soft delicate floral note reminiscent of magnolia or muguet, with the descriptor triad Floral - Magnolia - Muguet, and claims extraordinary tenacity: more than one month on a blotter. It is a branded multi-component base, not a single chemical. The pairing of a soft, low-impact floral with that much substantivity is the whole point of the material: it will not carry a top note and will not drive an accord on its own, so it is dosed as a fixative-weight floral that keeps a magnolia-muguet character alive through the drydown long after the lighter muguet alcohols and aldehydes have gone.
A soft, delicate floral lily-cyclamen, hydroxycitronellal-like base, sweet, light and tenacious; IFRA-50 and EU compliant replacement for HMPCC (Lyral / Kovanol).
Extremely powerful meaty-brothy, cooked-savory thiol; used in the sub-ppm range for meat, coffee and roasted accords.

The middle maturity grade of cold-pressed Citrus reticulata peel: brighter and cleaner than red mandarin, without the bitter-green sharpness of the green grade, keeping the dusty anthranilate sweetness that marks all mandarin. The balanced choice when red reads too syrupy and green too austere.
Wild apple-chamomile fruitiness over bitter green marigold leaves, strange and addictive. Micro-doses give juicy naturalness to apple, osmanthus and chamomile accords.
Sweet fruity-floral with anisic, cherry-vanilla and light powdery facets. Rounds lilac and heliotrope accords and adds a soft gourmand-floral sweetness to fruity compositions.

Mild balsamic clove, heavy and low-key, with none of the phenolic bite of eugenol. Used purely as a fixative to hold spice and carnation character into the drydown, where its tenacity far outruns eugenol or eugenyl acetate.

The solvent extract of Atlas cedar: the himachalene woodiness of the oil made thicker and darker, with a resinous-balsamic body and a warm tobacco-like sweetness the distilled oil never reaches. Used where the Atlas oil is too thin to carry a base, and as a tenacious fixative in chypre and amber woody accords.

(E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal, the cucumber aldehyde: piercing fresh cucumber-skin and violet-leaf greenness with watery, slightly fatty depth; among the most potent materials in perfumery. Trace amounts give realistic watery-green freshness to aquatic, fig and violet accords.
Winey, cognac-like fruity ester with grape and slightly waxy banana facets. The key 'cognac ester'; gives boozy-fruity sparkle to grape, wine and liqueur accords.

Mane describes a sophisticated, salty and woody profile with luminous ambery nuances, inspired by sun-bleached wood and built around the Ambramone captive; the supplier reads the same material as a soft cedar quality with the faintest hint of suede and ambergris, and Mane's own trade copy calls it an ambery woody note with salty and marine facets reminiscent of white woods. It carries over 44 hours on a smelling strip. Used in overdose it is an elegant wood note in place of common bases such as Vertofix or Iso E Super; in small amounts it nuances a formula, and blending it with green or fruity notes pushes those facets forward. It contains nothing harsh, which is what lets it be dosed heavily as a foundational wood.
Bright, fresh pink pepper with a terpenic, lemony opening over woody-resinous tones, and in some grades a soft rosy-green side; drier and more peppery-woody than the Schinus molle fruit.

Rugosa rose absolute: jammy and deep-rosy with a pronounced clove-eugenol warmth, a dried-fruit and raisin edge, and a rough leafy-green bite that damascena never has. Greener, more spiced and far less honeyed than damask rose absolute, so it reads as a wild hedgerow rose rather than a polished one. Use where a rose needs grit, spice or a northern-coastal roughness instead of Bulgarian opulence.
Pungent phenolic carvacrol-driven herbaceousness, dry, spicy and medicinal. Micro-doses lend rustic Mediterranean authenticity to herbal and leather accords.
Sweet cake and butter accord recalling freshly baked French madeleines.

Diffusive green-leaf note with lettuce, watercress and slightly metallic wine-like facets, more transparent than cis-3-hexenol. Gives modern salad-green freshness to fruity, tea and aquatic compositions.

IFF describes it as a fresh, clean, ozone marine complex with herbal aspects; TGSC classifies the odour type as floral at medium strength and writes "floral clean muguet ozone marine sandy balsamic", adding that it is a substantive floral muguet product with the odour of fresh outdoors over a green melony background. Despite the name it is a single molecule, the octahydro-dimethyl-naphthaldehyde, not a blend. Its value is durability: TGSC publishes 140 hours on the blotter at 100%, so it holds an airy marine-muguet transparency far longer than the ozonic top-note materials it is usually paired with.

Odorless, sweet-tasting humectant polyol used in water-based fragrance formats (body splashes, hair mists) to add skin feel and slow flash-off. Poor solvent for most aromatics on its own, so it is combined with ethanol or solubilizers.
Fresh, green-rosy and slightly leafy ester, sharper and more diffusive than geranyl acetate with a natural geranium-leaf character. Useful to open rose compositions with a crisp botanical top.
Sharp, crisp green hyacinth-leaf note preferred over phenylacetaldehyde for its superior stability. Delivers dewy garden greenness to hyacinth, lilac and spring floral accords.
Very faint delicate floral-green note. Used chiefly as a low-odor fixative, diluent and synthesis intermediate.

Symrise classify it citrus, floral and waxy; TGSC files it under the floral odour type and describes it as citrus-like, reminiscent of lemon peel with waxy and metallic nitrile-like shades, with muguet, lily and sweet facets behind. In a formula it is the stable way to hold a lemon-peel brightness inside a muguet or white-floral heart, and its nitrile backbone keeps it working in body lotion, shampoo, soap and cleaning bases where a citrus aldehyde would not survive. It is the saturated relative of citronitrile, a colourless to pale yellow liquid boiling above three hundred degrees, so despite the citrus reading it behaves as a heart material rather than a top note.
Soft, sweet, woody-rosy sesquiterpene alcohol co-occurring with guaiol in guaiacwood; mild and balsamic. Used to round and fix woody-rose accords.

Sweet powdery orris-violet with woody and slightly leathery-tobacco nuances, the classic methylionone blend of alpha, beta and iso isomers. Gives volume and a vintage powdery signature to floral, chypre and fougere hearts.

Turkish damascena absolute: dry spicy rose with a black-tea and dried-petal edge and a clearer green top, less jammy and honeyed than the Bulgarian. Sits well in tea-rose, chypre and leather accords where the Bulgarian absolute would read too sweet.

Givaudan describes a diffusive jasmine and muguet odour that gives an exceptionally full bodied floral character to compositions, with green, fruity and sweet facets around it. It is a volume material: rather than adding a sharp floral top it thickens and carries a white-floral heart, which is why it is recommended at levels up to 20%. Tenacity on blotter runs to about a week, and it shows exceptional substantivity on both damp and dry cloth, so it is a workhorse in soap, fabric detergent and shampoo as well as in fine fragrance.
Fresh lavender-like, lightly woody-floral ester. Economical freshness booster for lavender, pine and fougere fragrances.
Fruity, sweet apple-green odor with a winey nuance. Used in fruity and cognac-type accords.

A soft, creamy, luminous musk with a clean profile, subtle floral undertones and a light animalic signature. It is a ready-to-use Oliffac base rather than a single molecule, composed of 88% readily biodegradable ingredients and positioned by IFF as a modern alternative to legacy polycyclic musks such as Galaxolide, holding its performance at low dosage. In a formula it is a musk floor: it rounds and lengthens a composition, softens sharp edges, and adds a skin-close warmth through the drydown without the laundry hardness that a single nitro- or polycyclic musk brings. Debuted at SIMPPAR 2026.
Cinnamon/cassia character with a nitrile-metallic, deep cumin edge; balsamic, spicy and slightly fatty. A cinnamic-aldehyde-like note with better stability to acid, alkali and light.
An IFF specialty base with an animalic, costus, leather and labdanum character; used as a safe substitute for restricted natural costus root oil.

Ambergris, dry and woody: a powerful, very substantive ambery note with a tobacco facet, clean cedar-like wood, a subtle marine saltiness and a powdery-musky skin radiance. Givaudan's ambroxide, made by bioconversion from sugar cane.

Warm balsamic resin with medicinal, sweet and spicy aspects and faint smoky-leathery shading. Somalian Commiphora myrrha gum cold-extracted with ethanol; supplied as 50% TEC resin-absolute, not myrrh essential oil.

Intensely sweet-spicy, hot cinnamon candy character, harsher and more cinnamal-driven than Ceylon bark oil with a faint balsamic depth. Powerful in cola, red-hot and amber spice accords; heavily restricted for skin contact.
Sharp, fresh and tingling: a peppery top with bergamot, mandarin and petitgrain-like citrus and a faintly metallic edge, over a warm allspice-bay spice.

Rich honey with a fruity, rum-like warmth. The honeyed member of the allyl ester set: it links pineapple-fruity accords to honey, narcissus and tobacco themes, and like all allyl esters it needs free allyl alcohol below 0.1%.

Clover-herbal salicylate with a soft orchid-floral body, close to amyl salicylate but drier and a touch harsher. Fills the isobutyl gap in fougeres and green florals, giving white flowers a sunlit meadow lift.
Creamy-soft dry wood and amber with musky cedarwood facets; born from Cashmeran chemistry and released from IFF captivity in 2023. Gives plush, enveloping depth to woody, musky and ambery bases.

Phenolic castoreum and creosote smoke with a savory, horse-blanket edge; this is the Brettanomyces molecule behind barnyard wine and sweaty leather. A workhorse in ppm traces for castoreum, oud and animalic leather builds, doing the barnyard work that 4-ethylguaiacol cannot; harsh and medicinal if overdosed.

The great botanical musk: warm, sweet, musky-floral with winey, pear-brandy and slightly nutty ambrette facets from ambrettolide and farnesol. The natural perfumer's only true musk; superb in skin scents, iris and rose compositions.
Waxy, green-fruity orange odor with a winey nuance. Adds a fresh fatty-fruity naturalness to citrus and fruity accords.

Sweet spicy-balsamic ester with a soft grape-plum fruitiness over a cinnamon-tinged body, rounder and less sharply cinnamic than cinnamyl acetate. Useful in plum, apricot and dried-fruit accords and to warm the fruity side of ambers.

Givaudan's ultra-powerful benzodioxepinone: transparent sea-spray and wet-skin ozonic note with grapefruit and watery-floral facets, effective at parts-per-million levels. Cleaner and far more diffusive than Calone, it is the workhorse behind many modern transparent aquatics.

Clean fresh floral-woody with citrus-bergamot lift and a soft lavender-freesia petal character; among the most used materials in perfumery. Universal floralizer and blender bridging citrus tops to floral hearts; IFRA-restricted allergen (oxidation).
Light, fresh-fruity rose ester with a green, slightly herbal sharpness that evaporates cleanly. Gives naturalistic sparkle to the top of rose and geranium accords where acetates feel too sweet.

Solvent-extracted poplar buds: richly balsamic-fruity warmth of honeyed apricot and overripe plum over soft leather, spicy-cinnamic facets and a propolis-resinous depth (bees build propolis from this same bud resin). A base-note fixative that bridges benzoin and labdanum and anchors fruity-chypre, amber and incense accords; usually supplied at 50 percent in alcohol, so dose on the actual absolute content.
Fruity pineapple-banana ester with a waxy, slightly winey nuance, rounder than ethyl butyrate. A tropical top-note builder for pineapple and juicy-fruit effects.
Intensely powerful sulfurous-rubbery, faintly rose-and-beany thiol; used in extreme trace for realistic hyacinth, coffee and durian notes.

TGSC types it as herbal and describes the material as geranium, rose and fruity. Diluted it opens out as floral, rose and geraniol with herbal, green lavender and tea-like nuances, so it sits between a rose-geranium body note and an aromatic. It is useful where a rosy heart needs an herbal, leafy lift rather than more sweetness. Substantivity is about 20 hours neat on a blotter. The same molecule, p-menthane-3,8-diol, is the active of oil of lemon eucalyptus and doubles as an insect repellent.
Rich, sweet fresh-orange odor; the key sesquiterpene aldehyde character-impact molecule of sweet orange oil. Adds juicy natural orange lift.

Diffusive ethereal-fruity ester of unripe plum and apple with a light banana sweetness and a green edge. The sharpest and most fleeting of the hexyl esters, for a fast fruity lift on top of pome and plum accords.
Lush, creamy, banana-custard tropical floral with a spicy-medicinal edge. The complete ylang, warm and narcotic, a fixture of white-floral hearts.
Sweet, warm coumarin-like lactone with tobacco, hay and lightly coconut-caramel facets, the smallest of the fruity gamma-lactones. Adds a soft sweet-hay warmth to tobacco, fruit and gourmand accords.
Powerful, pungent aldehydic-fruity odor with an apple, cocoa and malty nuance. Trace-use for malt, fruity and fermented lift.
Fresh pine and fir-needle oil with woody, herbal, forest and clean disinfectant facets. A bright coniferous top note.
Fresh, diffusive marine-ozonic note with a muguet/lily-of-the-valley undertone and a distinctive cold, frozen effect that adds shivering freshness.

IFF's data sheet places it in the floral territory as muguet, fresh, freesia, and their perfumers call it a clear, crisp and clean straightforward note that gives volume and body to a fragrance. It rounds off green aldehydic muguet notes very well and is useful in building lemon and mandarin fresh citrus types and watery transparent effects. Note that IFF supply it as a blend, an isobutyl cyclohexyl propanal carried in Muguesia rather than a single molecule, so it has no single CAS and the strength on the bench is that of a solution; typical use is up to 5 percent, with substantivity over 72 hours.

Bench tincture of cured vanilla beans macerated in perfumer's alcohol at 10 to 20 percent: soft, rounded, boozy-balsamic vanilla keeping the bean's dried-fruit and faintly leathery complexity, far gentler than the absolute. The traditional way to carry vanilla into a formula at volume without the absolute's viscosity, cost or dark color.
Warm rye-bread spice: d-carvone freshness with earthy-sweet depth. A signature twist in aromatic fougeres and spiced citrus, unforgettable with lavender and bergamot.

Rich, creamy vanilla base with a smooth, unctuous character, enriched with Bourbon vanilla absolute and other naturals. A formulated replacement for Madagascan vanilla absolute, not the natural absolute itself.

Fresh fig-leaf and tomato-stem green with a distinctive watery, slightly minty naturalness. Signature material for fig accords and for giving stems-and-leaves realism to fruity and floral compositions.

Penetrating phenolic-floral ether at the heart of ylang-ylang's medicinal sparkle, with anisic and faintly animalic stable facets. Used in small traces to add ylang realism and a subliminal animal edge to florals.

Sweet licorice-anisic warmth, rounder and softer than star anise, with a faint carrot-seed herbal edge from the umbellifer terpenes. The Pimpinella anise of pastis and aniseed confectionery; interchangeable with star anise only in outline, and the gentler choice for anise in gourmands and fougeres.

Takasago describes it as floral, rosy, waxy and citrus, giving a clear, fresh and natural rosy note. It is the enantiopure (S) saturated alcohol sold as a Chiraroma grade, so it has none of the double bond that makes citronellol turn; that is exactly what it is for. In a formula it is the quiet, stable rose body used in rose, white floral and citrus work, adding a soft waxy petal weight and extending the reach and life of the florals around it. The house reports good substantivity on skin and hair with tenacity beyond twenty-four hours on the blotter, and it holds across the pH range, which is why it survives functional bases that eat prettier rose alcohols.

IFF's olfactive note calls it a unique warm spice reminiscent of cloves, carrying natural white floral notes along with smooth tobacco leaves; Perfumer's Apprentice list it plainly as clove, floral, herbal, and PerfumersWorld add spicy florals such as lily, carnation, tuberose and ylang with dry woody and leathery facets. It is sold as an enhancer and replacer for eugenol and isoeugenol, so in a formula it builds carnation and lily spice and a sweet tobacco-leaf warmth, and adds naturalness to rose and muguet, without leaning on the classic clove phenols. Blotter life is over 48 hours.
Rich amber with dry woody-labdanum depth and a camphoraceous top; a full amber accord in one material.
Creamy coconut lactone, sweet and slightly fruity-caramelic, cleaner and lighter than gamma-nonalactone. A staple of coconut, fig and tropical fruit accords.

Grasse-type centifolia rose absolute: luminous, honeyed, slightly green and peppery rose with a fresh dewy-petal quality, lighter and airier than damascena. Prized in classic French florals and as a natural radiance booster in rose and chypre hearts.

Nez describes Pyromist as an IFF captive whose sparkling scent ignites Jean-Christophe Herault's Speed Smelling 2022 composition, worked in tandem with pink pepper CO2 extract over a theme of raw minerality. The character is a dry, fizzing mineral brightness at the opening; the smoke in that fragrance came from patchouli and vetiver, not from Pyromist, so it should not be read as a smoky material. No chemical identity or technical data has been published.

Liquid wax ester from Simmondsia chinensis with a barely perceptible nutty odor; exceptionally oxidation-resistant carrier for natural perfume oils and skin-safe blends. Its wax-ester structure mimics skin sebum for elegant wear.
Woody-citrus specialty with grapefruit, green rhubarb and vetiver character. Adds sparkling, long-lasting grapefruit effects to modern woody-fresh accords.

dsm-firmenich describe it as an intense, very tenacious sensual dry woody note with an elegant ambery facet, and file it in their ambery palette. The HD grade carries a minimum 95 percent of the preferred isomer, at least three times what the regular Z11 holds, which the supplier calls cleaner and stronger, so it is dosed lower than the standard quality. It is made by sugar fermentation and green chemistry, is ultimately biodegradable and high in renewable carbon. In a formula it behaves as a fond material rather than a top effect: it does not jump off the strip, holding for about a month, and builds a dry radiant amberwood floor under woody and ambery accords while fixing everything above it. Perfumer's Apprentice note a strong trigeminal effect on the regular grade and recommend working Z11 at a 10 percent solution or less.
Fresh, sweet aldehydic-muguet note with citrus, melon-juicy and honeysuckle facets. Brings aldehydic sparkle to lily-of-the-valley and green florals, especially in functional perfumery.

Gourmand, musky, woody, ambery and powdery, classified by the house in the musky family. A FirAbs co-extraction of natural and synthetic ingredients in which the natural part is Hibiscus abelmoschus, the ambrette seed. Firmenich position the FirAbs process as a way to impart the natural feeling and evaporation profile of the botanical to a formula, so its job is to give an ambrette accord the roundness and gradual unfolding of the absolute while behaving predictably. In practice it sits where you would otherwise reach for ambrette absolute, but it is a different material and weighs differently, running more vertical and airy than the absolute it substitutes for.

Perfumer's Apprentice lists it in the floral family as lilac blossom, floral, powdery, and other suppliers extend that to floral, lilac blossom, sweet and powdery with a frankly vintage character. Ventos supplies it as a clear mobile yellow liquid and gives lilac blossom as the odour. It is a compounded reconstruction of a flower that yields no natural extract, and it smells of both the white and the purple lilac, sweet and slightly soapy-powdery rather than sharply green. Perfumers use it as a heart in florals and chypres, where it brings a romantic and somewhat nostalgic depth; on its own it reads as a base that needs support, so it is normally built on rather than used alone.
Sharp, sweet camphoraceous-herbaceous note with green and slightly wine-like facets, a traditional chartreuse-liqueur ingredient. Adds aromatic complexity to herbal colognes and fougère topnotes.

Perfumer's Apprentice files it under animalic and describes the odour as animalic, powerful, iodine and ozonic, supplied as a yellow liquid. The shop is explicit that it contains no animal extract and is not a natural blend: it is a built reconstitution of ambergris rather than a tincture. Bench reports on Basenotes describe it opening dry and woody, almost dusty like old paper, with the animalic sweetness arriving shortly after and holding well. In a formula it is used the way ambergris is used, as a salty mineral undertow beneath woods, amber and musk that stretches the base and lends radiance rather than reading as a note of its own.

The de Laire amber rebuilt by Symrise and presented as the vanillin of the 21st century, a modern successor to Ambre 83 rather than a rename of it. Scentspiracy describe a warm, long-lasting character that bridges gourmand, woody and ambery notes, more complex and nuanced than the 1874 original that first paired natural labdanum with synthetic vanillin, and the launch coverage adds a modern gourmand touch of toffee and precious natural woods. In a formula it is a fixative amber fond that already carries its own sweetness and wood, so it wants less vanillin and less cedar built around it than the old base did, and it reads cleaner and less floral-animalic than Ambre 83 in the drydown.

Firmenich's transparent woody-amber with metallic cedar, dry ambergris and a subtle smoky-incense facet; airy rather than dense. Excellent for diffusive modern woody structures where clean radiance is needed.
Fresh, dry, terpenic-woody oil with a green, resinous, gin-like and slightly peppery character. A crisp top note for fougere, gin and forest accords.
Dry, resinous pine needle: terpenic and balsamic over a woody base, with a sweet, faintly fruity nuance. A large germacrene D share gives it more tail than most pine oils.
Fruity-ambrette musk with a fresh apple-skin brightness and soft powder. A modern transparent musk that keeps fruity compositions airborne.
Faint sweetish, slightly caramellic-acidic character. Used mainly as a fixative and pH/functional adjunct in flavor and fragrance work.
Pyrazine specialty with an intense green galbanum character: sharp pea-pod, bell-pepper and hyacinth-leaf greenness of huge diffusion. Micro-doses electrify green florals, fig and galbanum accords.

Givaudan's own specialties catalogue describes it as a floral base built to match the scent of orris absolute, reflecting the different facets of the natural: gourmand, floral, woody and powdery. The odour index entry reads orris absolute, floral, woody, powdery; retailers add floral-orris and violet, very diffusive. In a formula it acts as a modifier of Isoraldeine 70 and ionone beta, boosting them and imparting a sparkling, vibrant effect, and it blends into floral-green accords and enriches woody and chypre themes. Unlike orris butter it is a mobile liquid, and the base does not cause discolouration.

IFF's data, as carried by Ventos, gives the olfactive description as fresh, pine, lime, herbal and lemon-like. It is supplied as a naturally derived, upcycled terpene fraction rather than a single molecule, which is why the profile spans several notes at once: it opens airy and camphoraceous like pine needle and dries toward a clearly lime and crushed-herb character with lavender and lemon nuances behind it. It is used as a booster for natural lime oil, which fades quickly on its own, and to put pine-like freshness into the top and heart of colognes and fougeres. Because it is a terpene fraction it should be treated as peroxide-sensitive and kept cold and full.

A well balanced, sophisticated synthetic oakmoss reconstitution: oakmoss with woody notes, a complex mixture containing patented Givaudan items that accurately reproduces the effect of natural oakmoss. Physically an amber to straw yellow liquid that may solidify and can be gently warmed back to liquid. Its whole reason for existing is regulatory: unlike the natural absolute it is not subject to IFRA restriction, and Givaudan states it can be used in the same applications and at the same level as the natural extract. That makes it the working chypre floor in a modern formula, where the extract can no longer carry the load.

The whole, undivided distillation of ylang ylang: rich, sweet and heady, jasmine- and neroli-like, with carnation spice. Keeping the heavier fractions makes it creamier and woodier in the dry-down than Extra, and softer at the top.

Not an odorant. Moellhausen sells it as a functional additive that makes the impossible possible, turning physically incompatible ingredients into the components of a single, stable and homogeneous liquid. In the house's words, MYSOL 381 is the key to solubilizing fragrance oils, lipophilic vitamins and other apolar substances in highly polar solvents such as water and ethyl alcohol. In a formula it contributes no scent of its own; it is used to carry a perfume oil into a water or ethanol base and hold it clear. The house describes it only as easy to use and publishes no dosage guidance.

Diffusive waxy aldehyde with a distinctive ambergris-incense dryness, herbaceous-fatty body and remarkable tenacity for an aldehyde; famously overdosed in Chanel No.5-style accords. Gives lift, dry sparkle and a slightly animalic-clean signature.
Sweet rosy-geraniol freshness over a dry grassy base, the budget rose of natural perfumery. Blends rose accords, softens citrus and stretches expensive rose oils gracefully.
Givaudan alicyclic ester musk: soft, creamy, fruity-musky with a serene powdery smoothness and excellent stability in aggressive media. Rounds and sweetens clean musk bases.

Intensely fresh cut-grass and crushed green leaves, the definitive 'leaf alcohol' with a slightly fatty, watery nuance. Used in traces to freshen almost any accord and at higher levels for realistic foliage, galbanum and violet-leaf effects.
Juicy pineapple-orange candy ester, the smell of fruit gum and tropical juice. Sparkles in tiny amounts through any fruity top.

Warm, sweet-spicy and diffusive with the true cinnamon-stick character, rounder and more refined than cassia thanks to eugenol and cinnamal balance. A classic warmth-giver for amber and gourmand accords; use sparingly as it dominates easily.
Dry woody, musty, camphoraceous patchouli-like note with a subtle leathery warmth. Grounds patchouli and woody accords and dries florals.

Symrise nitrile with a fresh sea-breeze, aldehydic-waxy character and citrus-clean facets, giving ozonic lift without aldehyde instability in functional bases. Good for airy, laundry-fresh top notes in both fine and functional perfumery.

Listed by dsm-firmenich in the Gourmand family. The house describes it as capturing the soul of Caribbean rum, authentic, richly fruity and with low alcohol, and says the supercritical CO2 extraction delivers a highly concentrated top note. In their trial compositions it softens a rum accord and sheds its candy-like quality, introduces what the house calls a delicate pink champagne bubble effect that adds brightness, and leaves the whole less powdery and sticky. It elevates the fruity notes with a sense of lift and vibrancy while strengthening the woody base into a deeper, more grounded structure, for a more cohesive result. Made at the Naturals Centre in Grasse from rum sourced in Jamaica and Martinique; the house works it at fractions of a percent and supplies it dilute for trials.
Spicy-camphoraceous Nepalese berry oil with cinnamon, cardamom-like and woody-balsamic facets. Distinctive natural spice note.

The Firmenich blackcurrant base, given by the supplier as green, fresh, floral, fruity and blackcurrant, a colourless to pale yellow liquid with a low flash point. Version F is the greener reading of Cassis 345 and keeps longer than the older B version. It carries the whole blackcurrant-bud effect on one line, so it greens and tartens a fruity top and cuts the sweetness of rose and green floral hearts without a perfumer having to build the accord from single cassis molecules.

Moellhausen names it in BoldBases #3 as the encounter of fascinating smoky notes, the doubled name marking it as an emphatic woody rather than a transparent one. It is a compounded base built around wood with smoke over it, so the burnt and the dry-timber sides arrive already reconciled. In use it behaves as a base-note foundation: it gives a formula a smoky woody floor in a single line, which is where the house positions the BoldBases as solid building blocks.

Roasted coffee with a sulfury, faintly eggy-meaty edge, quieter and less explosive than furfuryl mercaptan. A thioacetate that hydrolyses slowly to the coffee thiol, giving usable roast character with far better shelf life than the free mercaptan, which oxidises to the disulfide.

Galbanum pyrazine: overwhelming green bell-pepper and pea-pod note, the smell of fresh galbanum and Sauvignon grapes, detectable at parts-per-trillion. Use in extreme dilution to add natural leafy realism to green, fig and hyacinth accords.
Warm jasmine ketone with green, herbaceous and slightly fruity-woody facets; rougher and cheaper than cis-jasmone but very useful. Gives jasmonic warmth to soap jasmines and functional florals.

Lavandula latifolia oil: penetrating camphor-eucalyptus freshness over a rough herbaceous-lavender body, much more medicinal than fine lavender. Used for lift in fougeres, aromatic colognes and functional fragrance.

Symrise gives the odour as fruity, pineapple, pear, plum and jackfruit, and calls it an outstanding high-impact material. The published odour threshold in air is 0.00003 ug/l, roughly a thousand times lower than the other fruity esters in the same Symrise range, which is why it is dosed in traces: it is a top-note booster that implements natural effects and deep tropical fruit effects, adds volume to the fruit character and richness to the floralcy, and underlines juiciness and fully ripe fruit characteristics. Symrise recommends traces up to 1 percent.

Symrise woody-amber ketal with a rich, dry ambery-cedar body, faintly fruity-earthy patchouli nuance and outstanding tenacity. Builds dense, modern amber-woody drydowns and supports oud and vetiver themes elegantly.

Symrise's 21st-century reimagining of the 1922 de Laire base, deliberately lighter than the original. Scentspiracy describe an interpretation that emphasises the oakmoss character with iodized and marine notes, intentionally reducing the darkness of the bold leathery-green original while preserving its heritage; fucus absolute supplies the seaweed side that moss carries and the Symrise captive Spicatanate brings freshness, and the result is called very complex yet very true to the spirit of the original. In a formula it lays a modern mossy-marine chypre floor that a contemporary brief can actually carry. It is not interchangeable with the classic isobutyl-quinoline Mousse de Saxe recreation, which is far darker, more leathery and animalic, and it will be weighed differently against it.

Synarome gives it as woody, amber, dry and musky. The supplier lists it as the macrolactone 2-oxacyclododecan-1-one (C11H20O2, MW 184), a colourless to pale yellow liquid, so it behaves as a single macrocyclic base note rather than a compounded speciality. In a formula it is a dry ambery body: it warms and rounds woods without adding sweetness and lends a clean macrocyclic lift to amber and chypre bases.

TGSC types it green at medium odour strength and describes it as sweet, waxy, fresh, green, melon, fruity, pear and cucumber, with a matching fresh green waxy melon pear taste, and records a strip life of 48 hours neat. Bedoukian show BRI 338 in their 2026 fragrance range as a material that brings fruity and floral fresh top notes. In a formula it is the soft green lift that sits between a violet-leaf green and a melon-cucumber freshness: rounder, sweeter and far less aggressive than the parent 3,6-nonadienol, so it can open a fruity-floral or an aquatic accord with a juicy natural edge without the cut-grass bite the alcohol brings.

Bright peppery-green herbaceousness on a phellandrene backbone, drier and sweeter than the root oil and without its heavy celery-animalic floor; a soft musky-woody trail closes it. The gin-botanical top of choice for colognes and green chypres, and far easier to dose than angelica root because the furocoumarin load is low.

Guaiac wood pulled out as a single molecule: the warm dry sweetness of the oil without its smoke or its tar. Softly balsamic with a dusty powdery tail and a whisper of spice, low in contrast, and it works as a rounding agent under woods rather than as the wood itself.
Deep peppery, woody, fruity-spicy note reminiscent of rose absolute. Gives distinctive dark tones and extends rose ketones economically.
Egyptian geranium: greener, sharper and more rosy-minty than the Bourbon grade, with a bright leafy top. A workhorse rose modifier and a natural source of geraniol/citronellol.

Clean white-musk base combining volume and diffusion, with a persistent musky drydown. Fraterworks product 559547 is a proprietary blend, not a single musk molecule. The supplier suggests use from traces to over 20% of a concentrate and pairing with Helvetolide; this is creative guidance, not a finished-product safety limit. Reported blotter persistence exceeds one month, not a measured skin-life value. The named product's IFRA 51 Category 4 certificate is unrestricted, but the finished formula still needs aggregate constituent and safety review. Contains declared Cashmeran; the legacy allergen document does not establish expanded-list clearance.
Fresh minty-green note with fruity rhubarb nuances. Gives cool natural freshness without smelling of toothpaste.

Warm woody-ambery tobacco note, smooth and slightly sweet, sitting between Iso E Super and a blond tobacco absolute. A versatile, inexpensive blender that adds body and elegant amber-tobacco warmth to woody, opulent and fougere bases.
Ripe creamy fig flesh with crisp leaf, mild woody-green bitterness and coconut-lactonic warmth. A complete fig base or green-fruity texture for florals and woods.

Warm herbal-tobacco note with a caramel-like, nutty sweetness and hints of cherry-almond and anisic spice. A naturalising modifier for jasmine, champaca, tobacco and herbal accords. It is a rubefacient that can redden skin at higher doses, so start below 0.5% of the concentrate. The methyl ester of nicotinic acid.

Robertet describes it as floral with honey, green and aqueous notes, and presents it as a good alternative given the rarity and price of the natural raw material. The honey carries the heavy, faintly animalic side of narcissus while the green and watery facets keep it stem-like and fresh, which is the combination that makes narcissus read as a field flower rather than a perfume flower. In a formula it is used where narcissus absolute would be, adding honeyed weight to floral hearts at a workable cost. Flash point above 100 C. Applicable for a perfumery use only.

Macrocyclic diester musk with a clean, sweet, slightly fruity peach-skin muskiness and good stability in functional bases. A gentle, inexpensive musk that layers well under fruity-floral compositions.

Soft lily and rose floralcy over a waxy-green base, blander and quieter than hydroxycitronellal itself. The stable muguet workhorse: it survives soap, alkali and bleach where the parent aldehyde fades, so it carries lily-of-the-valley into functional bases.

Fresh floral-woody linalool homolog, slightly softer, more petally and less terpenic than linalool with a light magnolia-freesia character. Stable linalool alternative for functional bases and transparent modern florals.

Green vegetable sulfide with an onion-garlic bite and a wasabi-like, faintly metallic edge; in dilution a rounded passion fruit and geranium-green facet comes forward. Far softer and more forgiving to dose than the 3-mercaptohexanol thiols, used to green up tropical and cassis accords.

Sweet, warm anise-licorice character, intensely sugary at low levels with a clean, slightly floral-herbal softness. The core of licorice, anise, pastis and ouzo notes; sweetens gourmand and amber compositions efficiently.
Sweet, spicy-carnation with powdery, slightly vanillic softness, gentler and longer-lasting than isoeugenol itself. Used in carnation, ylang and warm-spice bases; carries its own IFRA restriction.

Sharp, diffusive cut-green over waxy and vegetal facets, the rawest and most volatile of the leaf esters. Use where leaf acetate is too heavy and a crushed-stem lift is wanted on the very top of green, fruity and gardenia accords.

Specified by Advanced Biotech as a colourless to yellow liquid with an odour characteristic of vanilla. It is neither vanilla absolute nor vanillin but a compounded natural complex, and the spec puts its alcohol content at 76 to 84 percent by volume, with a boiling point of 78 C and a flash point around 16 C, which tells you almost the whole story: this is a vanilla character carried in ethanol, pale rather than dark, and weak per gram compared with an absolute. In a formula it gives a clean rounded vanilla without the smoky, phenolic and resinous weight that a bean absolute brings, and without the flat single-note quality of vanillin alone. Because it is already four-fifths alcohol it is used neat and it contributes ethanol to the batch, which matters when the concentration is being computed. Twelve-month shelf life, so it is not a bottle to buy ahead.

Sweet rosy ester with red-rose depth, fruity-berry flesh and a honeyed, faintly storax-balsamic drydown. Sits between phenethyl acetate and phenethyl butyrate, adding warmth and body to rose and honey accords.
One of the most radiant sandalwood aroma chemicals, unusual in delivering the natural creamy top note of sandalwood that most substitutes lack. Prized for rich, lifelike santal effects.
Sophisticated woody-orris note with a distinct powdery iris character, warm ambery undertones and elegant tobacco nuances. A classic heart-base for masculine woody accords.
The sharper, more forceful citral isomer: fresh, zesty lemon peel, the backbone of a lemon effect.
Muted woody-ambery ionone with dried-fruit, tobacco and orris nuances, smoother and less floral than beta-ionone. Valuable in osmanthus reconstructions, tobacco notes and to soften woody-amber bases.

Marine specialty note with salty sea-water and watery-grapefruit facets over a slightly floral-ozonic body, drier and more saline than Calone. Used to bring realistic seashore saltiness to aquatic and citrus compositions.
Intensely fruity apple-pineapple odor with a rummy nuance. A classic commodity ester for jammy tropical and apple accords.

Green rose and honey with a waxy sweet-pea body and tropical kiwi-beany nuances. The heaviest of the leaf esters: it holds into the drydown long after hexenyl acetate and butyrate have gone, so use it to carry a leaf-green thread under honeyed florals, mimosa and sweet pea.
Explosive green galbanum top: raw pea pods, crushed leaves and gasoline-fresh bitterness. A trace replaces the fleeting sparkle that galbanum oil loses in compounding.
Fresh fruity-green ester of pear and unripe apple with a light waxy-herbal nuance. A clean, natural-smelling fruity lifter for pear, apple and fresh floral tops.

The Good Scents Company file 1,2-di((1-ethoxy)ethoxy)propane under the fruity odour type, describe it simply as "fruity", and give the functional note that it is an aldehyde generator used for enhancing the flavour of orange drinks. It is an acetal rather than a finished aroma chemical: it carries a light fruity note of its own and, under conditions of use, releases acetaldehyde, the pungent ethereal top that gives citrus and red-berry work its just-cut freshness. In a formula it behaves as a slow fuse under the top note, a way of keeping a citrus or berry accord smelling opened rather than a note you would build around, and it is honestly dull on a blotter compared with what it does in the finished thing. Nothing else in a normal palette performs this job, which is why it earns a bottle.
Creamy, buttery note with cooked milk, butterscotch and faint fruity-winey facets. A smooth dairy-cream builder for milk, caramel and dessert accords.

Bitter green-herbaceous sagebrush with camphoraceous thujone sharpness and a cedar-leaf nuance. Gives striking bitter-green lift to chypres and masculines (Aramis 900 style); thujone-rich and used with restraint.

Perfumer's Apprentice lists the odour as salicylate, green, rosey, freesia note. It is a fractional distillation of Michelia alba, taken from the leaves rather than the flower, with the floral fractions blended back together after fractionation. That leaf origin is why it reads green and freesia-like rather than creamy: it is not the soft citrus-green of a whole magnolia flower oil but a brighter, more salicylate-driven, almost transparent floral. In a formula it behaves like a natural freesia or muguet modifier, lifting a rose or a white floral heart and adding a sunlit salicylate warmth without the fatty weight a flower absolute would bring.

Soft floral hydrocinnamate with hyacinth and rose character over honey, fruity and rum-like facets. A gentle blender for jasmine, hyacinth and narcissus bases where a rounding honeyed floralcy is wanted without added lift.

Herbal, spicy celery and lovage character with warm maple and fenugreek sweetness, savoury brothy depth and phenolic nuances. A tenacious base-note aroma chemical used in savoury gourmand and floral reconstructions.

Crystalline acid with a faint dry balsamic odor over a sour, slightly urinous edge that reads as raw benzoin. A trace sharpens and authenticates benzoin, tolu and Peru reconstructions, and it doubles as a mild crystalline fixative.
Soft fruity-floral heliotrope with cherry, berry and powdery balsamic nuances. Rounds heliotrope and mimosa accords and adds fruity lift to powdery florals.

Fresh green herbal character, grassy and lightly minty, over a spicy cumin warmth with a citral-like citrus lift. Powerful enough to need 10% or less on the blotter; used in traces for perilla and green-spicy top effects, and IFRA restricted for sensitisation.

A deeper, richer relative of linalool: light, fresh muguet/lily-of-the-valley with lilac, citrus, rose, linden and soft fir-conifer facets. An all-purpose floralizer. Commercially a blend of tetrahydrolinalool and tetrahydromyrcenol, so no single CAS applies.

Soft, smoky-sweet rosy-woody oil from Bulnesia sarmientoi with tea-rose, slightly tarry and balsamic facets; semi-solid and rich in guaiol. Classic in rose bases, smoky woods, leather and incense fonds; inexpensive fixative.

A bright, natural-smelling chamomile-flower note: a fruity ester lift with a hint of pear over a clean herbal, softly floral body, without the medicinal edge of the oil. Small additions make synthetic accords read more botanical. An isobutyrate ester (Firmenich Isopentyrate).

Sweet cassia-cinnamon warmth with an oily, woody and slightly papery dryness and a medicinal-phenolic undertone, plus faint resinous nuances. A natural constituent of cassia and cinnamon bark oils; yellow crystals at room temperature. (E)-2-methoxycinnamaldehyde.

Soft violet with a light fruity-berry sweetness and gentle woody warmth, rounder and fattier than alpha-ionone and without its dry orris bite. Smooths violet, osmanthus and fruity-floral hearts, and blurs the edge of woody-amber bases.

Soft floral benzoate with bergamot, herbal-genet and tuberose-lily facets over a plum-grape fruitiness. Weak in impact but very tenacious; a quiet fixative for ylang, tuberose and white-floral bases where a balsamic anchor would sit too heavily.

Intensely bitter green absinthe herbaceousness, sharp, camphoraceous and slightly sweet-anisic in the dryout. Trace doses give an absinthe twist to green and fougere accords; thujone content demands caution.

Steam-distilled from lesser galangal rhizome (Alpinia officinarum), a pungent, warm ginger-like spice with peppery, fresh herbal and slightly camphoraceous, myrtle-like nuances. Distinct from greater galangal (Alpinia galanga); unqualified galangal-root names are not aliases for this material.

IFF's fresh-air aldehyde: clean ozonic sea-breeze note with light muguet-cyclamen florality and a faint metallic sparkle, less fruity than Calone. Excellent for lifting florals, adding laundry-fresh airiness, and building ozone accords with Helional and Calone.
Soft waxy-citrus aldehyde with grapefruit-peel and fatty-soapy nuances, the quietest of the classic series. Adds smooth waxy volume to aldehydic and citrus-floral compositions without harshness.

Powerful green-honey note with hyacinth, leafy and slightly harsh metallic facets that bloom into sweet honey on dilution. Key for honey, hyacinth and green-floral effects; a known sensitizer used at low levels and often stabilized as its dimethyl acetal.

DSM-Firmenich muguet aldehyde developed as a high-impact Lyral alternative: diffusive lily-of-the-valley with fresh watery-citrus sparkle and a magnolia character when overdosed. Extremely low odor threshold, so effective at fractions of a percent.

Sweet creamy coumarinic lactone with coconut, powdery tobacco and a clear spearmint signature from its peppermint origin. The only lactone in the catalog that brings herbal-hay warmth with a minty top; excellent in fougere, tonka and tobacco accords.

Givaudan's 70 percent gamma-methyl ionone grade: a dry, floral violet-orris character with woody and slightly leathery undertones, a creamy powdery body and a warm beeswax-like drydown. It is the muscular grade, drier and more orris-like than the 95 and with the substantivity to push through woods and leathers rather than sit above them; roughly 184 hours on a smelling strip. Core material for violet, orris, iris, leather and powdery accords, and the workhorse choice in fougeres and large-volume production where the 95 is too expensive. Not interchangeable with the 95: swapping grades changes the dryness, not just the strength.
Intense fresh-cut-grass and green-pea note, doubling the leafy character of both its halves. Reinforces natural grassy effects in violet leaf, fig and garden-green accords.
IFF's woody-ambery tobacco note: smooth, slightly sweet pipe-tobacco and cedar character with soft spicy warmth. Rounds tobacco and woody-amber bases and adds volume without phenolic smokiness.

An endogenous steroid, estra-1,3,5(10),16-tetraen-3-ol, that is essentially odorless and included in compositions as a putative human pheromone rather than for any scent contribution. Its role is claimed physiological signaling, adding no perceptible olfactory note to a blend.

Soft, powdery woody-amber ether with a smooth, slightly waxy ambergris character; discreet but very tenacious. Classic fixative for amber and fougere bases where a quiet, rounded ambery fond is wanted rather than a loud woody blast.

Soft, sweet balsamic floral with a lily-like heart, a neroli and labdanum-amber warmth and a quiet fruity, faintly herbaceous undertone. Low impact but persistent, it works as a blender and mild fixative in muguet, lily, freesia and oriental florals. The cinnamic ester of linalool.

A bright citrus note most reminiscent of grapefruit, but useful in lemon, lime, orange and mandarin. Firmenich's recreation of grapefruit oil, fruitier, juicier and more diffusive than their Grapefruit Base 15794 though not as long lasting as that base. It carries the freshness of lemon or lime alongside the grapefruit, so it supports those oils directly and gives a juicy quality to any fruit accord, and it has a distinct floral element that can be pushed further, turning it into a freshener inside a floral accord. It is a true top note and goes quickly on a blotter, so it wants pairing with a fixed citrus or a musk if the effect has to last.

Warm, radiant jasmine ketone with celery, herbaceous-fruity and woody-spicy facets; small amounts give jasmine accords their natural glow. Expensive but transformative in white florals, tea notes and fruity chypres.
Ripe strawberry with seed and green nuances and restrained candy sweetness. Supplier reports more than 400 hours on a smelling strip, not an exact duration or skin longevity.

Mane presents it as a natural molecule with sweet, smoky and clove-like notes, ideal for enhancing gourmand creations, produced with the house's biotechnology; show reporting from Grasse describes it as a natural isolate obtained from rice bran waste with a clove-like smoky vanilla scent and fruity undertones. Mane adds that its ambery notes create a warm atmosphere in compositions, contributing sweet incense and slightly smoky facets, and a spicy twist when it is dropped into a floral bouquet. In a formula it works as a clove-and-woodsmoke bridge into vanilla, caramel and tobacco accords, carrying an impactful signature through the drydown rather than sparkling at the top. Mane discloses no structure or CAS, so this is filed as its own captive and not as a synonym of any eugenol or guaiacol grade.

Soft, sweet, slightly waxy powdery musk with a faint ambrette-like floral warmth; one of the cheapest and most forgiving macrocyclic musks. Used generously (often 5-20% of a formula) as a smoothing fixative base for almost any style.

Mandarin leaf oil built on roughly half methyl N-methylanthranilate: sweet, dusty and deeply fruity, all Concord grape and plum over a narcissus-like floral body with a phenolic, shoe-polish edge. The natural route to the dimethyl anthranilate effect, but the same anthranilate load caps it hard in leave-on work, so it is a trace material.
Ultra-diffusive green apple-skin ester, sharper and more sour-juicy than ethyl 2-methylbutyrate, with a subtle strawberry facet. A trace electrifies fruity-floral tops with crunchy apple realism.

Green rose-leaf with a distinct mushroom-earthy nuance and a warm spicy walnut undertone. The shelf-stable form of hydratropic aldehyde: the same crisp hyacinth-leaf greenness, but it holds up in soap and alkaline bases where the free aldehyde oxidises.
Sweet, soft cold-pressed citrus peel oil, rounder and less tart than mandarin, with a juicy, slightly floral freshness. Bright, friendly citrus top note.
Intensely green, bitter foliage aldehyde of crushed stems and torn leaves that reads convincingly natural. Effective at traces as the green backbone of lilac, hyacinth, violet and muguet accords.

LMR Guatemalan Elettaria cardamomum seed oil: a sharp camphoraceous eucalyptus-mint opening, warm spicy-aromatic heart, sweet balsamic undertones and a persistent woody-floral drydown. It is a specific supplied grade, distinct from cardamom absolute and CO2 extract.
Soft, warm woody note with an orris-powdery, slightly fruity-woody amylene character. A gentle, elegant woody rounding agent for florals and woody bases.

Firmenich specialty delivering a watery floral-chypre freshness with clean marine transparency and a soft mossy-musky trail. Useful to carry aquatic effects from heart into drydown where most ozonics fade.

Listed by Bulkaroma as a colourless to pale yellow clear liquid with a blossom, floral, fresh, ylang character. It is a Givaudan Givco base, a composed ylang rather than a distilled Cananga odorata oil, so it reads as the blossom itself: the fresh top edge of ylang without the fatty, over-ripe weight a natural extra or first can bring.
