In a formula it is the ylang heart in one line, and it keeps a white floral or a solifleur legible where an essential oil would push the composition heavy and yellow.

Sweet powdery heliotrope with almond, cherry-pit, vanilla and faint spicy-floral facets; crystalline and comforting. Central to heliotrope, mimosa and powdery-amber accords and a softener in florals; subject to IFRA restriction.
Cleaner, sweeter and more refined than raw vetiver, with the earthy-smoky notes tamed into a woody, slightly floral dryness. A smooth fixative for fine fragrance woody accords.

Robertet describes a floral note reminiscent of orange flower water, very delicate and cosmetic, slightly green with ionone undertones. It is a fractionation of petitgrain bigarade essential oil reblended to its most floral and woody parts, which is why it reads as clean orange blossom rather than as the sharp green stem note a whole petitgrain gives. Perfumers use it as a neroli replacer or extender, since it carries the orange flower direction at a fraction of the cost and stays cleaner in an eau de cologne. Its restraint is the point: it will support neroli or orange flower absolute without competing with them.

Japanese sour citrus, cold-pressed: a sharp lime-yuzu peel cut with a dry herbal-green bite from its high gamma-terpinene and beta-phellandrene. Sharper and less floral than yuzu, and the natural way to put an austere, savoury edge on a modern citrus top.

Givaudan calls it a rich, natural and enveloping fragrance that reflects the characteristic sweet honey odour diffusion of a rose in the sun. Fresh, diffusive rosy elements give a floral transparency to what is otherwise a powerful and typically honeyed accord, so the honey never reads as flat or waxy sugar. Its sweet and velvety facets are described as particularly interesting in chypre, floral and heavy oriental accords, where the brochure says it gives a long lasting body effect: this is a base-register material used to warm and hold a rose rather than to open one.

Symrise present it as the most powerful amber ever with an unparalleled long-lasting effect, and as the third in the dry-woody ambergris trilogy that began with Ambrocenide in 1997 and continued with Ambrostar. Launch coverage describes a potent dry woody-ambery odour with musky aspects, giving a softer, more sensual-animalic character than its predecessors, with peppery accents that make it particularly suited to oud accords. It is built from sustainable alpha-cedrane and carries an unusually low perception threshold. In a formula it behaves like a super-amber with the edges taken off: use it at a trace where Ambrocenide would read too screechy and metallic, for round ambery power and a drydown that will not quit.

Transparent, radiant jasmine with a soft citrus-magnolia freshness; almost airy, more an effect than a smell on the blotter. A cornerstone diffuser used at high levels to add volume, lift and natural bloom to jasmine, floral and citrus accords.

Crystalline peppermint alcohol delivering intense cooling trigeminal freshness with a clean minty odor. Trace amounts sharpen fresh-aquatic and fougere top notes and add a cold-air sensation; easily dominates if overdosed.
Sweet, warm spicy-clove with a distinct tea-like, slightly herbal-carnation nuance, smoother than eugenol. Found in rose and bay oils; severely IFRA-restricted, used only in traces where permitted.
Dry, woody-minty freshness, less sweet and less cooling than menthol. Builds the body of peppermint reconstitutions and adds dry mint facets to geranium and herbal accords.

Fresh, clean waxy rose petal with a citrus zing and a cool ozonic air; fatty, but softer than the aldehyde, so it brightens florals with a dewy, just-washed sparkle. 10-Undecen-1-ol, the alcohol of aldehyde C-11 undecylenic.
Powdery violet and iris with creamy suede, restrained leather and warm wood. A proprietary orris-butter replacement base for floral, woody and chypre structures.

Floral, fruity and powerful. Robertet describes it as a marvelous interpretation of the ylang flower. It gives the creamy banana-and-custard fruitiness that distinguishes ylang from the other white flowers, in a compounded form that holds its character across batches where the natural grades (extra, I, II, III) each smell measurably different from one another. Being flagged powerful, it carries a heart accord on a small percentage.
Sweet cherry-almond aldehyde with a woody, slightly phenolic-cresylic nuance, more cherry-pit than benzaldehyde. Deepens cherry and amaretto accords and adds kernel realism to stone-fruit notes.

dsm-firmenich present it in their own 2025 annual report as a groundbreaking cedarwood ingredient with a rich ambery undertone, exceptional performance and impressive longevity, launched in early 2025 and reported around ten times stronger than the comparators it displaces, so far less material is needed. Fragrantica lists it as a dsm-firmenich captive woody-ambery molecule that adds intensity, power and diffusion, and it sits in the base of Cerruti 1881 Vivo Elixir beside oud, labdanum and Virginia cedar, where it reads as a smoky ambery trail with stronger lasting intensity. In a formula treat it as a woody-amber power material and a fixative rather than as a cedar in its own right: it carries the drydown and lends diffusion, and a purer crystallised version, Amberever Neo, followed in November 2025.
Light, dry hydrocarbon woody note with a fresh cedar-shavings character; the principal terpene of cedarwood oils. Used as an inexpensive woody top-to-heart extender.
Camphoraceous-minty with celery-like herbal and slightly fruity facets, characteristic of verbenone-type rosemary. Adds dry herbal complexity to rosemary and aromatic accords.

Winey, fruity-fermented note with sharp boozy lift, green apple-skin and slightly cheesy-waxy ethyl ester facets from wine lees. Adds authentic aged-spirit and champagne effects to boozy, fruity and chypre compositions.

Philippine calamondin peel, cold-pressed: a mandarin-lime hybrid, sweet-tart and almost entirely limonene, so it reads bright and juicy with very little bitterness. A cheerful natural top note; like sweet orange it is fleeting and oxidises quickly, so it wants aldehyde or citral support.

IFF's intensely dry woody-amber with a transparent, diffusive character and a slightly fruity-woody nuance; less aggressive than Amber Xtreme but from the same performance-driven family. Adds lift, dryness and enormous longevity to modern woody bases.

Floral with indolic notes. Robertet calls it a very powerful and sophisticated floraline that will enhance orange flower notes. That is its stated function rather than a standalone character: it is a booster, dosed under an orange blossom or neroli accord to deepen and animalise it. The house flags it as very powerful, so it belongs in a formula at trace level, and overdosing it will push a white floral straight into the sour indolic territory perfumers usually spend effort avoiding.
Fruity-oily, rose-cognac and waxy-nut note with a fatty body; used in fruity, brandy and rosy accords.

A powerful complex, green vegetative leafy aroma with a bit of sweetness on dry down, per the supplier listing. It reads as unripe fig and cut stem rather than ripe fruit: sappy, vegetal, a little bitter at the top before the sweetness arrives underneath. Exceptionally potent and persistent, still prominent at 5% and above, so it is dosed as a modifier and not as a main note. The working partners are the lactones (gamma-octalactone, jasmolactone) for the milky side of a fig accord, and florals or softer greens to take the edge off the stem.
Sweet caramel-fruity note with a jammy strawberry and toffee character, softer and longer-lasting than maltol. A smooth caramel extender for fruity-gourmand bases without ethyl maltol's sharpness.

Givaudan's linear watery-melon aldehyde: transparent watermelon and marine freshness with citrus and muguet nuances, smoother and more floral than Calone. Formerly captive; now a staple for contemporary clean-marine masculines.

IFF describes this material as "extremely powerful amber and woody", and supplier listings of the same solution give it as amber, woody and musky. ScenTree places the molecule itself in the woody / ambery-woods group with cedar, ambergris and milky facets. In a formula it behaves as a dry ambery fixative with a faint animalic-musky edge and no sweetness, working best as a modifier that adds body and length under existing woody-ambery materials rather than as a note that reads on its own. This grade is the ketal carried at roughly 8.5 percent in isopropyl myristate, so it pours and dissolves without warming, and it is weighed at roughly twelve times the dose of the neat crystal.

Soft honeyed floral with dewy hyacinth, dried tea-rose and a leafy-green edge, closing powdery with a faint petitgrain nuance. The slow-release form of phenylacetaldehyde: the same hyacinth-honey character without resinifying in the bottle, holding as a long quiet heart in floral compounds.
Sweet ripe pineapple with a banana-apricot roundness, less aggressive than allyl caproate. Reliable tropical juiciness for summer accords.

Givaudan's reading of the mamey, Mammea americana, a fruit of the Caribbean and northern South America. The Givco list describes it as powerful and long-lasting, providing a warm, fruity volume to chypre, osmanthus and spicy accords, and adding richness to jasmine and tuberose. It is a body note rather than a bright fruit top: it fills a formula out from underneath instead of flashing off, which is why it is reached for when a chypre or a white floral smells correct but thin.

Fraterworks 225868, a modern green floral hyacinth base with aldehydic radiance. Distinct from Hyacinth Absolute, Hyacinth Body, Jacinthia and Hyacinth TruAbs. Supplier strip life exceeds 48 hours; this is a lower bound, not an exact duration. Supplier IFRA 51 Category 4 maximum is 5.55% in finished product. Strength is an editorial estimate; 10% working dilution is a convention. The linked evidence does not include an SDS.
Sweet green-apple fruity note with pineapple, winey-estery and soft balsamic facets; a fresh top-note modifier lending grape, pear and apricot nuances.
Sweet burnt sugar, maple and caramel with a warm toasted edge. A gourmand modifier distinct from the 3,4-dimethyl isomer CAS 13494-06-9.

Sal tree resin (Shorea robusta) destructively distilled in a sealed clay pot: dry smoke and charred resin with a pine-terpenic edge, settling into leather and a soft amber sweetness. Less phenolic than Choya loban and without the marine funk of Choya nakh; it is the smoky backbone of shamama and hina attars. Use in traces.

Warm, spicy-balsamic and distinctly medicinal-bitter resin note with mushroomy, licorice-anisic and sweet ambery undertones (furanoeudesmadiene character). Adds mysterious depth to incense and amber accords; powerful and slightly rubbery in overdose.
Sweet, very tenacious lily and linden-blossom Schiff base with orange-flower undertones. Long-lasting muguet-lily heart for soaps and fine fragrance.
The generic pencil-shavings cedar: dry, soft, woody and slightly sweet. The affordable backbone of woody bases and a natural cedryl source.

IFF's Schiff base of indole and hydroxycitronellal, listed simply as floral, jasmin, animal. The condensation creates a jasmine character that neither parent molecule has on its own: the raw fecal edge of indole is tamed into a warm, narcotic white-floral body with only a slight animalic growl left showing. Exceptionally tenacious. Sold only as a 50 percent solution in benzyl benzoate or DEP because the neat material is an intensely coloured viscous liquid, so it is weighed at double the neat dose. Use it to extend and deepen natural jasmine absolute, or to give a synthetic jasmine, tuberose or orange blossom accord the indolic weight it otherwise lacks.
Radiant, velvety cedar-wood blend with subtle green facets and smooth volume, incorporating rare natural oils. A formulated woody base, not an alias for Iso E Super.
Honeyed floral-hay sweetness with green tobacco, beeswax and slightly animalic facets. Adds sun-dried floral warmth to chypres, hay accords and narcotic florals.
Rosy floral ester with a green geranium body and a lemony verbena edge on the dryout. Used where a geranium-inflected rose wants sweetness and lift without the harshness citronellol brings.

Givaudan files it in the herbal-agrestic family with notes given as herbal, spicy and celery. It is a modifier rather than a lead: the house calls for it in aldehydic chypres and fougeres, pairing it with basil and tarragon oils in the top and using it to complement jasmine complexes, and recommends it wherever lovage and celery notes are desired. In practice it supplies the savoury, slightly soupy green-spice bite that makes a herbal top read as a real plant rather than a clean terpene, and it carries far enough that a small overdose will dominate an accord.

Bedoukian describes it as aldehydic with peely, fresh notes of tangerine and orange. Their captive BRI 387 is the cis C12 aldehyde, so under the citrus there is the fatty, waxy character long-chain aldehydes always carry, and that is what separates it from a plain citrus oil. In a formula it puts the zest back into a top note: a trace over sweet orange or mandarin restores the bitten-peel effect that distillation strips out, and it gives a classic aldehydic opening a fresh citrus direction instead of a soapy one. The house works it around the one percent mark in the concentrate, which tells you it is potent and easy to overdose into candle wax.

The high-purity cis isomer of methyl dihydrojasmonate, and the most concentrated expression of the Hedione effect: a wide, luminous jasmine transparency with a fruity-magnolia softness that lifts everything placed beside it. Used where radiance is wanted without weight, at a fraction of the dose plain Hedione would need.

The key odorant of saffron: powerful spicy-phenolic, hay-tobacco and leathery note with a metallic-sweet edge, harsh neat but magical in traces. Use highly diluted to authenticate saffron, leather and tobacco accords.
Sweet floral-fruity note of orange blossom and strawberry over a clean musky-naphthyl base with honeyed jammy undertones. Fixative for neroli and berry accords.
Sweet floral note with grape, orange-blossom and wintergreen facets; milder and less harsh than methyl anthranilate.
Dry, clean, slightly sweet nitro musk that was the cheap workhorse of soap perfumery for a century. Effectively banned (REACH/IFRA prohibitions); included for historical formula reference.
Sweet, fruity rum-like odor with pineapple and grape facets. A simple commodity ester for fruity lift.
Mild, sweet floral alcohol between rose and muguet with a slightly herbaceous, powdery-lime blossom nuance. A quiet blender that adds petal volume to rose, muguet and lilac accords.
Powerful nutty popcorn note with roasted peanut and hazelnut facets. Used in trace amounts for roasted, cereal and nutty gourmand effects.
Juicy peach-apricot note with a warm woody-musky undertone, more diffusive and less creamy than the lactones. Builds radiant modern peach accords and pairs beautifully with osmanthus and rose.

Specialty aquatic blender with a soft watery-green freshness, light melon-cucumber facets and a clean floral transparency. Handy as a rounder in marine accords where neat high-impact ozonics would feel harsh.
Fresh, sweet piney-citrus terpene with a slightly anisic, plastic-lime nuance. Used in lime and pine accords and to give a natural terpenic edge to citrus reconstitutions.
Fatty, waxy, soapy-rancid odor with a sour-goaty nuance. Trace-use acid for waxy, cheesy and skin-like effects.
Warm phenolic-medicinal thyme, sweeter and less tarry than carvacrol. Trace doses give herbal-spicy warmth to fougères, chypres and mouthwash-fresh accords.

Odorless light emollient ester (bis(2-ethylhexyl) adipate) used as a phthalate-free solvent and plasticizer in perfumery, candles and cosmetics. Gives good spread and solvency with a drier feel than IPM.

IFF's sandalwood base from the Oliffac range. Perfumer Supply House lists it plainly as a warm buttery sandalwood note; perfumers working it describe it as creamy and soft with something animalic underneath that makes it friendly rather than austere, and a distinct grain or malt-cereal facet that earns it a place in gourmand work. Scentspiracy's account of the range calls it a creamy, milky-wood heart that is velvety and exceptionally tenacious, dosed from around one percent to the high single figures of a formula. In a formula it is a whole sandalwood accord in one bottle rather than a single santalol molecule, so it fills the woody base with far less building than Sandalore or Javanol alone, and its musk and phenolic constituents mean it fixes the blend as well as scenting it.
The full fresh-peel lime: zesty, green and slightly floral, richer and more complex than distilled lime. Phototoxic; the cola-and-mojito sparkle of classic colognes.

Mothball-fecal in concentration yet luminous and narcotic in dilution: the molecule that gives jasmine, orange blossom and tuberose their living animal breath. Essential in trace amounts for realistic white florals and animalic accords; discolors formulas over time.
Softer, sweeter and more rounded than methyl salicylate, with a wintergreen connotation over a heavy floral-fruity body. A wonderful blender for ylang-ylang, cassie and mimosa.

Givaudan gives Gardamide as a zesty grapefruit citrus heart note with aspects of crisp rhubarb, delivering long-lasting citrus freshness and working well alongside other citrus and earthy green notes. Being an amide, N,2-dimethyl-N-phenylbutyramide, rather than a terpene, it holds for several days on the blotter and stays put in fabric conditioner, antiperspirant, shampoo and detergent bases where citrus oils vanish. In a formula its job is to keep grapefruit alive past the top: it sits under bergamot and grapefruit oils and carries their zest into the heart, with the rhubarb edge sharpening green and earthy accords.

Soft, long-lasting green-floral with a balsamic salicylate sweetness, like ivy leaves in warm sun. A discreet fixative-blender that carries green freshness into the drydown of florals, fougeres and suntan accords.

Published by IFF with the same olfactive description as Ambermor: a strong woody amber, sweet earthy and musky, with a delicate animalic tonality, high heart and base impact and substantivity beyond forty-eight hours across fine fragrance, soap, shampoo, deodorant and detergent, used from traces upward. It is a readily biodegradable, stabiliser-free quality. In a formula it does what Ambermor does, giving amber-woody volume, diffusion and fixation to the whole composition. Distributor specifications give the same ambroxan CAS and describe the physical form as white flakes rather than the crystalline powder of Ambermor, so the difference on record is presentation and specification, not a published change in odour or strength.

Sharp, ethereal fruit ester: a quick, juicy flash of apple and pineapple with a sweet tutti-frutti edge and a faint floral hint. Its odour threshold is very low and it evaporates within about an hour, so it serves only as a top-note lift. Methyl 2-methylpropanoate.
Drier and more resinous than Indian album, with a woody-balsamic and slightly rooty character from Osyris heartwood. Used as an alternative natural sandalwood source.
White grapefruit: brighter, sharper and more bitter-pithy than the pink grade, with a crisp sulfurous sparkle. A distinct expression of grapefruit peel.
Soft peony-mimosa floral with fresh rosy and slightly green facets. Rounds and naturalizes light floral hearts.
Powerful, diffusive amber-woody note with ambergris, tobacco, vetiver and smoky nuances and a slight musky undertone. A tenacious fixative for woody-amber bases.
Rustic cousin of ylang-ylang: sweet floral with leathery, smoky-green undertones. Cheaper and rougher than ylang, useful in soap and masculine florals.

Symrise's blend is described as musk, cosmetic, creamy and balsamic. It is not a single molecule but a ready-made musk accord built primarily on Globanone, so instead of the flat linearity of one macrocyclic musk it reads as a soft, skin-close musk with a milky cosmetic roundness and a faint balsamic sweetness underneath. In a formula it is dropped in wholesale as the musk foundation, anywhere from 1 to 20 percent, to give a drydown that soft powdery lift and to hold heavier materials down without imposing a character of its own.

Natural coumarin isolated from cassia bark: warm, sweet hay and tonka with a spicy, cinnamon-like edge and hints of almond, tobacco and custard. Spicier and more pungent than synthetic coumarin, without its cherry note; for fougeres, tobacco and vanilla accords.

Mane's gourmand speciality base opens on a dank earthiness before turning into a rich gourmand accord that the supplier describes as reminiscent of carrot cake, caramel, liquorice and spices, then dries down exceptionally balanced and vanilla-leaning. It is built on an overdose of Mane's Presantone H captive, which is what gives the accord its baked, syrupy body rather than a flat vanilla sweetness. In a formula the loamy opening pairs with rich patchouli while the vanilla-leaning drydown modernises classic-inspired blends; it holds over 24 hours on a smelling strip. Supplied unfiltered to preserve olfactory matter, so it is usually macerated for up to a month, then chilled and filtered before use.

Fatty melon-rind aldehyde, waxy and green with violet-leaf and cucumber facets over a chicken-fat base, sitting between 2,4-heptadienal and 2,4-decadienal on the dienal ladder. Captured by the IFRA 2,4-dienals group prohibition, so it is reference only rather than a usable trace material.

The Good Scents Company records this IFF alcohol at medium odour strength with the description "floral minty earthy leather", and notes hyacinth, minty and woody character. It is the (2,4-dimethylcyclohexyl)methanol behind the Floralol family: a soft, non-shouting floralising alcohol rather than a top-note lift. TGSC publishes a blotter life of 28 hours at 100%, which places its work in the heart, where the minty-earthy shadow underneath the floral keeps hyacinth and muguet accords from reading sugary.

A dry woody vetiver-like ester (also sold as Vetynal) with an earthy, ambery character brightened by a grapefruit-like sparkle, more transparent and contemporary than natural vetiver oil. A cost effective vetiver modifier and woody-amber building block for vetiver reconstitutions, chypres, fougeres and functional bases.
A synergistic nitro musk base with a powerful, silky-smooth musk character; clean, delicate and sensual. Contains IFRA-compliant Musk Ketone, 300+ hour tenacity.
Intensely fresh, sparkling citrus-lime top note with floral rose-lavender nuances. Very volatile burst used in eaux de cologne and fresh top-note constructions.
Neo-gourmand amber base with dark rum, caramel and red fruit over gentle florals, then vanilla, tonka, patchouli, vetiver and labdanum.
Sweet rosy-honey ester with fruity champagne and slightly balsamic nuances; soft, rounded and very stable. Adds honeyed rose body to florals and works beautifully in soap.
Sweet, diffusive fruity ester of apple and blueberry character with a slightly cheesy-fermented undertone. Adds juicy realism to apple, berry and tropical accords at low dosage.
Musty, pungent, leafy-green with vegetative and fruity apple-banana nuances.

Glyceryl triacetate: odorless, water-tolerant solvent and mild fixative used in perfumery, flavors and e-liquid style bases; good for dissolving vanillin and crystalline sweet materials. Safe, biodegradable, and helpful in candle and functional applications.

Coconut lactone with an oily body and green, hay-like edges, drying to a creamy coumarinic tonka nuance. Completes the delta series next to gamma-heptalactone, which is sweeter and nuttier; use it where coconut should read fresh-husk rather than candied.

Symrise describe a complex animalic note reminiscent of ambergris, civet and musk laid over a rather sweet lactone accord; the datasheet lists it as animalic, white flower, civet, ambergris, and The Good Scents Company reads it at 10% as dry, animal, amber, ambergris, civet, musk. In a formula it does two jobs at once: it imparts the opulence of gardenia and tuberose while carrying the animalic weight underneath, which is why it is a standard component of civet and castoreum reconstitutions. Used at traces up to about 1 percent, and it still measures 52 hours on the blotter from a 10 percent solution.

Sparkling, sweet-tart citrus with a distinctive floral-lavender and slightly spicy tea-like nuance, more refined than other citrus oils. The backbone of colognes and fougeres; perfumers use it generously in top notes to lend elegance and lift. FCF grade: bergapten/furocoumarins removed for photo-safety; the scent profile is essentially the same, marginally less full in the deep facets.
Dry fruity ethereal note with pineapple, brandy and banana facets; adds lift to citrus and fruity topnotes, alkali-stable.
Sharp fatty-acid odor, cheesy and sweat-like. Trace ingredient for natural animalic, dairy and fruit nuances.
Sweet cinnamic-vanilla balsam, drier than Peru

Givaudan gives it as a fresh herbal note with hints of rhubarb and banana and a lilac background, filed under the fruity family with rhubarb, aromatic and lilac facets. It is a soft, generous top-note material rather than a sharp one: it blends into fruity, citrus and herbal accords and lifts their freshness without pulling the accord toward solvent. The house reports it performing well in toiletries, soaps and detergents, and it can be used at generous levels for a molecule of this weight.
Fresh, green, gin-like juniper berry: coniferous, peppery and clean. A crisp lift for aromatic and woody-fresh accords.
Odorless crystalline coolant with a slow onset and an unusually long cold tail. Chosen over the menthol derivatives when the cooling should build gently and last, with no minty smell of its own.

A Givaudan speciality supplied in triethyl citrate. Perfumer's Apprentice describe it as cocoa, vanilla and powdery: it brings a rich cocoa note together with a warm vanillic background, with the powdery effect of chocolate just as when a tin of drinking-cocoa powder is opened. It is built on Givaudan captives, Levistamel, Isobutavan and Ultravanil, where Isobutavan carries a sweet creamy vanillic character reminiscent of white chocolate and cream soda with a soft apricot feeling and Ultravanil boosts it with a very powerful vanilla-absolute note. In a formula it is the shortcut to a chocolate accord and a warm, slightly dusty sweet fond under gourmand, oriental and tobacco compositions, sitting in the base and dragging the drydown sweeter.
Bland, oily fixed carrier oil used for massage-oil bases and occasionally as a natural-perfumery diluent; add an antioxidant to slow rancidity.
Floral hyacinth-rose with chocolate, narcissus, lilac and reseda facets. Widely used in hyacinth and tropical floral accords.

Solvent-extracted from the flower of Humulus lupulus and sold at 50% in triethyl citrate. Bulkaroma tags the material bitter, green, herbal and spicy; a working perfumer's account of the Payan Bertrand grade puts it more plainly as a beer intensified, with a herbal character, fruity and slightly butyric, meaning cheesy albeit subtly. That butyric edge is what makes it interesting and what makes it dangerous: owing to its unique profile and its potency it is used, if at all, in traces, worked into fruity, herbal, woody and spicy accords for a bitter green realism nothing else gives. Being a 50% cut in TEC, it is weighed at double to land the same absolute in the formula.

Green-floral hyacinth with earthy mushroom and rose-stem nuances, much smoother and more stable than the free aldehyde. Workhorse for hyacinth, lilac and green rose effects in soaps and fine fragrance.
Warm, sweet-spicy oil from the aril of nutmeg, brighter and more terpenic-fresh than nutmeg seed oil, with a delicate balsamic sweetness. Spicy top-heart accent for ambers.
Deep aquatic-floral with hay, anise and leathery-fruity undertones, mysterious and dense. A drop adds exotic wet-flower realism to aquatic florals and incense compositions.
Warm, creamy, natural-smelling sandalwood with a soft, slightly floral-musky character; a very versatile woody smoother. Marketed under several names across houses.
Soft fruity-balsamic with wintergreen and ylang nuances, gentle and blending. A quiet fixative-modifier for heavy florals and fruity chypres.

The Corsican verbenone chemotype: soft green-herbaceous rosemary with only a whisper of camphor, a hay-sweet body and a fruity, almost apple-like edge. Where the cineole and camphor grades bite, this one folds into lavenders, fougeres and green colognes without the medicinal sharpness.

Powdery icing-sugar character with strawberry and light fruity facets. Supplier description accompanies its 10% DPG stock; this row identifies the underlying chemical, not that diluted stock. Heart filing is a catalog convention, not measured evaporation or longevity.

Bedoukian describes it as a green, cucumber, floral with orris and honeydew melon notes. The Good Scents Company reads it as fresh green violet cucumber at 1% in DPG, opening at 5% into green, melon, fatty cucumber with oily mushroom and faintly fishy nuances, rates the strength high and recommends smelling it at 1% or less, with substantivity greater than 24 hours at 100%. In a formula it is the natural-green top that makes melon, cucumber and violet-leaf accords read as fruit and leaf rather than as a flat chemical green, and a trace lifts orris and iris reconstructions.
Fresh, dry, woody-camphoraceous alcohol with a slightly earthy-pine and lime-like nuance. Used to add a crisp, dry woody-coniferous edge.
Powdery ylang floral character with a light fruity, wild-blackberry nuance. Heart filing is a catalog convention, not measured evaporation or longevity.

PerfumersWorld list it as ambergris, sweet, dry, amber, woody, mossy, with an odour life of 400 hours on the smelling strip and a base-note placement; suppliers describe a fumey, extremely radiant ambroxan-type dryness with an animalic, old-wood edge. IFF built it as a direct replacement for natural ambergris tincture, roughly equivalent to a 5 to 10 percent tincture and therefore stronger than most tinctures, and it contains no animal extract. In a formula it is the dry ambergris floor that stretches a base out and adds skin-radiance without sweetening it. A compounded base, so no single CAS.

A fresh and powerful fruity grapefruit-zest odour with hints of green, floral and transparent notes. Suppliers describe it as stronger, much longer lasting and more grapefruit-like than the natural oil, without decaying into the sulphurous notes that spoil aged grapefruit oil, and with minimal photosensitising effect. In a formula it is the workhorse grapefruit: used generously it becomes the body of a grapefruit accord, and at low levels it lifts and sharpens any citrus opening while surviving far longer than the oil would.

Herbal, dry and spicy, with oregano and thyme character, leafy green nuances and a light citrus-peel undertone. Less phenolic than carvacrol. Used in aromatic, fougere and citrus compositions. Fraterworks rates direct strength 3/10 and blend impact 4/10. Its reported blotter life is greater than 8 hours, a lower bound rather than an exact measurement. Lluch's IFRA 51 certificate lists Category 4 at 100%; this is not a recommendation for undiluted skin use. The expanded EU allergen declaration lists each reported allergen below 0.001%, not necessarily absent.

Powerful sweet vanilla-anisic note with a spicy, slightly medicinal-clove undertone, several times stronger than vanillin. A booster for vanilla and licorice effects where high impact at low dosage is needed.
The (S)-(-) enantiomer found in rose oil: finer, softer and more petal-like than racemic citronellol, with less citronella harshness. The choice for prestige rose bases where naturalness matters.

Sparkling, sweet-tart citrus with a distinctive floral-lavender and slightly spicy tea-like nuance, more refined than other citrus oils. The backbone of colognes and fougeres; perfumers use it generously in top notes to lend elegance and lift. FCR grade: the FURANOcoumarins are rectified and REDUCED rather than removed. That is the only claim the grade carries: one supplier also prints coumarin-free, but rectification targets the phototoxic furanocoumarins and bergamot's other coumarins are not what it removes, so this row does not repeat it. Coumarin is an EU-declarable allergen and a free-of claim about it belongs on an analysis, not in a description. The residual figure is the supplier's own spec rather than a standard, so treat it as restricted until that figure says otherwise; the FCF grade is the bergapten-free one. Scent is essentially the plain oil, marginally less full in the deep facets.

Deep, dense and tenacious creamy-woody extract with a slightly resinous, sweeter facet than the distilled oil. Used in trace amounts as a rich fixative and to reinforce natural sandalwood impressions.
Dry, bitter camphoraceous note with earthy fennel character, harsher than camphor. Adds authentic bitterness to fennel, absinthe and lavender-spike reconstructions.

Fresh, sweet pine-fir balsamic ester with a camphoraceous-herbal edge and a light citrus lift; milder and sweeter than fenchyl alcohol. Supports pine, lavender and fougere structures where bornyl acetate reads too sharp, and it flashes off quickly.

Symrise's datasheet gives floral, jasmine, lactonic, tuberose, yellow plum; The Good Scents Company reads it as fresh, waxy, coconut, jasmin, spicy and natural, with sweet, lactonic, creamy, coconut, fatty, powdery and coumarin nuances. In a formula it gives opulent white flowers such as jasmine and narcissus a creamy, rich body with a faint animalic edge, puts a milky accent into sandalwood, and underlines the fruit in osmanthus and the tropical side of frangipani, at roughly 0.05 to 3 percent. Very tenacious for a heart material, around 192 hours on the blotter at full strength.
Fruity ester: apple and pear with a sweet, green pineapple-peach character.

A vivid fruity freshness carrying apple, pear, banana, strawberry and fig nuances, with the apple and pear accents leading. IFF positions it for high impact at low dosage: it enhances both the top and the heart, brings out their diffusion, and extends brightness and longevity rather than flashing off like a simple ester. In a formula it is the material that keeps a fruity opening legible into the heart, and the house cites an allergen-free profile plus stability in demanding media including water-based systems, so it also serves where a natural fruit note would collapse. Debuted at SIMPPAR 2026.
Very faint waxy-oily, mildly iris-like note; used mainly as a soft, low-odor diluent and body-builder in fine fragrance.

Robertet describes it as floral, spicy, fresh orange flower and honey. It is made by refining a floral alcoholic infusion of Tunisian Citrus aurantium blossom through supercritical CO2 fractionation followed by partial concentration, so it reads as the living flower rather than the heavier sweetness of an absolute: bright and slightly green on top, honeyed and faintly clove-spicy underneath. In a formula it is the naturalist's orange flower, used to give neroli and white-floral hearts a freshly picked lift the absolute cannot supply, and to warm a citrus cologne without dragging it into indolic territory.

The key odorant of natural Tonkin musk: warm, sweet, powdery-animalic musk of great elegance and skin-like sensuality. Used at low levels to give authentic animal warmth to musk accords and reconstitutions of deer musk.

Woody, resinous, sweet, sugary, toffee, fresh, slightly phenolic, in Robertet's own words, supplied as a natural on an MPG carrier. It carries the toffee-balsamic sweetness of fir balsam with a fresh coniferous edge on top and a faint tarry phenolic corner underneath. It works as a fixative and a warmth source in fougeres, chypres and conifer accords, and the carrier makes it far easier to dose accurately than the neat absolute.

Bedoukian describes the neat material as a powerful green cucumber and violet leaf with orris notes, and elsewhere as an intense green floral with notes of violet and hints of walnuts. The Good Scents Company reads it at 10% in DPG as green violet floral walnut, rates the odour strength high and records substantivity greater than 400 hours at 100%. It is the nitrile route to a violet-leaf green: extremely diffusive and very tenacious, so it is dosed in traces, and because nitriles hold up where the corresponding aldehyde would not, it is the usual choice for green floral character in bleach, detergent and other aggressive bases. Bedoukian sells it neat as BRI 640N and at 10% in DPG as BRI 640DPG; this row is the neat material.

Dark, savoury forest floor: wet soil and damp moss under an intense dried-porcini umami, turning faintly musky-animalic and dark-chocolate as it settles. A trace-level fixative that gives leather, chypre and vetiver bases a living, rotting-wood depth no synthetic mushroom note reaches.
Dry, fresh, coniferous-woody oil with a slightly smoky, resinous and green-terpenic character. A crisp top-heart note for fougere, forest and masculine accords.

The Good Scents Company describe it at twenty-five percent in dipropylene glycol as "mild cooling mentholic minty" and rate the odour strength low; the taste is "Medicinal, menthol", an initial menthol note that fades into a lingering cooling feel. Advanced Biotech go further and sell WS-23 as the coolant that gives a clean, long-lasting cooling sensation without the accompanying minty flavour or odour. Both readings are true at their own dose: concentrated it is faintly mentholic, at use level it is close to odourless and works as sensation rather than smell. That is exactly what separates it from WS-3 and from menthyl lactate, which bring mint character along with the cold. Reach for it when a fresh or aquatic accord needs to feel cold without any mint arriving in the top, and expect it to add nothing to the pyramid.

Givaudan calls it green and powerful, with floral shades of hyacinth and rose and a hint of watercress, giving a natural green freshness to top notes. It is phenethyl isopropyl ether, and the useful thing about it is that the green reads as a living stem rather than the sharp cut-grass of a leaf aldehyde, so it opens a floral without the metallic bite. It lasts about a day on the blotter, which places it firmly in the top, and it is used up to 3 percent; it holds up well across soap, shampoo, fabric conditioner and antiperspirant bases where softer green naturals would simply disappear.
Sweet, warm balsam with vanilla, cinnamic and ambery facets and a powdery, woody-resinous dry-down. A fixative in amber, leather and vanilla accords.

Fresh, tangy-bitter citrus peel with a subtle sulfurous, juicy pulp nuance from trace nootkatone and mercaptans. Used for sparkling modern freshness; often boosted with methyl pamplemousse or a trace of grapefruit mercaptan. FCF grade: bergapten/furocoumarins removed for photo-safety; the scent profile is essentially the same, marginally less full in the deep facets.

The main odorant of natural civet: a macrocyclic ketone that is smooth, warm and musky-animalic without civet's fecal harshness. Key building block for clean synthetic civet bases and sensual musk accords.

Bedoukian's copy, carried by Perfumer's Apprentice, gives herbaceous, leathery, peppery, with notes of elemi oil and thyme and a touch of citrus. TGSC files the same CAS as a phenolic odour and adds spicy, styrene, eugenol and guaiacol-like with musty, coffee and nutty nuances, and one supplier there reads it as burnt wood and roast coffee. Perfumer's Apprentice reports tenacity over an hour on a blotter, very good substantivity on damp cloth, and recommends traces only. In a formula it is a naturaliser: a trace roughs up a herbal, fougere or citrus top so it stops smelling reconstituted, and it carries a dry leathery-peppery edge into elemi and thyme accords.

Steam-distilled sweet orange leaf: softer and sweeter than petitgrain bigarade, with a sabinene-peppery green lift in place of bigarade's dry woody-bitter edge. Use where bigarade reads too austere, or to round an orange-blossom top without pulling it green.

The house describes it as green, floral and slightly powdery, built around a tiny musky muguet with an innocent, half-shadowed character. It is a compounded lily-of-the-valley accord rather than a single molecule, so it drops a finished muguet heart into a formula without the perfumer assembling one from hydroxycitronellal-type and Lilial-type building blocks, and its powdery-musky tail lets it sit under other white florals instead of shouting over them.

dsm-firmenich lists Dorinia as floral, with rose, apple and violet as its olfactive descriptors, and calls it a well balanced association of ingredients, some of them captives, blended into a speciality. It was built with the house's Natural Ingredients Centre of Expertise as a technical solution for natural reconstitutions and belongs to the Grasse GI absolue collection. In a formula it drops in a finished rose heart, the fruity apple and powdery violet facets covering the parts of a rose natural that a reconstitution usually leaves flat.
Waxy, fresh green-rosy odor with a mushroom-fruity nuance. Adds a fresh natural facet to florals and greens.
Dry, woody-camphoraceous with a peppery, slightly earthy balsamic nuance, softer and more natural than camphor. Adds authentic dry-herb character to lavender, rosemary and incense accords.
Woody-orris violet, drier and more masculine than the alpha isomer, with a slightly leathery dryness. Useful in woody-floral bases, iris for masculine fougeres and to dry down violet accords.
Green, fruity and slightly vinous, suggesting unripe apple and grape stems. Adds juicy leafiness to fruity topnotes and modern green colognes.
Powdery, sweet indane nitro musk of the classical era with a warm, slightly animalic softness. PROHIBITED by IFRA; historical reference only.

Fraterworks 777206: a synthetic reconstruction of aged white ambergris, with salty, metallic, marine-sweet and warm animalic character. Supplier strength 5/10 and blend impact 6/10; 240 hours on a blotter is not a skin-wear claim. Sold without alcohol. The supplier describes substitution for a 3% natural ambergris tincture, not a 3% dilution of this product. Supplier IFRA 51 Category 4 maximum: 8.3333% of the finished product. The disclosed restricted constituent is p-cresol at 0.06%; this is not the complete proprietary composition.

Robertet describes it as gourmand, powerful, with a cocoa powder effect, and adds that it is one of the few cocoa extracts used in perfumery as it is. It is a decolorised cocoa natural on a triacetin carrier, so it delivers the dusty, barely sweet cocoa-powder impression without the dark colour or the heavy roasted body of cacao absolute. Reach for it when a gourmand needs bitter cocoa dust that will not stain the juice or drag the drydown down.

Fresh linalool-orange blossom anthranilate with herbal and gardenia facets over a quiet woody base. Very tenacious and cheap, which makes it the standard fixative for neroli, orange flower and petitgrain accords.
Sweet, fruity-balsamic and spicy-floral, suggesting cinnamon softened with pear and hyacinth facets. Useful to round spice accords and add a fruity-spicy sparkle to ambers and heavy florals.

Givaudan describes Jasmonyl as giving a lactonic jasmine effect with a mushroom-like note that blends well with lavender, and says it enhances the diffusion of a fragrance. The house supplies it as a two-isomer material, 3-pentyl-4-tetrahydropyranyl acetate together with 5-methyl-3-butyl-4-tetrahydropyranyl acetate at CAS 63270-14-4, and classes it floral / jasmine / lactonic with several hours of blotter tenacity. In a formula it is the creamy, slightly damp side of jasmine rather than the indolic side: it fattens a jasmine or muguet heart, pushes the whole accord outward, and its earthy mushroom edge is what makes it sit so naturally under lavender.
Fresh citrus-citronella nitrile, lemony-rosy and metallic-green, very stable in bleach and detergents. Used for persistent lemon-lime freshness in functional products and sporty fine fragrances.
Soft, dry, powdery woody-cedar with a subtle ambery sweetness; smoother and more refined than cedar oil. A tenacious fixative used widely in woody and fougere accords.

ScentScientists, who sell it at 10 percent in DPG, describe a fresh, balsamic, smoky natural aroma of styrax resin. Perfumer's Apprentice describe the product itself as a purified styrax specialty blend in IFF's Oliffac series, light in colour, far less viscous than raw styrax and much easier to work with; it carries no single CAS, being a mixture. In a formula it is the smoky-leathery balsam behind chypres, leathers and incense accords, contributing the cinnamic sweetness and phenolic smoke of styrax while pouring and dosing like an ordinary liquid instead of a tar.
Mild woody-floral, apple-lily nuance, good blender
Bright green-citrus freshness in the lemongrass direction with juicy apple-pear facets and herbaceous verbena nuances. Excels in lemongrass reconstructions and citrus colognes.

Noble, diffusive amber-woody ketal of great elegance, reminiscent of the finest ambergris tinctures with a dry cedarwood undertone. Long-lasting and radiant; lends expensive-smelling depth to woody and amber fragrances at low dosage.

Givaudan describes a floral tea-rose note with a fruity balsamic character and a hint of honey sweetness. It is 2-phenylethyl pivalate, and the house positions it as a modifier for the common rose alcohols and esters rather than as a rose in its own right. In practice it goes in beside phenylethyl alcohol and the rose esters to pull them toward dried tea petals and honey, taking the greenish sharpness off a rose accord and giving it a warmer, slightly balsamic sweetness. Used up to 3 percent, with good bloom in soap and strong performance in fabric conditioner, shampoo and all-purpose cleaner bases; substantivity is medium on damp substrate and slight on dry.

Rosy-green leafy freshness with minty rhodinol facets and a slightly fruity, earthy depth; the Réunion (bourbon) quality is the benchmark. A fougère pillar alongside lavender, and the green backbone of rose accords and masculine florals.

Mane calls it a magnificent marriage between the powdery elegance of orris and the sturdy woodiness of cedar, giving powdery floral softness over a dry, structured woody backbone with delicate violet nuances. It is made by co-distilling orris roots together with rectified cedarwood essential oil, one raw material acting as co-solvent for the other, so the two fuse into a single tailor-made identity with facets Mane states are impossible to obtain by conventionally blending the separate extracts. In a formula it enriches woody accords with depth and complexity and lends a luxurious, long-lasting character, sitting where an orris butter and a cedarwood would otherwise have to be balanced against each other by hand. It won Most Innovative Ingredient at WPC 2026.
Powerful aldehydic-citrus top note with intensely metallic, clean-laundry nuances. Boosts sparkle in colognes and fougeres; extremely strong, typically used at 1% dilution or below.

Fresh, waxy rose-petal alcohol with dewy, slightly aldehydic-citrus and iris facets; smells like the cool moisture on a rose petal. Excellent freshness booster for rose, muguet and clean-skin accords.

Givaudan's definitive modern muguet aldehyde: luminous watery lily-of-the-valley with clean petal freshness and huge diffusion, created as a safe successor to Lilial. A little goes far; anchors contemporary muguet and water-lily accords.

TGSC records it as floral, waxy, green, watery, muguet, orchid, cyclamen and creamy; Takasago prints floral, aldehydic, green and aquatic. It is the aldehydic half of Takasago's muguet pair: a luminous green-floral lily-of-the-valley with aldehydic lift over a creamy body, which harmonises with marine and citrus notes and, combined with Biocyclamol, extends a natural and linear muguet-ozonic radiance into the drydown. Dosed anywhere from 0.2% to 15%, with substantivity over 168 hours at full strength. Made from sugar-cane derived farnesene and fully bio-based.
Sweet fruity, estery and slightly sour with strawberry, pineapple, green, creamy, waxy, peach, berry, tutti-frutti, apple and banana facets. Best used in dilution.

Indian Arabian-jasmine absolute: greener and fresher than grandiflorum, with orange-blossom and jasmine-tea facets, banana-fruity nuances and a pronounced indolic, almost feral undertone. Superb in white-floral bouquets, tea accords and modern solifleurs.
Extremely powerful sulfurous, cabbage-and-corn odor; at extreme trace lends a fresh marine, tomato-leaf and blackcurrant lift. Ultra-trace use only.

Odorless emollient ester similar to IPM but slightly richer in skin feel, used as a carrier in oil perfumes, solid perfumes and body products. Good solvency for most aromatics; can be comedogenic in leave-on skin products.

Symrise's own datasheet types it Floral, Green, Reseda, Vegetable Green: a true-to-nature foliage green, the crushed leaf and stem side of reseda rather than the flower. In a formula it gives natural green aspects to violet and mimosa complexes and builds a convincing leaf-green accord without the harshness of a leaf alcohol. Symrise recommend 0.1 to 3 percent in the concentrate, and record an odour threshold of 0.02 micrograms per litre, so it carries a long way for a green.
Simple, fresh orange-peel terpene note, light and diffusive but very fleeting. Used as an inexpensive citrus filler and solvent-like lifter in top notes; prone to oxidation, hence IFRA-flagged.
Waxy, fresh floral-green odor with an orange-blossom nuance. A soft fatty-green diluent-strength material for naturalness.
Extremely dry woody-amber, powerful and slightly animalic; pure dryness as a material.
Green galbanum-like with fruity pineapple-apple facets and a slight floral lift. A stable, soap-friendly way to add galbanum character to functional and fine fragrance alike.

A dark, fruity black tea: plummy dried-fruit notes over an unsweetened cocoa undertone, soft tobacco-like smoke, toasted grain and a delicate floral facet; darker and fruitier than a plain black tea note. Supercritical CO2 extract of Keemun black tea leaves from Qimen county, Anhui (Firmenich), supplied diluted in ethanol.
Powerful jasmine-fruity cyclopentanone with celery-herbaceous and slightly rooty facets, drier than jasmatone. Adds jasmonic naturalness and diffusion to white florals and chypres.

A nature-identical reconstitution of oud oil. Suppliers describe it as woody, animalic, balsamic, earthy, spicy and leathery, with a good dose of the barnyard smell present in a lot of oud oils. It is a pale brown to brown viscous liquid, specific gravity around 1.0, miscible with alcohol, DPG, IPM and most carrier oils, with a published blotter substantivity of 240 hours. In a formula it is the affordable stand-in for oud oil: a heavy animalic base that anchors woody and amber accords and carries the funk that a cleaner oud base deliberately leaves out. Retailers point perfumers wanting a drier, cleaner, woodier profile to a plain oud wood base instead.

White Nelumbo lotus absolute: cleaner and greener than the pink, with a cool anisic-hay lift over a soft waxy floral body and a watery undertone. Less dense than pink lotus and less honeyed than blue; use it where a lotus note has to stay luminous rather than narcotic.

Bulgarian and Serbian white rose absolute: cool green rose with a clean, lightly fruity-honeyed body from its phenylethyl acetate, and none of the damascena's spice or jam. The white rose most catalogs skip; use it where a damascena would read too warm, and alongside violet leaf, orris and green notes.

An extremely powerful woody and ambery note with a slightly animal undertone, developing a dry woody direction toward patchouli. A house speciality base described as a well balanced association of ingredients, some of them captives, built by Firmenich perfumers with their natural ingredients centre of expertise as a technical route to natural reconstitutions. In a formula it is a drydown engine: it supplies dry woody-amber volume and a faint animalic warmth underneath, so it anchors a woody accord and lends a patchouli-like earthiness without the camphoraceous top of patchouli oil itself. Its power means it is easy to overdose into flatness.

IFF's branded heliotropin replacer, sold as a mixture rather than a single molecule. The Good Scents Company files it as floral and describes it as sweet balsam heliotrope cherry anisic, sweet and mealy with coumarin, coconut, anise and almond notes. Perfumer's Apprentice calls it a deep and mysterious exotic floral with sweet, balsamic and spicy undertones and nuances of almond and berries. It is built to give the soft powdery vanillic-blossom of heliotrope where piperonal is unwelcome, and it holds on a blotter well past two days, so it works as a fixed base under floral, gourmand and oriental accords rather than as a top-note effect.

Earthy patchouli base with woody depth and peppery accents. Fraterworks product 861088 is a compounded interpretation of Akigalawood, not the Givaudan material. Supplier-reported persistence exceeds 280 hours on a smelling strip; this is a lower bound, not a skin-wear estimate. Supplier IFRA 51 Category 4 maximum: 33.18% in the finished product. Exact declarations cover only part of the mixture; grouped allergens and remaining SDS intervals require review before a formula-level safety clearance.
Sweet herbaceous lactone with tobacco, coumarinic and caramelized facets. Distinct from beta-Angelica lactone CAS 591-11-7.
Sweet, bready, almond-caramel note with woody-brown, freshly-baked facets. Adds toasted, oven-warm realism to bread, coffee, nut and caramel accords in traces.
Oily fixed carrier oil with a bland, near-odorless character and slow skin absorption. One of the most popular bases for massage-oil blends, where it can make up to 80% of the total.
Woody-green vetiver-style note with dry grapefruit and earthy facets. Reinforces vetiver and adds transparency to woody bases.

Dense green-woody absolute: a cooked-banana fruitiness at the opening, then an intensely green, mossy-woody heart with iodine nuances, drying down smoky and iodine-like. It lacks the urinous note of the living shrub and is offered as an oakmoss/treemoss alternative in chypres. Absolute of Buxus sempervirens twigs (Mane).
Dry mahogany-style precious wood note, warm and slightly spicy. A woody specialty for elegant dark wood effects.
Creamy, buttery peach-cream lactone, more dairy and less fruity than gamma-decalactone. Gives fragrances a smooth creme-fraiche fruitiness; lovely in fig, gardenia and tuberose bases.

Mild solvent with a faint sweet, slightly rosy-almond odor, excellent for dissolving crystals and stubborn resins; also a common preservative component. A declarable allergen in the EU, so account for it in labeling.
Sweet tangerine-mandarin citrus note with soft floral nuance. Reinforces mandarin oils and adds natural juicy zest.
Green-tea-like, leafy floral oil from champaca foliage, herbaceous with soft floral undertones. Unusual natural bridge between green and white floral notes.
Unmistakable fresh mushroom and forest-floor earthiness with a surprisingly fresh herbaceous hay facet. Powerful naturaliser used at traces in gardenia, fig and earthy chypre accords.

Givaudan places it in the floral family with a floral / tuberose / lactonic note, and describes its characteristic effect as imparting a natural touch of white flower, such as tuberose and gardenia. What it does in a formula is give a white floral its creamy, slightly waxy skin instead of a flat indolic one, and the house notes it can be used effectively in combination with fruity lactones to provide lift. It is worked at 0.1% to 1%, lasts about a week on a blotter, and shows excellent stability in soap and shampoo. Supplier listings for the same material read it as a lactonic white floral with waxy, metallic tuberose character.

Built from the scent of Philodendron solimoesense, whose aerial roots hang from canopy trees in the rain forest of French Guyana: cut one and you immediately perceive a grapefruit scent against the background of a woody accord. The base has a refreshing effect in every application. Perfumers reach for it to modernize masculine accords, where its citrus-woody character reads as natural rather than compounded, and it bridges a bright citrus top into a woody body without a seam.

A Givaudan fragrance precursor for hair care, reported launched 23 June 2026. Trade coverage describes it as delivering a soft, fruity-floral scent with lasting freshness, built on green melon and orange blossom notes. Like the rest of the Scentaurus palette it is oxygen-activated, releasing its fragrant molecules gradually on exposure to light, humidity and oxygen for what Givaudan claims is a lasting sense of cleanliness, freshness and naturalness over several days. It is biodegradable per OECD guidelines and made on green chemistry principles. Weighed into a formula it is a slow-release freshness carrier, not an opening note; the melon and orange blossom read on the hair over days rather than off the blotter.

Large cardamom fire-dried over an open flame: warm seedy spice wrapped in wood smoke and a huge cineole-camphor blast, closing dry and resinous. Nothing like the green Elettaria cardamom, and the smoke makes it a direct route into smoky chai, leather and campfire-amber accords.
Roasted, nutty aroma with hazelnut, cocoa and coffee facets. Top filing follows the catalog's pyrazine convention, not measured evaporation or longevity.

Animalic and phenolic, with urinous, leather, tobacco and fermented facets and a warm musky-balsamic drydown. Fraterworks rates strength 6/10 and blend impact 7/10. More than 400 hours on a blotter is a lower bound, not an exact measurement or skin-wear claim. This record represents the supplied product: 40% Hyraceum extract in DPG, not neat extract. Its 1.28% Category 4 limit and disclosed constituents apply to that supplied product. Any bottle dilution is additional dilution of this product; do not apply the factory 40% a second time.

Hexane extract of soft wheat bran, washed of its waxes with alcohol into a viscous brown absolute. Cocoa and tea over dried fruit, with a balsamic honeyed warmth underneath. A material for nuancing a base rather than leading one, and awkward to dissolve: get it into solution and it stays there. Not the rice bran oil of the same family name, which is a fixed carrier oil and carries no smell.

Potent waxy orange-peel aldehyde with soapy, slightly floral-fatty body; a defining note of sweet orange oil and of Chanel-style aldehydic tops. Trace doses give sparkle, diffusion and citrus-waxy shimmer to florals.
Fresh pine-woody, herbal, earthy seashore complex showing fruity apple aspects at low concentration. Versatile fresh-woody modifier.

Paprika oleoresin, fractionally distilled until the colour and the burn are gone, then standardised to 5 percent in monopropylene glycol so it doses straight from the bottle. What survives of the pepper is its dried-fruit side: sun-dried tomato above all, over hay and the tannic edge of black tea, closing warm and faintly bready. No capsaicin heat, which is the whole point. It gives a spice accord body without adding another sharp top.
Sweet milk-chocolate accord with butter, caramel, butterscotch, vanilla and creamy pastry effects. A synthetic ready-made accord, not cocoa extract.
Praline accord with roasted hazelnut, toffee and chocolate character. Fraterworks supplied base 502630; a formulated blend, not a hazelnut extract or a synonym for Prunol.
Sparkling, slightly sweet grapefruit note with green and metallic-fresh facets, clean and non-sulfurous. Extends and modernizes grapefruit and generic citrus tops with excellent stability.

Warm maple, caramel and burnt-sugar cyclopentenolone with a nutty, faintly smoky depth, the ethyl homologue of cyclotene and a touch rounder. Interchangeable with cyclotene in maple, praline and tobacco accords where the licorice edge of the methyl grade is unwanted.

Osmanthus flowers co-distilled into a molecular distillation of cedarwood oil. The supplier describes a sophisticated leather scent with prominent oud-like character, combining delicate osmanthus florals with apricot fruitiness over a refined cedarwood backbone. It lasts more than 240 hours on a strip and the house advises using it boldly: one natural material that supplies a leathery-floral base where a formula would otherwise need an osmanthus absolute, a cedar and a leather accord, and it is where the oud-like impression comes from without any agarwood.
Soft coconut-milk lactone with buttery, slightly waxy-fruity facets, smooth and rounded. A blender for creamy fruit and dairy nuances in gourmands and tropical accords.

Sweet, warm balsamic resin from Myroxylon balsamum with cinnamic, vanilla and faint floral-hyacinth facets; drier and spicier than Peru balsam. Classic fixative for amber and floral-balsamic bases; IFRA-restricted, use compliant qualities and levels.

Givaudan describe it as a base built on a reconstitution of the concentrated essential oil, with a typical orange note and good stability, containing less than 2% limonene. Their odour index entry reads orange, aldehydic, fruity, powerful; suppliers list it as a top note and describe it as diffusive, juicy, aldehydic, fresh orange with peel. In a formula it replaces or extends orange oil where the natural would fade or discolour: it holds the zest far longer than the essential oil, and it is potent enough that perfumers report a 20% dilution reading roughly as strong as a standard orange oil neat.

Softer, sweeter and more carnation-like than eugenol, warm-spicy with powdery floral and slightly woody-vanillic depth. The heart of classic carnation accords; strongly IFRA-restricted, often replaced by Methyl Diantilis.

Sweet balsamic ester with a green, waxy edge and a soft fruity-tropical nuance underneath. Quiet and blending rather than characterful, with medium impact and mild fixative value. Used to give body and weight to ylang, jasmine and tuberose bases without pushing any note of its own forward.
Fresh grassy-green, oily aldehydic note with spicy nutmeg-cortex character and exceptional tenacity. Clean green lift for functional and fine fragrance.

Reflects the typical odour of a juice cocktail based on papaya, mango and maracuja, sweet and slightly syrupy, the poolside umbrella-drink effect. In a formula it gives lift and radiance to floral bouquets, brings a sophisticated natural freshness to citrus accords, and adds attractive effects to chypre and oriental concepts, so it works as a rounding and radiating agent as much as a fruit note in its own right.

Steam-distilled lemon peel: thinner, sharper and more terpenic than the expressed oil, with less of its juicy zest-cell richness. Distillation leaves the furocoumarins behind, so this is the lemon to reach for in leave-on skin products where the expressed oil's phototoxicity cap bites.

Sharp, pungent green-leaf aldehyde with bitter almond and apple-skin facets, the 'leaf aldehyde' counterpart to cis-3-hexenol. Powerful in traces for realistic crushed-leaf and fruit-skin effects; harsh if overdosed.

Balsamic ester with a pronounced earthy, mushroom and vegetative body and an almond-nutty sweetness underneath. A background note and mild fixative in rose and reseda types, where the musty-earthy undertone reads as naturalness alongside vetiver and oakmoss.

Kao describes it as a privet blossom note: tulip flower, deep green, oily, filed under the descriptor triad Green - Plastic - Floral and placed in the house's GREEN family. It is a green floral rather than a leafy or a grassy green, the smell of a hedge in flower, with a thick oily body under it and the faintly synthetic edge Kao itself names as plastic. In a formula it gives a floral heart a deep, wet green underlay that cis-3-hexenol-type materials cannot supply because they evaporate away; as a 1,3-dioxane it holds through the heart instead.
Grapefruit floral with rhubarb-rose nuances, fresh and long-lasting. Extends citrus grapefruit effects into floral hearts.

A green, natural tomato leaf note. Used as a top note ingredient it imparts powerful fresh-natural effects and gives green volume to a whole perfume, which is its real job in a formula: it opens up and enlarges a green accord rather than merely tinting it. It performs well in hair care and in soap, and offers excellent malodour coverage on that base. Part of the Leaf Givco family alongside Birch Leaf and Green Ivy, and not to be confused with the natural tomato leaf extract or with single molecules such as 2-isobutylthiazole.
Fresh green-floral acetal of rhubarb, grapefruit and chrysanthemum with cypress and gardenia nuances. Brings sparkling fresh-floral lift to muguet, gardenia and fruity-green accords.

The Good Scents Company records monomenthyl succinate as odorless at full strength, with an odour strength of none; what registers is a slight coolness on the strip and a lingering coolness with good mouthfeel on the palate. It is a sensate, not an odorant, and adds nothing to the pyramid. Its value in a formula is timing: the patent literature describes menthyl succinate being paired with menthyl lactate or with WS-3 precisely because their release rates differ, giving a fast cooling onset and a long-lasting cooling tail in the same product, so MMS is the slow, persistent partner rather than the immediate hit that menthol provides. This is the synthetic grade, which is how the material is made commercially.

Very natural leafy-rosy ester with a geranium bite and balsamic fruity undertones, closing on a dry tea note. More substantive than citronellyl acetate, which makes it the better choice for rose-leaf and geranium facets and for geranium oil reconstructions.

The supplier listing gives the odour as tobacco, powdery, spicy, gingerbread, floral, and describes a refined tobacco foundation enriched by elegant powdery facets, subtle floral tones and warm spicy accents. It is a French-made dark brown liquid and is classed as a base note and a fixative, so in a formula it is both the tobacco itself and the thing that holds the rest of the dry down down. The powdery and floral side is what separates it from a raw tobacco absolute: it reads as cured pipe tobacco in a tin rather than smoke, and the gingerbread nuance gives it a warm spiced sweetness that lets it sit under fougeres, chypres and leather accords without turning tarry.

Robertet describes it as floral, a sophisticated orris note, precious and powdery, with violet and watery facets. The house calls it reminiscent of the orris butter at a good price/quality ratio, so it is the material a formula reaches for when it wants the cosmetic-powder, violet-tinged rootiness of orris without paying orris butter prices. In a blend it works low and slow as a soft powdery cushion under florals, adding a faintly damp, precious quality rather than any brightness of its own. Sold for perfumery use only.
Sweet hawthorn-heliotrope note with coumarinic hay, tonka and faint fruity nuances; crystalline and diffusive. Reinforces mimosa, hawthorn and heliotrope themes and sweetens powdery amber bases.

Extremely diffusive green-herbal ether: a camphoraceous, cool burst recalling crushed rosemary and eucalyptus leaf that settles into a softer vegetal green with apple-blossom and transparent rose nuances. Short-lived; lifts herbal, aromatic and fougere tops and boosts apple or rosy top notes. 3,3,5-Trimethylcyclohexyl ethyl ether.

Sweet jasmine ester with an oily-fruity body, a faint rosy edge and tropical sweetness underneath. Softer and rounder than benzyl butyrate, so it fills out jasmine, ylang and gardenia hearts without adding sharpness.

Realistic fresh-cracked coconut: creamy, buttery and milky with waxy-nutty facets, a gentle toasted sweetness and a bright fruity lift at the top. Adds fleshy, creamy texture to white florals without reading overtly tropical. Mane low-temperature CO2 extract of coconut.

A powerful dry woody amber powerhouse from Symrise, delivering pencil-shaving cedar dryness and a diffusive ambery woodiness that structures drydowns from top to base. Firmenich sells the same alcohol as Norlimbanol; traces carry a formula, and overdose turns harsh and cardboard-dry.
Roasted cocoa, coffee and baked-potato earthiness with a nutty, musty-brown character. Trace additions bring roasted realism to chocolate, coffee and peanut accords.

Sweet dry-woody note with clove, powdery and smoky facets; at dilution it opens into phenolic guaiacol, smoke and a ham-like nuance over woody vanilla. The acetate of guaiacol, far less medicinal and tarry than the free phenol, so it doses phenolic-smoky character into leather, whisky and incense accords without the harsh edge.

Jammy, deep-green balsamic absolute from Abies balsamea with remarkable raspberry-jam, honeyed and coniferous-resinous facets. Adds a plush, sweet forest depth to amber, incense and chypre bases; a little goes far.

Natural bitter almond and stone-fruit kernel character, essentially pure natural benzaldehyde with a softer, rounder edge (free from prussic acid). Lends authentic marzipan and amaretto warmth to almond and cherry gourmands.

Robertet lists it as tobacco, jam, fruity, dried apricot, fig, again a natural put onto an MPG carrier. The mate leaf is still present but sits beneath a stewed dried-fruit sweetness, which is precisely why a formulator picks this grade over the plain mate. It bridges fruit and tobacco inside a single material, so it works where a separate apricot lactone plus a tobacco base would argue with each other.

Sweet, fresh berry ester with raspberry and strawberry facets over a green, tutti-frutti body and a soft rosy undertone. Pairs with neryl acetate to build the cis side of a rose alcohol blend, where it supplies the fruit the geranyl esters cannot.
Sharp, volatile boozy-rum note with fruity, ethereal and slightly smoky-woody facets. Gives an instant alcoholic-spirits lift to rum, whisky and boozy-vanilla gourmands; very fleeting.

Soft, waxy-rosy petal note with a fresh, slightly citronella-green edge; one of the two structural pillars of every rose accord. Blends seamlessly with geraniol and PEA, and its cleanness makes it ubiquitous in functional perfumery.
Creamy, peachy-coconut lactone that occurs naturally in jasmine, tuberose and gardenia; sweet, fruity and slightly buttery-tropical. A little gives white florals their fleshy, petal-cream carnality.
Powerful aldehydic-ozonic note with metallic marine freshness. A little gives sparkle and sea-air lift to fresh accords.

Soft green leaf with a melon-waxy sweetness and a milky edge carried by the lactate. The most tenacious of the leaf esters, so it holds a green signature into the heart long after hexenyl acetate has gone.
Soft, sweet citrus-floral ester with rosy, slightly raspberry-fruity facets, reminiscent of neroli and helichrysum. Rounds citrus tops and adds a natural bergamot-neroli smoothness to colognes.

Musk, animalic, leathery and sweet: an IFF Oliffac speciality built on a Galaxolide (HHCB) skeleton, roughly 55% in dipropylene glycol, deliberately tweaked away from the usual clean Galaxolide signature and toward the depth of natural deer musk. The wider profile runs musk, amber, woody, powdery, balsamic, creamy, old wood and leather. Neat it opens with a feral, almost phenolic leather punch reminiscent of wet hide, then settles into a honeyed, skin-warm sweetness. In a formula it is the animalic backbone under a musk accord, giving body and a naturalistic dirtiness that a plain polycyclic musk cannot. It solidifies when cold and will re-crystallise even at moderate temperatures, so warm it gently in a water bath before weighing.

The Good Scents Company records it as long lasting, strong, refreshing and decidedly jasmin-like with an intriguing wine bouquet, and a pear, floral, ozone, luminous, transparent note; under their jasmin descriptor it reads methyl dihydrojasmonate, fruity jasmin, waxy, herbal. In a formula it is a transparent jasmin body note, lighter and more luminous than an absolute, carrying a fruity pear and wine lift down into the heart and keeping a jasmin accord airy where lactones would thicken it. Substantivity is 92 hours neat, and it is used up to 10 percent of the concentrate.

Green sulfurous thiol bursting into passion fruit and box tree, brighter and more overtly tropical than 3-mercaptohexanol, with a savory caramelized-onion background and a catty drydown. The acetate ester of 3-MH: use at ppb to ppm for the lifted, exotic top of passion fruit, cassis and Sauvignon accords.
Rich, sweet fruity odor of apricot, banana and pear. Used to build juicy stone-fruit and tropical accords.

Sparkling, rosy-spicy and slightly fruity-juniper like, brighter and more lifted than black pepper with a modern cologne freshness. A signature contemporary top note pairing beautifully with rose, citrus and woods.
Soft creamy sandalwood alcohol with milky-woody smoothness. Blends beautifully with musks and ambers.
Soft herbaceous-sweet ester with bergamot-lavender, cardamom and faint pine-lilac facets. Inexpensive blender for lavender, cologne and pine themes and a smoothing agent in functional perfumery.
Green, herbal-spicy leaf oil with a warm, slightly citrus-terpenic and nutty-savory character distinct from culinary curry powder. Novel green-spicy note for exotic accords.

Spicy, sweet-phenolic and clove-like with fresh aromatic and slightly smoky facets; the classic bay rum note. Traditional in masculine grooming, bay rum and fougere accords; eugenol/chavicol content flags it.

Robertet gives the odour simply as floral, jasmine, and describes the product as a jasmine flowers-like reconstitution. It is a straight drop-in jasmine heart rather than a character base: where a formula needs the flower itself and not an absolute's animalic weight, this carries the note on its own. Robertet lists its flash point at 55 C, which is a flammability figure and not a ranking of volatility, so nothing here is inferred from it. Applicable for a perfumery use only.

A fresher, fruitier cut of Moroccan armoise, richer in thujones than the whole oil and correspondingly more diffusive. The parent LMR armoise oil reads as an aromatic and camphoraceous note with a thujone character and a minty cooling effect, its fruity and green facets fading to resinous pinewood undertones; the Heart concentrates the bright fresh-fruity end of that and leaves the heavier resinous tail behind. In a formula it is a lift material: a small dose opens a fougere or a chypre with a cool green herbal snap that carries further than the oil does, and it stays legible over aromatic lavender and clary accords instead of muddying them. Obtained by precision molecular distillation and fractionation. LMR Naturals, SIMPPAR 2026.

Woody-balsamic oil from Dipterocarpus oleoresin with a dry, slightly smoky ylang-woody nuance and prominent alpha-gurjunene. Workhorse extender for woody, balsamic and patchouli-type bases; also used in ylang and vetiver reconstructions.

IFF publishes it as a diffusive spicy, woody ambery note with great rounding and smoothing properties, and suppliers reselling it describe an extremely rich musk that is stronger and spicier than Cashmeran itself. In a formula it behaves less like a note and more like a finishing agent: it rounds off edges between woods, ambers and musks, adds diffusion and a plush warm body to a drydown, and holds a structure together at very low dose. IFF lists it as a mixture rather than a single molecule, so it carries no CAS of its own; it is sold diluted (one supplier at thirty percent in DPG) because it is potent enough that neat handling is impractical.

Soft blue oil carried by aliphatic esters rather than azulene: sweet fruity apple and wine over a gentle herbal-floral haze, rounder and less bitter-medicinal than German chamomile. Adds a fruity-herbal glow to lavender, tea and chamomile accords where the German oil would read too sharp.
Fresh orange blossom-neroli ether note, radiant and slightly green. Natural-smelling floralizer for neroli and cologne accords.

dsm-firmenich compounded base 109223 GEB, a balanced association of ingredients built by the house's perfumers with their natural ingredients specialists. The house describes a fruity note in the direction of kiwi, mango, peach and lactonic citrus, so it delivers a rounded tropical fruit accord that is creamy and juicy rather than sharp. It is used as the fruit centre of a formula, where a single fruity molecule would read one-dimensional, and it sits across the top and heart.

Warm, honeyed, waxy note with hay, tobacco, pollen and soft animalic facets true to a working beehive. Adds natural honey depth and vintage waxiness to honey, tobacco, mimosa and amber accords. IFF's LMR beeswax absolute carries no hazard classification and no IFRA standard of its own; its IFRA 51 certificate allows 40% of a fine fragrance (category 4), 10% of a deodorant and 2% of a lip product, and its allergen declaration lists fifteen declarable allergens, the largest sclareol at 0.16% and benzyl cinnamate at 0.10%, isoeugenol at 0.002%. Those figures are the constituents the checks here use.
Tocopheryl acetate. Almost odorless viscous emollient and antioxidant additive used at 0.5-1% to enrich blends, slow absorption and prolong massage bases.

Sweet herbaceous lavender with bergamot and slightly rosy-fruity facets, a natural minor component of fine lavender oils. Rounds and naturalizes lavender accords beyond what linalyl acetate alone achieves.

The house sheet gives it as the smell of a delicate bouquet of white flowers with fruity notes reminiscent of banana and pear, with nuances of solar flowers giving a sunny and radiant effect, and files it under FLORAL, WHITE FLOWER. Its job in a formula is spelled out plainly: it is used as a salicylate top note in place of hexyl or amyl salicylate, or as a versatile floral building block, and the sheet stresses that it is much more stable than the salicylates it stands in for, especially in home care, blending particularly well with all kinds of floral or fougere accords. That stability is the whole point of reaching for it. The sheet marks it as a top and heart note and it lasts two days on a smelling strip, which puts its real centre of gravity in the heart. Fine fragrance dosage runs from a few tenths of a percent up to a couple of percent, so it is a body material rather than a trace one, and it is a Firmenich signature molecule with no other existing supplier.

Woody-ambery agarwood reconstruction with olibanum, balsamic and patchouli nuances. Givaudan product 215/2, not natural agarwood oil.
